en: The Man Who Painted the Ground
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: A cod fisherman whose crewmates had a whip-round to send him to art school — and who ended up with **5,405 of his works** in the city's collection and a museum on the hill with his name on it.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: **Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval (1885–1972)** is one of the **central pioneers of modern Icelandic painting** — that is how the museums put it, and it is the honest framing. "Iceland's greatest painter" is an opinion, however widely held.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: He came to it the hard way, off a fishing boat, and trained in **Copenhagen**. What he did with it was the un-obvious thing: he **got down on the ground**. Icelandic landscape painting had been all mountains and distance; Kjarval knelt over the **moss, the lava and the cracks** and painted the three feet in front of his face.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: In among the rock he painted **faces and figures** — that is real, and it is where the elf stories come from. But be careful with it on the mic: the **fantasy forms appear in parts of his work**, not in every canvas, and **not every odd-shaped rock he painted is a documented hidden person.** The lava is the subject. The faces are the seasoning.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: **Kjarvalsstaðir**, on **Klambratún**, opened in **1973** — the formal opening was **24 March** — and was designed by **Hannes Kr. Davíðsson**. It is **one of the three buildings of Reykjavík Art Museum**, alongside **Hafnarhús** and **Ásmundarsafn**. It carries special responsibility for his work, but it is a general exhibition space too, not a one-man shrine.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: The numbers behind that responsibility are startling. The city's own 2019 operating report lists its registered Kjarval holdings as **5,405 works** — **195 paintings, 5,167 drawings and 43 other pieces** — out of **17,495** works in the whole museum collection. **He is very nearly a third of it.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: And the honours story is better than the version you usually hear. He did **not** simply refuse the **Order of the Falcon** out of modesty. An honour proposed in **1965** was **initially declined**, and what followed was a negotiated arrangement, with the insignia ending up associated with the **National Gallery**. A man who said no, then let them find a way round him.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: The Brewery That Outlived Prohibition
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: A brewery founded in **1913** — and **two years later Iceland banned the lot.** It is still here. It outlasted the ban by seventy-four years and then sold the country its Christmas drink.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: **Tómas Tómasson** founded **Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson** in **1913**, and the company's own history dates the first production and delivery to **17 April**. A newspaper from **March 1914** already names him as owner and notes he had worked at the **Sanitas** soft-drink factory — so he learned fizz before he learned beer.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: It is named after the saga poet and warrior **Egill Skallagrímsson**. The company links him to ale; **why Tómas actually picked him is not recorded anywhere I can stand behind**, so anyone who tells you it was because Egill was a famous drinker is guessing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: **Prohibition did not arrive in one go.** The law was passed on **30 July 1909**; the **import ban** bit on **1 January 1912**; the **general sales ban** on **1 January 1915**. **Wine came back in 1922**, **spirits in January 1935** after a referendum — and **beer stayed illegal until 1 March 1989.** Seventy-four years. A country that allowed you brandy but not lager.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: Here is the part everyone gets wrong: **"pilsner" was never alcohol-free.** Icelandic law set the line at **2.25% ABV** — at or below that, a drink was legally not *áfengi* at all. So the shelves held real, weak beer the whole time. Ölgerðin sold **malt drinks, soft drinks and 2.25% beer** for three generations.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: And there was one loophole with a uniform on. From **1940** Ölgerðin brewed **Polar Ale for the occupying forces**, whose bases sat outside the domestic rules. **Full-strength beer was being made in Reykjavík — Icelanders just were not allowed to buy it.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: **1 March 1989**, beer came back, and Icelanders called it **Bjórdagur** — Beer Day. Not an official holiday. Just a nation marking the end of the daftest rule it ever wrote.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: The other legacy is in every fridge at Christmas: **Egils Malt mixed with Appelsín**, the orange fizz. The argument about **which one you pour first** is genuinely national, and there is **no single correct ratio** — anyone insisting on equal parts is stating a preference, not a tradition.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: One modern footnote, because it changed six months ago: in **February 2026** shareholders renamed the listed parent company **Bera hf.** — the Nasdaq Iceland ticker went **OLGERD → BERA on 4 March 2026** — and the drinks business now trades as **Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson ehf.** The brewery is still at **Grjótháls**. Same beer, new letterhead.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: One small river feeds the city, waters it, lit it, and holds the argument about where its parliament began. Most capitals would settle for the water.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: We counted the salmon with a camera, bought the river outright, and got a king to pull the switch. For a stream you could throw a stone across, it has had a career.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: The Valley That Runs the City
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: Most capitals get a grey, sad little river. Reykjavík's hands you **dinner, drinking water, electricity — and an argument about where parliament started.** Show-off.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: Meet the **Elliðaá** — one of very few **capital-city rivers anywhere with a wild Atlantic salmon run.** And I can give you the real count, because they put a **camera counter** in it: in **2009** the whole run was **1,533 fish** — **1,242 through the counter and 291 caught below it** — and the report is explicit that these were **naturally produced salmon, because no smolts had been released the previous year.** In **2003** it was **1,067**. (If you have heard "two and a half thousand salmon", that number is real but it is the wrong animal: **2,500 is a batch of smolts**, not returning adults. I have said it wrong myself.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: The stock has been **monitored continuously since 1988**. It **crashed in 1997**, they moved fish and stocked fry where spawning had failed — and the line that matters is this one: **all stocking has since been stopped, because the run now renews itself.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: The city was so taken with the river it **bought it in 1906**, for hydro power. (Your city buys parks. We bought a river.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: **The tap water your hotel keeps bragging about starts here too.** **Vatnsveita Reykjavíkur was formally founded on 16 June 1909**; water was taken **straight out of the Elliðaár that summer**, and from **Gvendarbrunnar**, the springs by **Elliðavatn**, later the same year. Two different supplies, same valley — and the Gvendarbrunnar water is the one you are drinking.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: **The lights: Elliðaárstöð, switched on 27 June 1921** — and not metaphorically. **King Christian X and Queen Alexandrine were inside the station and started the first two machines themselves.** It opened as a **1,500-horsepower plant producing 1,000 kW**, and was expanded over the years to about **3,150 kW by 1933.** I will not tell you it was Iceland's second power station or its biggest, because **neither of those rankings survives checking** — plenty of small plants were already running by 1921.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: **Iceland's first was humbler.** In **1904** the Hafnarfjörður carpenter **Jóhannes Reykdal**, with **Halldór Guðmundsson**, wired a **9 kW** generator to his workshop stream and lit **sixteen houses and four street lamps.** Officially the country's first power station. Realistically, a shed with big ideas.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: Upstream, on a low spit in **Elliðavatn** called **Þingnes**, sits a cluster of settlement-age ruins the state registers as *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður* — the ancient Kjalarnes assembly place. **Whether it actually is is a genuinely open question and always has been.** Six seasons of excavation never settled it; **Adolf Friðriksson's position is that the archaeology does not establish a þing-site at all.** **Ari fróði** put that assembly on **Kjalarnes**; the ruins are here, **fourteen kilometres away**, and nobody has ever closed the gap. And the old ground now lies **partly underwater** since the river was dammed. Very Icelandic: invent democracy, mislay it, then flood it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: **The heat, too — and this surprises people.** Reykjavík's hot water did not start with a volcano out in the lava. It started **inside the city**: **low-temperature fields at Laugarnes and here in Elliðaárdalur**, plus **Mosfellsbær** out of town. Those wells still work, and neighbourhoods get deliberately swapped between sources **so the reservoir under the city can rest.** Yes — the ground gets a lie-down.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: A Layer Cake of Climate
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: That is not a mountain. It is **at least two dead volcanoes wearing one name** — and the honest position is that **nobody can tell you exactly how old it is or exactly how tall the top is.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: **It is not one mountain, and it is certainly not one volcano.** The rock records **more than one extinct central volcano**: an older **Kjalarnes** centre in the west — which some publications call **Viðeyjareldstöðin**, and whether those are one volcano or two is still argued over — and the younger **Stardalur** central volcano in the east, with its own caldera. Volcanism migrated **eastward** across the whole pile. "Esja" is the name of the eroded mountain mass you are looking at. It is not the name of a volcano.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: **The stripes are climate, and you can read them from your seat.** **Dark basalt** flowed in warm, ice-free spells and cooled in peace. **Pale móberg** is lava that picked a fight with a glacier and lost — erupted under ice, shattered, welded into rubble. **Dark means warm. Pale means frozen.** That is the whole code, and it is the one part of this mountain nobody disputes.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: **How many ice ages are stacked in there? Here is the honest answer.** The peer-reviewed survey — **Leó Kristjánsson, Ingvar Birgir Friðleifsson and Norman D. Watkins** — logged a **2,100-metre composite section across Akrafjall, Eyrarfjall and Esja** and read **at least 11, possibly 16 glaciations** in it, plus **at least 13** across western and south-west Iceland between **3.1 and 1.8 million years ago**. But **that count is for the composite, not for Esja on its own** — several of the lower horizons sit in Akrafjall and Eyrarfjall before the section even reaches this mountain. So you are looking at a stack of ice ages. The number everybody quotes belongs to a bigger profile than the thing out the window.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: **How old? Also genuinely disputed.** That composite section is dated **4.2 to 1.8 million years**. Two University of Iceland theses put Esja's oldest rock at **2.8 million years** and the youngest Stardalur rhyolite at **1.8** — but both trace back through the same 1985 account, so that is **one source wearing two hats**. And the actual **potassium–argon measurements** on the upper rhyolite come out at **1.89 ± 0.08**, **1.78 ± 0.04** and **1.85 ± 0.18 million years.** "Exactly 1.8" is a rounded interpretation, not a reading off a machine.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: **The heights are not settled either**, which for the most-looked-at object in Reykjavík is quietly hilarious. **Hábunga** is the name usually given to the true summit at **914 m** — not confirmed against any official survey record I would stand behind. **Þverfellshorn**, the one everybody actually climbs, is usually quoted at **780 m**; the nearest real published measurement is a **weather station at 783 m** *near* Þverfell, which is a different object on a different spot. And the boulder called **Steinn** is a genuinely documented route landmark — a **kennileiti** — but it has **no registered elevation anywhere.** Touch the rock and you have climbed Esja. Nobody checks. Nobody could.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: **Which is exactly how the city uses it anyway.** Reykjavíkers do not open the weather app. They look out of the window and see whether Esja is still there.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: The Parliament Before the Parliament

en: Iceland's world-famous parliament at Þingvellir? Not even the first. There was a **Kjalarnesþing** before it, set up by the founder's son. Nepotism: also a Viking value.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: **Ari fróði** wrote the only near-contemporary line about it, around **1122–33**, and it is worth having in full: *"Alþingi var sett at ráði Úlfljóts ok allra landsmanna þar es nú es, **en áðr var þing á Kjalarnesi**, þat es **Þorsteinn Ingólfssonr** landnámsmanns … hafði þar ok höfðingjar þeir es at því hurfu."* Before the Alþingi, a þing on Kjalarnes, held by the first settler's son and the chieftains who joined him.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: Notice what Ari does **not** say. He gives no meeting place, describes no structures, does not call it a vorþing, and never says it was Iceland's first. **Jakob Benediktsson** flagged the open question: was it a district assembly, or an embryo of the national one? Even "the parliament before the parliament" is an interpretation.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: **And nothing has ever been found on Kjalarnes.** The candidate everyone points at is **Leiðvöllur**, a gravel spit out past **Mógilsá** on the north side of Kollafjörður. **Sigurður Vigfússon** searched it properly — the spit, the slope above it, both sides of the channel — and published in the **1880–81 Árbók**. He found **one very indistinct small ruin**. His answer was to suppose the sea had eaten the site, which is a hypothesis, not a find.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: The ruins are **13.8 km south**, at **Þingnes** on **Elliðavatn** — and that is where **Jónas Hallgrímsson** actually dug, on **21 June 1841**, with four hired labourers. He counted **about twenty ruins** plus a stone circle, opened the biggest, and reasoned that a þing-site this size in this district could hardly be anything but the Kjalarnesþing. Morphology, density and the name **Þingnes**. No inscription, no dated find.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: The National Museum went back for **six seasons, 1981 to 1986**, under **Guðmundur Ólafsson**. The 1984 instrument survey recorded **16–17 surface ruins and at least 18 structures** — and they are **not all booths**: one looks like a permanently occupied house, one held **slag** and reads as a smithy, and some unexcavated ones may be later sheep houses or barns.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: The famous **"judgement ring"** is two circles, not one: an outer ring built **purely of stone**, about **18–20 m overall and 14–15 m inside**, with a smaller **turf** circle nested in it and paving from a different phase inside that. **No entrance was ever found.** Guðmundur allowed it might be a **lögrétta** — and also weighed a livestock pen, which the central position and missing doorway argue against. The archaeology calls them *circular structures* and leaves the function open. **"Dómhringur" is an antiquarian label, not a result.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: **There is no radiocarbon date from Þingnes at all** — the 2004 report says plainly that its charcoal was never submitted. What the ground gives is tephra: the **Landnám ash (c. 871)** sits *inside the turf* of several walls, so those walls were cut and built after it. At one structure the activity layer lay **3.5 cm** above that ash, and at an assumed **1 mm a year** that works out at the **early 900s** — the report calls that an estimate, and it is. Activity runs from about **900 into the 1200s**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: So: **plausible, unproven, and the experts have never agreed.** **Kålund** accepted it looked like a þing-site but said it was unresolved whether Kjalarnesþing ever met there. **Brynjúlfur Jónsson** thought it might be a single chieftaincy's assembly instead. **Guðmundur Ólafsson** called Kjalarnesþing the obvious candidate and stated outright that it could not be asserted as certain. **Adolf Friðriksson** went further: the archaeology does not independently establish a þing-site at all.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: The state, meanwhile, wrote it down as fact and never took it back. The register reads *"Mannvirkjaleifar á **hinum forna Kjalarnessþingstað** í Þingnesi"* — **signed 25 October 1930, registered 16 November 1938** (so if the sign at the lake says 1938, it is not contradicting you — that is the second date). **Inherited legal wording, not archaeological proof.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: **Footnote from the same peninsula, and it is a good one.** Landnámabók has **Örlygur Hrappsson** building a church at **Esjuberg** in the settlement period — by tradition Iceland's earliest. In **1981** the National Museum opened the mound locals call **Kirkjurúst Örlygs**, the ruin of Örlygur's church. It turned out to be an outbuilding from the **16th or 17th century**. A debris slide off the gully above has since buried the ground around it, so Guðmundur concluded further digging there would be pointless. The church may well be under the landslide. It has simply never been found.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: The laws, at least, are solid. The chieftains sent one man — **Úlfljótr** — to **Norway for three winters** to learn the **Gulating law** and adapt it. Nothing was written down, so he **carried the whole code home in his head**, and it came back with one radical edit the Norwegians never made: a parliament with **no king**. Stole the software, deleted the boss.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: And the line everyone hangs on him — **"með lögum skal land byggja"** — **he almost certainly never said.** Its first appearance in Icelandic writing is **Njáls saga, chapter 70**; it enters Icelandic *law* only with **Járnsíða**, the Norwegian king's code of **1271–74**, and it is **not in Grágás** at all. The phrasing comes from Norway's **Frostaþingslög**. Roughly **three and a half centuries** too young to be his.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: There is a second history under the music. After the British landed on **10 May 1940** the Americans took over in **July 1941**, and the US Army's own medical history puts **80% of the entire American force in Iceland** in a coastal strip **centred on Álafoss** — this town. In **April 1942** the **167th Station Hospital** moved into fresh **Nissen huts at Álafoss**, and they plumbed the **hot springs** in to heat the wards. A field hospital, warmed by the ground.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🎵 Mosfellsbær

en: It is still in the soil. Minjastofnun's **2022 survey at Lágafell** records a circular **gun-pit, 3.5 by 3.1 metres**, and an intact **34-metre trench** — both still there. **Lágafell Camp** itself, a depot and vehicle workshop on land requisitioned from **Thor Jensen**, has vanished completely under later housing. The camp went. The hole somebody dug to shoot from did not.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🎵 Mosfellsbær

en: Up the coast at **Hvalfjörður** the Royal Navy ran **HMS Baldur** at **Hvítanes** from 1940 to the end of the war, and the Americans built a fuel depot of **44 oil tanks**. **Convoy PQ17 sailed out of that fjord on 27 June 1942** — **35 merchant ships** bound for **Arkhangelsk**. **Eleven arrived.** And a myth worth killing: **HMS Hood did not sail from Hvalfjörður** on her last voyage — she was on her way *to* it when she was turned west for the Bismarck.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🎵 Mosfellsbær

en: **The silver (from Egil's saga):** in old age the warrior-poet **Egill Skallagrímsson** — sitting on two chests of silver gifted by **King Æthelstan of England** (the same Egill the brewery back in town is named after) — slipped off during the Alþingi with the silver, a horse and two slaves. The horse came back. Egill came back. The slaves and the silver didn't — he killed them to keep the spot secret. A thousand years of treasure hunters later: score **zero**. (Saga, not survey — treat it as legend.)

en: The typist was **Auður Sveinsdóttir**, born at **Eyrarbakki on 30 July 1918**, and she didn't just type it — she ran the build. She married **Halldór Laxness** that **Christmas Eve, 1945**. The architect was **Ágúst Pálsson**; the house was home from **1945** until Halldór died on **8 February 1998**. Auður outlived him by fourteen years, dying **29 October 2012**, aged **94**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: **1955:** Halldór takes Iceland's **only Nobel Prize in Literature** — *"for his vivid epic power which has renewed the great narrative art of Iceland."* Auður marked it the way a textile artist would: she made **Maríuklæðið**, "Mary's Cloth", to commemorate it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: **Kjarval's altarpieces, chapter one:** in **1914** the people of **Borgarfjörður eystri** commissioned him to paint one for their church at **Bakkagerði**, and the women of the district kept him fed while he worked on it. It is still there. And the famous part — that the rock Christ preaches from is **Álfaborg, the elf city**, with **Dyrfjöll** behind — is the reading absolutely everybody gives it, **including me**, but **no church, museum or art-historical source documents Kjarval ever saying so**, and nobody has produced a record of a bishop refusing to bless it. It is a wonderful story. I am telling you it is a story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: **Chapter two, and this one is documented — by the museum that owns it.** Kjarval painted an altarpiece for **Rípurkirkja** in Skagafjörður. In **1925**, **after the church had already been consecrated**, the clergy turned the painting down, and their objection is on record: *"Þetta er söguleg fölsun. Hér sýnir málarinn Krist sem ungling, en Jóhannes skírara sem öldung"* — this is a historical falsification; the painter shows **Christ as a youth and John the Baptist as an old man.** Not blasphemy. **Bad chronology.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: The picture then wandered. It ended up with a farmer called **Ólafur**, and when he died **his widow wrote to Halldór and offered it to him.** He took it. It hangs in the **entrance hall** of this house — so the first thing you see on the way in is a painting a parish sent back.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: **And there is a coda.** Kjarval came here later to sign it, and while he had the brush out he wanted to **add a beard to John the Baptist.** Halldór stopped him. **You can still see the faint marks he got in before he was stopped.** The painter, the brewer's Viking and the novelist — the morning's three pocket names — all tie off in this one valley.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: The **Icelandic state bought the house and its art in 2002**, a hundred years to the year since Halldór was born, and opened it to the public on **4 September 2004**. His **typewriter is still on the desk**.

en: **Vínland — the one hard proof, and it is now dated to the year.** The Norse site at **L'Anse aux Meadows**, Newfoundland — **found by Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad in 1960**, the Norse remains confirmed by excavation **from 1962**, **UNESCO-listed 1978** — is the **only confirmed Norse archaeological site in North America.** In **2021** a *Nature* study found the **993 cosmic-ray radiocarbon spike** in three wood samples and counted the rings out to the bark: **the trees were felled in 1021.** That is **471 years before Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492** — and be precise about what it dates: **1021 is when they cut wood there**, not when they arrived or how long they stayed.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🚢 The Norse Expansion (793–1066 CE)

en: Legacy: English law and language, the sagas, **the Alþingi — founded around 930 and one of the world's oldest parliamentary institutions** (say it that way: the year is a reconstruction, and it was **abolished in 1800 and restored in 1845**) — plus the birth of **Normandy** and **Kievan Rus'**.

en: By tradition, in **874 CE** Iceland was all but empty. By **930**, it was full. Settled, mapped and **booted up with a national parliament** — in a single human lifetime.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏘️ Landnám

en: The **Landnám** ("Land-Taking") is the **~60-year window** when 9,000-plus Norse, Celtic and other settlers grabbed every habitable bay and valley on the island. (**874 is the traditional date**; Ari the Wise points nearer **870**, and a nationwide ash layer — the **871 ± 2 tephra** — timestamps the whole business to the second.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏘️ Landnám

en: The textbook source is **Landnámabók** (*The Book of Settlements*) — **400 settlers** named, their farms, feuds and home-towns mapped in detail no other Viking-age country can match.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏘️ Landnám

en: The trick: Iceland had **no locals to fight** — just a handful of Irish monks (the **Papar**) who legged it the moment longships appeared.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏘️ Landnám

en: By **930** the population (and the feuds) were big enough that the chieftains met at **Þingvellir** to launch the **Alþingi**, the world's oldest parliament still in use.

en: You are in the **gap between two continents** — and no, they do not meet here. They are tearing **apart**, at the speed your fingernails grow, and this valley is the hole they have left behind.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: Forget the postcard version where you "touch two continents at once." **Þingvellir** sits on the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, and what you are standing in is a **seven-kilometre-wide graben** — a strip of valley floor **sinking between two fault walls** as the plates pull apart about **2 cm a year**. The plates never touch here. The valley **is** the gap.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: The cracks have names. **Almannagjá**, the big one you are walking through, is the **torn edge on the North American side**; its twin **Heiðargjá** marks the far side of the rift. The floor between them belongs to **neither continent** — it is the seam, still ripping.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: The plain is **Þingvallahraun**, a **9,000-year-old** shield lava that spread down from **Skjaldbreiður**. Since then the floor has sunk **over 40 m** and the rift has pulled open by about **70 m**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: It does not creep smoothly — it locks, strains, then lets go. The last big pulse came in **spring 1789**, dropping the valley floor about **2.5 m in roughly ten days** and flooding the paths around the assembly ground.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: Since **930** the assembly ground itself has dropped some **3–4 m.** The parliament you are about to stand in met noticeably higher up than the ground you are on.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: For two weeks every summer the country **shut down** and came here: laws made, marriages arranged, murderers tried, beer drunk.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: The **Lögsögumaður** (Law-Speaker), elected for a **three-year term**, had to recite **a third of the entire legal code from memory each year** — three years to deliver the lot. Drop one clause and you could change a verdict.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: And there was **no king** — roughly **36 goðar** (chieftain-priests) ran the whole thing by consensus. One law, one people, zero crowns.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: They chose this ground carefully: reachable from north, south and west inside about **seventeen days' travel**, a natural stage of cliffs and level floor, and **common land confiscated after its owner was outlawed for murder.** Practical, dramatic and pointedly neutral.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: It met here every summer until **1798**, sat two more summers in Reykjavík, and was then **abolished outright by royal decree on 6 June 1800.** Re-established on **8 March 1843**, it sat again on **1 July 1845** — in Reykjavík, in a school building. So not a thousand unbroken years. A thousand years with a **43-year hole** that Denmark put there.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: ⚖️ Kristnitaka
ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Standing at Lögberg. This is the exact ground where it was decided.
ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Most national religions are imposed by kings or won by armies. Iceland's was decided **on this rock, by a man having a lie-down.**
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Calmly, collectively, and after a really good night's sleep. That is how Iceland became Christian — standing where you are standing. Most countries were not given the option.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Weather pivot: "Þorgeir lay under a fur cloak for a day and a night. In this, you can see why."
ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: The Day Iceland Changed Religion, Lying Down
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Around **the year 1000**, Iceland changed its national religion **without a single sword being drawn** — right here. No army. No martyrs. Just one pagan chieftain, one cloak, and a really long nap.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: By **999** the country was split — Christian districts against pagan strongholds — and Norway's King **Ólafur Tryggvason** was squeezing hard: he welcomed Christian traders into his ports, barred the pagans, and **held Icelandic hostages** as leverage. Convert, or lose the trade route you cannot live without.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Persuasion had gone badly. One Saxon priest, **Þangbrandur**, allegedly **fought duels and killed poets** who mocked his sermons. Not a charm offensive.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: By **AD 1000** (the sources wobble between 999 and 1000) the **Alþingi** met on this spot facing two religions, two law codes and one looming civil war — so both sides handed the verdict to one man: **Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði**, the *pagan* Law-Speaker.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: He lay down under his cloak **a full day and a night**, then stood up on this rock and ruled: **one law, one people, one faith — Christianity** — so the young commonwealth would not split in two. Private sacrifice, horse-meat and infant exposure were quietly tolerated at first, then dropped. Food is food.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: The white church and the five-gabled farmhouse on your right, at the bottom of the wall.
ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: A thousand-year-old church, a Prime Minister's summer house, and a national shrine containing two poets — one of whom may not be the right man.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: They built this to hold the greatest Icelanders who ever lived. Two people went in. Then everyone thought about it a bit more and decided, actually, we'd rather be buried at home.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: Weather pivot: "The white church against a grey sky is the photograph everybody takes anyway."
ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: A Westminster Abbey With Two Occupants
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: There has been a church on this spot since **1017**. Beside it is a **national burial ground built to hold Iceland's greatest artists** — and in eighty-five years it has managed to bury exactly **two people**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: The church first went up around **1017**, the present building dates from **1859**, and the bell tower was added in **1907** — the date is on the weather vane. It has no resident priest; the one who serves it **comes out from Skálholt**, which we pass later today.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: The five-gabled farmhouse beside it is **Þingvallabær**, built in **1930** for the Alþingi millennium festival by **Guðjón Samúelsson**, the state architect. He turned its face deliberately toward **Almannagjá** — the older turf farmhouse it replaced had looked out at the lake. It began with **three gables**; two more were added after a **1970 fire** destroyed the king's house next door. Since **1974** it has been the **Prime Minister's summer residence.** One gable belongs to the church.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: Behind the church is **Skáldareitur**, the poets' plot — and it exists because of an argument over a corpse. When **Einar Benediktsson** died in **January 1940**, his ex-wife and his companion could not agree who had the right to bury him. **Jónas Jónsson frá Hriflu** saw the opening and proposed a national honour ground here, modelled on **Westminster Abbey**. Einar went into it on **27 January 1940**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: The second and last arrival was **Jónas Hallgrímsson**, Iceland's national poet, who had died in Copenhagen on **26 May 1845** of blood poisoning after breaking his leg on a staircase. His bones came home and were buried here on **16 November 1946** — over the objection of the man who dug them up, who wanted him in **Öxnadalur** where he was born. The Prime Minister, **Ólafur Thors**, overruled him. The government's position was that **Jónas's bones were state property.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: And nobody is sure they are his. Two other people had been buried on top of him in **1875** and **1900**, and both had to be lifted out first. The doubt has never gone away — there are still calls to open the grave and test what is in it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: Two graves. That is the whole national pantheon. **Halldór Laxness**, whose house we passed this morning, is not here. **Kjarval**, who opened this tour, is not here either. Iceland built itself a Westminster Abbey and then quietly stopped using it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: The Waterfall, the Drowning Pool and the Fake Wishing Well
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: A waterfall that was **moved here on purpose**, a pool where **at least eighteen women were drowned**, and a wishing well invented by **a sign put up in the 1930s.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: The **Öxará** comes over the wall at **Öxarárfoss** and runs down through the assembly ground. It is the main open river feeding the whole valley — and it is doing a job it was very probably given, diverted to bring water to the assembly.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: Below the falls the river widens into a still green pool: **Drekkingarhylur**, the drowning pool. After the Reformation Iceland adopted a severe moral code, **Stóridómur**, in **1564**, and Þingvellir doubled as an execution ground — men **beheaded, hanged or burned**; women convicted of **adultery, incest, perjury or infanticide** were **drowned here**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: Court records point to **at least eighteen women killed at this pool between about 1618 and 1749.** A memorial plaque now names them. Two weeks a year this place made the law. It also carried out the sentence.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: And then there is **Peningagjá** — the crack full of coins by the bridge, properly the southern end of **Nikulásargjá**. The coins have nothing to do with the sagas. The **bridge went up in 1907** for the visit of the Danish king **Frederick VIII**, who is said to have thrown the first one in.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: The wish came later, and from a signpost. In the **1930s** somebody put up a board reading **"to the wishing well"** — and that is the entire origin of the tradition. The national park's own record is blunt about it: **no older Icelandic folk tale or story about wishing here exists.** An ancient custom, ninety years old, invented by signage.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: Two continents pulling apart, the cleanest drinking water on the planet running through the gap, and a fish quietly turning into four other fish while nobody watches.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: Iceland's answer to a tectonic disaster: turn it into a reservoir, then drink it.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: Weather pivot: "If the far shore has gone, that is the rift you cannot see across — which is rather the point."
ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: The Cleanest Water on Earth, and Four Fish That Are One Fish
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: Meltwater that left a glacier **thirty to a hundred years ago**, filtered through lava the whole way — **drinkable from your cupped hand**, with **120 m** of underwater visibility. And one fish in it that has quietly become four.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: **Þingvallavatn** is Iceland's largest natural lake: about **84 km²**, up to **114 m deep**, averaging **34 m**, sitting at roughly **100.5 m above sea level** — and its bed lies **below sea level** because of the rifting.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: About **nine-tenths of everything entering it arrives from below**, seeping up through porous lava at **3–4°C**. Only about a tenth comes in as visible surface water, most of that the **Öxará**. The catchment runs to some **1,300 km²**, of which the lake is only about **six per cent** — the rest is plumbing you cannot see.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: The water begins as snow on **Langjökull** and spends **thirty to a hundred years** underground before it surfaces. Clear pools like **Silfra** are that meltwater arriving. The water in front of you fell before some of you were born.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: In that lake, one Arctic charr arrived after the ice left and split into **four separate forms in about 10,000 years.** **Kuðungableikja**, the snail charr. **Dvergbleikja**, the dwarf. **Murta**, the small open-water one. **Sílableikja**, the fish-eater. Two feed on the bottom, two feed in open water — and they are **all one species**, *Salvelinus alpinus*. They can interbreed and produce fertile young. They largely decline to.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: **Three of the four are genetically distinct.** The fourth, sílableikja, comes out muddled — some read as murta, others as crosses. Vísindavefurinn's assessment is that this may be **sympatric speciation**, one population dividing with no physical barrier between the halves, and that another **10,000 years** could produce genuinely separate species. Evolution has not finished tidying up.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: That island out in the lake is **Sandey**, a **tuff cone** built by **Hengill** about **1,900 years ago** — the same eruption that laid down **Nesjahraun** at the north end. An eruption happened in the middle of a lake and built itself an island out of it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🌋 Hekla

en: Last erupted **February 2000** — and Hekla is so eerily quiet beforehand that seismographs picked up its run-up only about **80 minutes** before it blew.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🌋 Hekla

en: She is a great deal older than her CV suggests. The story of the Hekla we would recognise today begins **just over 7,000 years ago** — she was already in business long before anyone was here to take notes. **1104** was her **first eruption after the settlement of Iceland** — and it is still **her own largest explosive eruption in historical time.** (The bigger explosive eruption in Iceland's historical record belongs to a rival: **Öræfajökull in 1362.**) She had been quiet for roughly **three centuries** beforehand, which means nobody then alive had the faintest idea what she was capable of.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🌋 Hekla

en: The ash of 1104 went north, and the farming districts of **Þjórsárdalur** and **Hrunamannahreppur** were **abandoned** because of it. Iceland got a thousand years of European publicity out of that eruption and **wrote none of it** — the people actually living underneath were otherwise engaged, emptying two districts.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🌋 Hekla

en: The Judas story has a date and a document. **Within ten to twenty years of 1104** an **English poem** was already asserting that **Judas** — the arch-traitor himself — was imprisoned inside Hekla, and European clergy positively welcomed eruption reports, because to their minds an eruption **proved that Hell existed.** The image that fixed it was a woodcut in the history of the Northern Peoples by the Swedish churchman **Olaus Magnus (1490–1557)**, published in **Venice in 1555**, showing Hekla with a set of tunnels running down out of the mountain. **Vesuvius and Etna never acquired the same reputation** — and Vísindavefur offers the driest explanation available. They were **too close to civilisation.** A volcano safely off the edge of Europe made a far more convincing front door.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🌋 Hekla

en: Her longest eruption began on **5 April 1766** and continued with breaks until **May 1768** — **just over two years**, including a **six-month pause** in the middle that must have felt to everyone like the end of it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🌋 Hekla

en: Warm Water, Cold Politics
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

en: What happens when you put the leaders of an entire country into the **same hot water** to settle an argument? Iceland has been finding out for a thousand years — and the answer, twice, was **not what anybody promised.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

en: **Laugarvatn** — "Pool Lake" — **280 people at 1 January 2026.** Hot springs feed the lake, and along parts of the shore the water genuinely runs bath-warm in mid-winter. **I am not going to give you a temperature for the lake**, because there is no single honest number: different outlets run at different heats. What *is* measured is the spring above **Vígðalaug**, which runs **up to about 90°C and often between 70 and 80** — and **Þorvaldur Thoroddsen measured 54°C** in the built pool there back in **1889.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

en: **Its moment came around the year 1000.** **Kristni saga** — not Íslendingabók, the two get mixed up constantly — says that once Christianity had been voted through at Þingvellir, **the northerners and the southerners were baptised at Reykjalaug in Laugardalur**, and gives the reason with beautiful bluntness: **they did not want to go into cold water.** A whole country changes religion, and the sticking point is the temperature.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

en: **Now the part every guide gets wrong, including the version I used to tell.** The pool you can walk to today is called **Vígðalaug**, the Consecrated Pool — but **Kristni saga never renames anything.** It says Reykjalaug and stops. **Kålund** described the pool in **1873** without identifying it as the baptism site at all; **Thoroddsen** in **1889** wrote only that Reykjalaug was *probably* at Laugarvatn and that **certainty was lacking**; and the identification of *this* pool with *that* text appears **not to have been made until the twentieth century.** A **1999 excavation found no tephra and nothing datable** — archaeologically, it **cannot** be dated to the year 1000.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

en: So: a real pool, a real text, a tradition joining them that is about a hundred years old. **That is still a good story. It is just not the same story as a fact.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

en: **Next door is Apavatn — "Marsh Lake" — and this is where the cold politics happened.** In the **spring of 1238**, **Sturla Sighvatsson** did not ambush **Gizur Þorvaldsson** out of nowhere: he **summoned him**, and Gizur came with **forty selected men.** Sturla said he meant no betrayal, and then **had the lot of them seized and disarmed by force.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

en: **A book was brought out** — the saga says *bók*, and **it does not say Bible** — and Gizur swore on it: **to sail abroad, and to keep faith with Sturla.** Note what is *not* in the oath: **he never swore to give up power.** That was handled separately, when **Hjalti Magnússon** took over his **goðorð**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

en: **Gizur broke it anyway.** What happened five months later is the next block, and it is the worst afternoon in Icelandic history.

en: **Brúará** ("Bridge-River") is a clear, spring-fed river feeding the Hvítá; its showpiece is the electric-blue waterfall **Brúarfoss**. For centuries a natural **stone arch** here was the only crossing for miles.

en: The Civil War That Ended the Republic
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: Iceland governed itself without a king for three hundred years. Then a handful of families decided that was inefficient — and **burned the whole arrangement down.** Literally, in one case, with the wedding guests still inside.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: The **Sturlungaöld** is usually dated from **about 1220 to 1262** — **Sögufélag says 1264**, because the submission to Norway went **district by district** rather than all at once. Iceland's longest and ugliest internal war.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: Power had pooled into a few big clans, above all the **Sturlungar** — the family of the saga-writer **Snorri Sturluson**. Disputes stopped going to the Althing and started going to **swords, fires and assassinations**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: **Spring 1238, at Apavatn** — the lake we just passed. **Sturla Sighvatsson summoned Gizur Þorvaldsson**, who came with **forty picked men**. Sturla swore he meant nothing by it, then **had them all seized and disarmed.** A **book** was produced — the saga says *bók*, not Bible — and Gizur swore **to sail abroad and keep faith**. He did neither.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: **Five months later, on 21 August 1238, they met at Örlygsstaðir.** Be honest about the numbers, because the tidy version is wrong: **Íslendinga saga gives shifting totals** as forces joined and split — Gizur and **Kolbeinn ungi** with **1,300** at one point, about **1,300** again at Reykjarlaug, then **Brandur arriving with another hundred**, against **four hundred with Sighvatur** and others besides. A modern Icelandic reconstruction puts it at **more than 1,600 against more than 1,200.** It is **often described as the most populous battle ever fought on Icelandic soil** — and I will give you that description, but **nobody has ever demonstrated it.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: **Sturla's spear has a name and a problem.** **Grásíða** was **large, old, and not very stiff**: he thrust so hard that men went down in front of him, but **the spear kept bending, and he had to put it under his foot to straighten it** between attacks. A family heirloom, failing in real time, in the middle of the worst afternoon of his life.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: **How he died is not one blow, and the saga is specific.** **Húnröður Magnússon** stabbed him through the right cheek. **Hjalti Magnússon** through the left cheek and the tongue. **Böðvar kappi** into the throat. **Gizur** then struck a great axe wound **behind the left ear**. **Klængur Bjarnarson** thrust into the wound already in his throat. **Markús Marðarson** stabbed his belly. **The text names no single fatal blow** — so when you hear that Gizur killed him, that is a summary of a queue.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: **Snorri Sturluson — the man who wrote down Norse mythology — was killed at Reykholt on the night of 23 September 1241.** King **Hákon** had sent a letter demanding he come to Norway and answer for himself; **Gizur Þorvaldsson**, his own former son-in-law, brought **seventy men**. **Five went down into the cellar**: Markús Marðarson, Símon knútur, Árni beiskur, Þorsteinn Guðinason and Þórarinn Ásgrímsson. **Símon told Árni to strike.** Snorri said **"Eigi skal höggva"** — *do not strike* — **and the saga records that he said it twice.** They struck. (Íslendinga saga, chapter 156.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: **The low point was the Burning of Flugumýri, 22 October 1253** — a wedding ambush, the hall fired with the family inside. It is often compared to a certain television wedding; that comparison is a modern one and I will label it as such.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: **And the ending is messier than the textbook.** Beginning in **1262** and finished by **1264**, the districts accepted the King of Norway one by one. The document we call **Gamli sáttmáli** records the conditions — but **no original signed 1262 treaty survives.** The manuscript it comes down in, **AM 45 8vo**, is a **damaged law book written in the second half of the sixteenth century**, and Sagnfræðistofnun at the University of Iceland suggests the text is better read as **a homage document, a list of conditions**, than as a treaty between two parties. **Three hundred years of self-government ended, and we cannot produce the paperwork.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: One farm in this steaming valley bred a **dynasty**: the first bishop's family, the household that raised the man who wrote Iceland's memory down — and the one who **ended the republic**. Meet the **Haukdælir**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

en: **Haukadalur** reads as **"Valley of the Hawks"** — *haukur*, hawk, and *dalur*, valley — though I will be straight with you: **that is the obvious reading, not a documented etymology.** Nobody has proved that is where the name came from.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

en: Known now for steam, but for two centuries this was a **chieftain's seat**: the home farm of the **Haukdælir**, one of the great power families of the Icelandic Commonwealth.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

en: **Teitur Ísleifsson** — son of **Ísleifur Gissurarson, Iceland's first bishop** — is the man the family line runs through, and this valley held **a learned household**, not a school in any modern sense. (The *school* crown belongs to **Skálholt**, down the road.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

en: **And here is what it produced.** **Ari fróði Þorgilsson** — "the Wise", **1068 to 1148** — **came to Haukadalur at the age of seven and stayed fourteen winters.** He grew up to write **Íslendingabók**, between **1122 and 1132** — the reason Iceland has any firm early dates at all. **A boy was sent to a farm in a steaming valley, and the country got its memory.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

en: The family stayed at the top for two centuries — bishops, lawmen, and finally **Gizur Þorvaldsson**, the oath-breaker of Örlygsstaðir: a **Haukdæling**, and in **1258** the Norwegian king made him **jarl — earl** — of Iceland, though at first **only over some districts and with his authority unclear.** Four years later the republic he had helped bury was handed to Norway.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

en: **The valley also holds Geysir and Strokkur** — the original *geysir*, the Icelandic verb *að geysa*, to gush, which gave the word to every language that has one. Geologically it is the **Geysir high-temperature geothermal field, on the eastern margin of Iceland's Western Volcanic Zone** — a **borderline field**, in the literature's own phrase. (I used to say "the Hreppar block". The Hreppar **microplate** is real, and it is real regional context between the two volcanic zones — but it is not the description of this field, so I have stopped using it here.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

en: **And be honest about the star turn: Geysir is dormant.** It woke up briefly after the earthquakes of **2000** and its **last known eruptions were in 2016.** The one you are going to watch is **Strokkur** — and its interval is **not** "every five minutes" either: the monitoring study gives an **observed range of 3.7 to 16.4 minutes.** Point your camera and be patient. It owes you nothing.

en: Iceland gave the world the word **"geyser"** — from one hot spring, in one field, on one farm.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: The original **Geysir** is first recorded in **1294**, when earthquakes reshaped the field's springs — at its peak it threw water **60–80 m** up. **It is dormant: its last known eruptions were in 2016.** The one you are here for is its cousin **Strokkur** ("the Churn"), **15–20 m** high and occasionally 40 — and its interval is **not** the five minutes everyone quotes. The monitoring study gives an **observed range of 3.7 to 16.4 minutes.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: Watch the **dome** bulge just before it fires: a thin layer of cooler water over near-boiling water below, pressure building until it punches through.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: Geologically this is the **Geysir high-temperature geothermal field, on the eastern margin of Iceland's Western Volcanic Zone** — the literature's own word for it is a **borderline field**. Water seeps down, hits **200°C+ rock**, flashes to steam and comes back up. (I used to say "the Hreppar block" here. The Hreppar **microplate** is real and it is the regional context between the two volcanic zones — but it is not the name of this field.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: The name **Geysir** (from *geysa*, "to gush") first appears in writing in **1647** — and as Enlightenment scientists took an interest, the word spread to **every language on Earth**, all from this one field.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: **Geysir runs on earthquakes.** Born in the annals after the **1294** quakes, it roars back after every big southern shake — **1630**, **1896**, then **June 2000** — and dozes off again between them, sometimes for decades. **It stirred twice more in early 2016**, which is the last anybody has recorded, and the experts were quick to say that did not mean it was back.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: Icelanders never quite accepted the naps: they used to **shovel rocks and turf in** to provoke it, and from **1963 to 1981** the official trick was **soap** — lower the surface tension and the superheated water boils over. The country literally **washed its geyser into performing**. (We've since let it sleep with dignity.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: At its most active it took **8 to 10 hours** to refill between eruptions. In **1896** it came back erupting **several times a day**, then fell dormant around **1915**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: A **channel was cut in 1935** to lower the water surface and restart it, then **re-cut and deepened in 1981**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: **Strokkur** is straight thermodynamics: **one metre down the water is 90–95°C**, at **ten metres 112°C**, and at the bottom of the **23-metre shaft about 130°C** — held liquid only by the weight of water above it. Take the lid off and it flashes to steam.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: Measured eruptions in **2000** threw between about **270 and 425 litres** of water, or **300 to 500 litres** once you count what leaves as steam.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: **Strokkur's** reliability is younger than most of its audience. Its nineteenth-century performances are said to have **lasted an hour and reached up to 60 metres** — then it fell silent for decades. In **1963** the decision was taken to **drill about 40 metres into the gosskál**, the eruption basin, and it has been **extraordinarily active** ever since. The most dependable natural spectacle in this country is not entirely natural.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: One more number for the shaft: a **cold vein comes in at about 13 metres** down. That is part of why height, duration and interval all vary — and why nobody will ever hand you a timetable, so keep looking at the water rather than at your phone.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: In **1907** an investor tried to dam this waterfall — and a farmer's daughter, **Sigríður**, fought it all the way to Reykjavík. She **lost in court** — and the falls are still here anyway.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: **Gullfoss** ("Golden Falls") drops the **Hvítá** down two staircase tiers, **32 m** total, in a narrow canyon — spray throwing rainbows so consistently it looks staged.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: The Hvítá is **glacial meltwater** from **Langjökull**, silt-laden enough to glow gold in summer light.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: In **1907** an Englishman leased the falls from farmer **Tómas Tómasson** for a **hydro plant**. His daughter **Sigríður Tómasdóttir** spent her own savings on a Reykjavík lawyer — **Sveinn Björnsson**, later Iceland's **first president** — and fought for years to void the lease. The famous "walked barefoot to Reykjavík / threatened to jump" details are **romanticised**; she genuinely **lost in court**, but the lease then **lapsed because the developers stopped paying the rent**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: Gullfoss survived, became a **nature reserve in 1979**, and Sigríður — remembered on a memorial above the falls — is now called **Iceland's first environmentalist**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: The gorge below runs about **2.5 km long and 70 m deep**, and mean flow over the lip is **109 m³/s**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: The Englishman's offer, early in **1907**, was **50,000 krónur** — and Iceland passed a law that same year restricting **foreign ownership of waterfalls**, after which foreign parties obtained rental rights anyway.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: **Sigríður Tómasdóttir**, **1871 to 1957**, came from the farm **Brattholt** above the falls, and what she spent years trying to void were the agreements **her own father had signed**. The judgement went against the Brattholt family.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: What actually saved it was duller than the legend: in **1928** the rental payments stopped and the agreement fell void. The reserve declaration was signed on **9 March 1979** and covers **164.2 hectares**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: Her lawyer was **Sveinn Björnsson**, who went on to become Iceland's first president, **1944 to 1952**. (Losing that case turned out to be quite good for his CV.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: Iceland Through the Years
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: Forty-three tracks in three acts, and the whole story of how a country with fewer people than most cities ended up on everybody's playlist. We get through the first two today.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **ACT I — Borrowed clothes.** Iceland still working out who it sounds like. Five of the biggest singalongs here are secretly Anglo-American hits in Icelandic disguise — *Mambo Italiano*, *California Dreamin'*, *I Will*, Ray Sharpe rockabilly, and a Brita Borg banger out of Stockholm. The mambo arrived secondhand, via 1950s Manhattan. Post-war crooners, dancehall ballads, and Keflavík kids who saw The Beatles in Bournemouth and ran home to start a band.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **01 · Jeg vil ha' morfor med mig ud på sjov** — *Raquel Rastenni*. Plot twist — the Danes nicked it. The song is actually “Jag ska' ta' morfar med mej ut i kväll,” a 1949 Brita Borg banger out of Stockholm, dressed up in a Danish coat a year later. Same writers (Peter Spar / Jessup Sandy), different *morfar*.  [Secret-cover thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **02 · Litla flugan** — *Sigfús Halldórsson*. Iceland's most beloved earworm started as a bar bet. December 1951, Reykhólar farm — the manager Sigurður Elíasson tells Sigfús he can't turn that poem into a tune in ten minutes. Ten minutes later: a national standard. Drinks were *not* on Sigurður.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **03 · Bláu augun** — *Haukur Morthens*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **04 · Vor við flóann** — *Ragnar Bjarnason*. Two-for-one. The 1959 7″ gives you Ragnar singing “Vor við flóann” on the A-side — flip it over and **Guðbergur Auðunsson** takes the mic for “Hvítir svanir.” Same record, two singers, no warning.  [Recorded somewhere unusual]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **05 · Æskuminning** — *Alfreð Clausen*. 1953. Iceland's first-ever ballad recorded with a full orchestra, Carl Billich on the baton. Walked it into the SKT dance-song competition the year before — and *lost*. The audience promptly overruled the judges and handed it the people's prize. Iceland figuring out who runs music: the people. Always the people.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **06 · Hæ Mambó** — *Haukur Morthens*. Yes — *that* Mambo Italiano. The Rosemary Clooney one. Loftur Guðmundsson Icelanded the lyrics and Reykjavík caught the mambo bug secondhand via 1950s Manhattan.  [Secret-cover thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **07 · Lilla Jóns** — *Guðbergur Auðunsson*. It's a Ray Sharpe rockabilly tune in Icelandic drag. Jón Sigurðsson took the American melody, dressed it in his own words, and out came “Little Jónsi.”  [Secret-cover thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **08 · Sveitapiltsins draumur** — *Hljómar*. California Dreamin'. With Icelandic lyrics. About a country boy. Yes, really.  [Secret-cover thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **09 · Sveitin milli sanda** — *Elly Vilhjálms*. There are no lyrics. None. Elly sings the entire thing on one open vowel — wordless, weightless, pure *Aaaaaa*. It started life as the score to a 1962 Ósvaldur Knudsen documentary; Magnús Blöndal Jóhannsson never bothered to add words and nobody ever asked.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **10 · Vor í Vaglaskógi** — *Vilhjálmur Vilhjálmsson*. Akureyri, February 1966. Two lovers go camping in Vaglaskógur — a 300-hectare birch forest in Fnjóskadalur — and Iceland gets its forever-song. The hook line every Icelander mouths on first beat: *Draumar þess rætast, sem gistir Vaglaskóg* — “the dreams of those who sleep in Vaglaskógur come true.” Kaleo dragged it onto the global stage in 2016. The forest has not stopped collecting tourists since.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **11 · Kling Klang** — *Dátar*. 1966 Keflavík teen-rock — fine. But the keyboard player? **Þórir Baldursson.** Twelve years later he'd be playing organ on Donna Summer, Giorgio Moroder and ABBA records. Pop is a small world. Iceland is an even smaller one.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **12 · If you knew** — *Thor's Hammer*. Recorded on Parlophone — *the Beatles' label* — in London, 1966. The “Umbarumbamba” EP that houses it now goes for thousands at auction; among 60s garage-rock collectors it's the white whale, the holy grail, the EP they'll remortgage their flat for.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **13 · Tætum og tryllum** — *Stuðmenn*. From the soundtrack of *Með allt á hreinu* (1982) — Iceland's biggest film of all time. 120,000 tickets. In a country of 230,000. Half the country watched it. Half the dialogue was improvised on the day, and the rival on-screen girl-band “Gærurnar” was actually Grýlurnar (skip ahead to track 19) — meaning the battle of the bands was real on screen *and* in the bar afterwards.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **ACT II — Finding the voice.** Iceland stops borrowing and starts getting copied. *Með allt á hreinu* eats half the country's box office — **120,000 tickets, 230,000 people**. Grýlurnar weaponise punk, and the band rivalry becomes the actual plot of the film. The Sugarcubes go global. Björk goes solo. GusGus turn out to be a twelve-person filmmaking collective who picked up instruments halfway through.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **14 · Reyndu aftur** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Mannakorn*. Track 2 of Mannakorn's January 1977 sophomore LP *Í gegnum tíðina*. The voice you're hearing? Pálmi Gunnarsson — same Pálmi who'd open Iceland's Eurovision account in Bergen 1986. Track 21 is also him. The man gets around.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **15 · Skólaball** — *Brimkló*. Plot twist confirmed by RÚV in 2021: *Skólaball er um stúlku sem síðar varð konan mín* — “the girl in the song became my wife.” Magnús Kjartansson met her at an actual school dance and wrote the actual song. The most romantic Reykjavík origin story that doesn't involve a horse.  [Song about someone]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **16 · Gáta dagsins** — *Spilverk þjóðanna*. Twenty seconds. *Twenty.* “Today's Riddle” clocks in shorter than a cigarette break — a deliberately cryptic micro-piece slipped in among the album's full-length songs. Blink and you've missed it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **17 · Á Sprengisandi** — *Þú og ég*. A 19th-century Grímur Thomsen *ghost poem* turned into a 1980 disco track. Yes. The placename comes from *sprengja* — “to ride a horse to death” — because the highland route was so brutal travellers were said to kill their mounts crossing it. Now picture that on a glitterball.  [Debut-LP opener]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **18 · Sísi** — *Grýlurnar*. It's not about anyone. The whole song is laughter and “vo-oh-oh”s and the name “Sísí” chanted as a hook — pure rhythm, no narrative. From *Mávastellið*, 1983. (The band's name means “the Grýlas” — Iceland's child-eating troll-mother, the lady who shows up at Christmas to scare your kids straight. Sweet branding.)  [Song about someone]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **19 · Svart-hvíta hetjan mín** — *Dúkkulísurnar*. Forty years and she still won't crack. Gréta Sigurjónsdóttir wrote both words and music in 1986 and Icelanders have been begging ever since: *who is the black-and-white hero?* Not telling. “Their best-kept secret.” Stop asking.  [Song about someone]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **20 · Þorparinn** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Pálmi Gunnarsson*. The song is about its own singer. Magnús Eiríksson watched his friend Pálmi Gunnarsson hauling fish in Vopnafjörður before fame found him — and wrote it down. The voice you're hearing is the voice of the song's own subject. Meta-loop activated.  [Song about someone]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **21 · Deus** — *The Sugarcubes*. “Deus does not exist… but if he does, he lives in the sky above me.” Sing-songed like a kindergarten chant. Delivered in fluent Icelandic blasphemy. Whole band straight-faced through the entire thing. The Sugarcubes never did anything halfway.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **22 · Venus As A Boy – 7″ Dream Mix** — *Björk, Mick Hucknall, Gota Yashiki*. Now for the most-WTF production credit on this entire playlist — the 1993 “Dream Mix” was produced by **Mick Hucknall.** As in: Simply Red. As in: *Holding Back the Years* Mick Hucknall. He had a side production company called Dream that year and Björk used it. Pop is so weird.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **23 · Lög unga fólksins** — *Unun*. Title nicked straight from RÚV — *Lög unga fólksins* is Iceland's long-running pop-request show, “Songs of Young People.” Naming your 1994 alt-rock single after the state-broadcast request show is the indie equivalent of calling your album *Top of the Pops*.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **24 · Oh – Edit** — *GusGus*. Hidden inside this slick Reykjavík club banger: a 1959 *tiki-bar* instrumental. Hawaiian exotica composer Arthur Lyman's “Taboo Tu,” sampled in. GusGus reached back forty years and pulled out a luau.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **25 · Sá ég spóa** — *Savanna tríóið*. Authorship: nobody. It's a *þjóðlag* — an anonymous Icelandic folk song that Savanna tríóið nailed down in the now-definitive arrangement. The lyric is twelve seconds of pocket-sized natural history: a curlew on the marsh, a golden plover singing “bí-bí-bí,” and that's it — that's spring, officially clocked in by the *lóa*.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **26 · Serenade** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Album closer of *Fisherman's Woman* (Rough Trade, 2005). Torrini said the entire album was “a letter I wrote to a person that I lost at that time. I coped by thinking I was with a fisherman.” Serenade is the dream-state final page of that letter — the bit where she lets him go.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
