en: Iceland grows **tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and strawberries** a shade south of the latitude of **Fairbanks, Alaska** — and the heating bill is a hole in the ground.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: **Reykholt** ("smoky hill") in **Bláskógabyggð** is the village; **Friðheimar** is its headline farm, a working greenhouse where you eat lunch **among the vines**, soup ladled three feet from the plant that grew it. And the village is booming — **474 people on 1 January 2026**, up from **321 three years before**. Grow tomatoes, apparently, and people follow.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: The heat comes out of the ground **200 metres away** and arrives in the houses at **about 95°C**. The glass is only **4 mm** thick — you want every scrap of daylight, so you accept the heat loss — and the place therefore drinks roughly **200,000 tonnes of hot water a year**. The source is **Reykholtshver**, an old geyser that still erupts about **every ten minutes** and delivers **14 litres a second at 100°C**, heating the village's houses and glass alike.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: Here's the bit most guides get wrong: **geothermal gives you heat, not light.** At this latitude the sun effectively resigns in November, so the plants run on **grow-lights powered by hydro**, and **CO₂ drawn from natural geothermal steam** is piped in to speed up photosynthesis. Volcano heats it, waterfall lights it, volcano feeds it. Heat **plus** light, never heat alone.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: The hardest-working department is one nobody applies to: about **1,200 bumblebees**, a species brought into Iceland specifically to pollinate greenhouses. Each can work **around 2,000 flowers a day** in good conditions — and it needs to, because there are **25,000 plants** in there, every one of them opening two to four fresh flowers a day. No sick days, no HR complaints, paid entirely in pollen.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: The output is **up to two tonnes of tomatoes a day**, every day of the year. About **5%** come out scratched, undersized or misshapen — those go straight into the kitchen behind you, which is the real reason the soup exists. Even the green ones left on the plants at changeover get used. Nothing is thrown away.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: **Knútur Rafn Ármann** and **Helena Hermundardóttir** bought the place in **1995**: two greenhouses and a big farmhouse nobody had lived in for years, though there had been growing under glass here since **1946**. In **2008** they opened the farm to visitors as a small sideline. Today **tourism is two thirds of the turnover** and the tomatoes are one third, with **110 year-round staff** and another 15–20 in summer. The sideline ate the business.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: They are still building. **17,000 m² of glass**, of which **6,000 m²** has already swapped the old sodium lamps for **LED** — about **half the electricity** — and the rest follows by **2028**. In **2025** they took over **Jarðarberjaland** next door, Iceland's strawberry specialist, and are taking it from **3,600 to 6,000 m²**, lifting it from **60 tonnes of strawberries a year to 100**. Icelandic strawberries are still only **three to four percent** of the market, so there is room to grow.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: None of this is new here. Iceland's **first geothermally heated greenhouses went up at Reykir in Mosfellssveit in 1924** — three of them in a single spring and summer — and that is the year the whole industry dates from. The **first greenhouse in Biskupstungur came in 1932**, built at Reykholt by the local schoolmaster, **Stefán Sigurðsson**. Down the road, **Espiflöt** has been going since **1948** and now grows flowers only. And the **very first greenhouse in Iceland**, at Sauðárkrókur in the late 1890s, was heated by **fermenting horse manure** — so on balance, the volcano was an upgrade.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: The horse in that field is a **direct descendant of a Viking horse** — a bloodline effectively **closed for ~1,000 years**. Just don't call it a pony. That's the one hill Iceland will genuinely die on.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🐎 Icelandic Horses

en: The **Icelandic horse** is small (**~132–145 cm**), shaggy, long-lived (often **30 years**), tough and frankly opinionated — and by breed convention and national insistence, **always a "horse," never a pony**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🐎 Icelandic Horses

en: No new bloodstock has arrived since roughly the year **1000**, so it's essentially a **closed, disease-naïve population** — one of the purest native breeds on Earth. Tradition says the **Alþingi** slammed the import door around **982**; the documented ban dates to **1882** — and it still stands.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🐎 Icelandic Horses

en: Most breeds have three or four gaits; the Icelandic has up to **five**, including the famous **tölt** — a four-beat running walk so smooth you could carry a full beer and not spill it. The extra gaits trace to a **single gene mutation**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🐎 Icelandic Horses

en: Population ~**78,000** in Iceland and ~**195,000 abroad** across 30+ countries — the diaspora outnumbers the home herd two to one, and **not one of them is ever allowed back** (biosecurity enforced by MAST, the food and veterinary authority).

en: For **700 years**, this farm was Iceland's **capital, university and cathedral** rolled into one. Then a **1784 earthquake** ate the lot — and the country never gave it back.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: **Skálholt** was Iceland's first **episcopal see**, founded **1056** — for 700 years the country's brain: bishops, Iceland's **first school** — **Skálholtsskóli**, a school from Ísleifur's time — a scriptorium and a library, all bankrolled by a guaranteed **church tithe from 1097**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: It gave Iceland its **only saint** — **Þorlákur Þórhallsson**, declared holy by the Alþingi in **1198** and formally made **patron saint of Iceland by the Vatican in 1984**; his feast on 23 December still anchors the Icelandic Christmas.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The **Reformation** arrived on **7 November 1550** with the beheading here of **Jón Arason** — the Catholic bishop of *Hólar*, the northern see — and two of his sons. The Lutheran takeover, sealed in blood on this lawn.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: A **~magnitude-7 earthquake** (South Iceland Seismic Zone) in **1784** levelled the cathedral; the Danes used it to abolish the bishopric and shift the see to a fishing village called **Reykjavík** — formally, in **1801**. (The last bishop to live at Skálholt, **Hannes Finnsson**, died here in **1796**; the lights went out slowly.) The current church is a **1963 reconstruction** — where the blues-rock band **Kaleo** later recorded a track live, because Iceland.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: Its first bishop, from **1056**, was **Ísleifur Gissurarson** — whose son ran the school up at **Haukadalur**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The district around it is **Biskupstungur**, **the bishop's tongues** — the wedge of land between the **Hvítá** and the **Tungufljót**. A **tunga** is a tongue of land between two rivers, and the bishop in the name is the one on that hill.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The church came before the bishop. **Gissur hvíti** — Ísleifur's own father — is said to have raised the **first church at Skálholt** after the conversion at the **Alþingi in the year 1000**, and **Ísleifur Gissurarson was consecrated the first bishop of Iceland in 1056** and took his seat there. Minjastofnun's phrase for the place is the **head place of Iceland for about 700 years**, and the bishopric ran **continuously from 1056 to 1801**, moving to **Reykjavík** only in the wake of the great natural disasters at the end of the eighteenth century.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The school ran from **Ísleifur's time until 1785**, with short interruptions. Seven centuries of teaching, on a farm.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The 1550 beheading has names and a run-up. **Jón Arason** was executed here on **7 November 1550** together with his sons **Ari** and **the Reverend Björn** — and two years earlier, in **1548**, the Skálholt men had thrown up a **fort east of the churchyard** to hold off his attack, the remains of which are still identifiable on the ground. In **1912** an Englishwoman, **Disney Leith**, paid for a **monument** to him at what is taken to be the execution spot.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The site carries **ten protected archaeological monuments** and **well over a hundred** further age-protected remains. The cathedral standing there now was designed by the state architect **Hörður Bjarnason** and consecrated in **1963** — and Skálholt got a bishop back, a **vígslubiskup**, in **1992.** (Seven hundred years as the centre of the country, ended by an earthquake rather than by politics.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: A red crater with a blue lake in the bottom — and in 1987 a county sports club that had just lost a fortune put **opera singers in boats on that lake** and pulled **seven thousand people** in to bail them out.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: **Kerið is about 6,500 years old** — that is the figure in its own geological description, and a scientific outreach article puts it at about 6,600. **You may have heard me say five to six thousand. That was wrong and I have stopped saying it.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: It is **about 270 m long, 170 m wide and 55 m deep** — deep enough to swallow a seventeen-storey building. The lake in the bottom is **groundwater, 7 to 14 metres deep**, rising and falling with the water table rather than being fed by any stream. It looks turquoise because water absorbs red light first and the floor is dark. And there is life in it: a **2014 paper found ten zooplankton taxa**, mostly rotifers.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: **The walls are red because the iron in the scoria has oxidised** — it is rusting, and it is young enough to still be doing it. Give it a few thousand more years and it will blacken like its neighbours. (I used to name the mineral. **Nobody has actually published a mineral analysis of this crater**, so I have stopped doing that too.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: **How it formed is genuinely argued over, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.** Kerið's own geological account says a **scoria cone that collapsed when the magma drained away beneath it** — explicitly not an explosion. A **2024** scientific article says it is probably a **maar**, blown out where magma met groundwater. **Two respectable accounts, opposite mechanisms, same hole in the ground.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: It is the **northernmost crater of the Tjarnarhólar row**, and the **Grímsnes lavas came from twelve separate eruptive centres** covering about **54 km²**. No single big bang — built up in instalments, the way Iceland does most things.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: **It is privately owned, and that matters for the ticket.** It has charged a small admission **since June 2013**, which is unusual in a country where walking into a landscape is normally free — the money goes on the path and the stairway down the north wall. The owner is **Kerfélagið ehf.** — a company, not, as I used to say, an association of local farmers: **Arctic Adventures bought all the shares in 2023.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: **And now the concert, because the version on the internet is wrong.** On **Sunday 16 August 1987 at three in the afternoon**, Kerið hosted what Morgunblaðið called ***fyrstu tónleikar í eldgíg á Íslandi*** — **the first concert ever held in a volcanic crater in this country.** The musicians performed **from boats out on the lake**; DV's headline the next day was ***"Fljótandi tónleikar"*** — floating concerts.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: **The bill, as the paper printed it two days before:** the opera singer **Kristján Jóhannsson** with **Lára Rafnsdóttir**; **Kristinn Sigmundsson** with **Jónas Ingimundarson**; **Bubbi Morthens**; **Björgvin Halldórsson**; **Magnús Kjartansson's band** with **Erna Gunnarsdóttir**; and **Ásgeir Steingrímsson** on trumpet. **Every one of them played for nothing.** Tickets were **500 krónur**, free for under-fourteens and pensioners.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: **Björk was not there.** I told that story for a long time and it is not in a single contemporary report. The rock name on that bill was **Bubbi**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: **Why they did it is the good bit.** **Héraðssambandið Skarphéðinn**, the district sports association, had just lost a fortune on an outdoor festival at **Þjórsárdalur** over the August bank holiday. **Árni Johnsen**, then a member of parliament, got this up to dig them out of it — and **about seven thousand people came.** DV reported the turnout beat the most optimistic hopes in the association and **the debt was paid off.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: One detail from Tíminn that tells you exactly what it was like: **the sound took so long to climb the slope, and the applause so long to come back down, that when the crowd tried to clap along with the singers it threw everybody out.**

en: A river only **20 km long** — and for a generation it carried **half of Iceland's electricity**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: The **Sog** is the **only river draining Þingvallavatn**, Iceland's biggest natural lake, and it runs south to join the **Hvítá** and become the **Ölfusá**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: Short, but enormous in volume — **Iceland's largest spring-fed river**, averaging about **100 m³/s** of lake-clear, gravel-filtered water.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: That single outlet is the whole reason the engineers loved it. Þingvallavatn behaves like an **enormous header tank**: it refuses to flood and it refuses to dry, which makes the Sog **one of the steadiest rivers in the country** — exactly what a turbine wants.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: Three stations sit on it, and they were built a generation apart. **Ljósafossstöð** (1937), **Írafossstöð** (1953) and **Steingrímsstöð** (1959) — together about **88 MW**, which ran roughly **half of Iceland's electricity** through the 1960s and 70s, until the big highland plants on the **Þjórsá** took over.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: **Ljósafoss** opened in **1937** with **two machines of 4.4 MW**; a **third of 5.8 MW** followed in **1944**, taking it to **14.6 MW** — about **105 GWh** a year. Scale was never the point. **Being first was.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: **Írafoss** came online on **16 October 1953** with **two machines of 15.5 MW**. The **third, 16.8 MW, was not added until 1963** — so the famous "48 megawatts" is a *1963* number, not a 1953 one. It harnesses two waterfalls, **Írafoss and Kistufoss**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: **Steingrímsstöð** started up on **6 August 1959**, **26 MW**, and it is the one that dams the **outflow of Þingvallavatn itself**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: And the consequence was entirely domestic. **Ljósafoss quadrupled the electricity available to the capital region**, and **Reykjavík households swapped their coal ranges for electric cookers.** A whole city stopped smelling of smoke because of a drop in a river almost none of them had ever visited.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: Where did Iceland's electric age actually start? Not here — in a **carpenter's workshop in Hafnarfjörður**. On **12 December 1904**, **Jóhannes Reykdal** ran a **9 kW** generator off the stream behind his joinery and lit **15 houses — the school and the Good Templars' hall among them — plus the workshop and four street lamps**, in time for Christmas. From one carpenter's stream to all of this, inside a single lifetime.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: **The bill came due in the lake.** Damming **Efra-Sog** in 1959 diverted the water past its own channel and into Steingrímsstöð's tunnels, and the flood thrown up by the construction **swept the spawning gravel out of the Útfall**. The Efra-Sog stock had been **the largest brown-trout population in Þingvallavatn**; as a distinct spawning run, it **disappeared**. The lights went on and a fish went out — and that trade is the honest version of this river's story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá

en: Four rivers walk into a valley. Only one of them comes out with a name — and it is carrying more water than anything else in the country.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá

en: **Ölfusá is Iceland's biggest river by volume.** Orkustofnun's long-run measurements put it at about **400 m³ every second** at Selfoss, averaged over **44 years** — against **363 m³/s** for Þjórsá at Urriðafoss, the runner-up. It is emphatically not the longest. It is simply the one nobody could get across.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá

en: It is **four systems wearing one name.** The glacial **Hvítá** runs south from **Langjökull** past **Gullfoss**, gathering **Tungufljót** and **Brúará** on the way. The spring-fed **Sog** drains **Þingvallavatn** — Iceland's largest natural lake — down through **Álftavatn**. The two trunk rivers meet under the **eastern flank of Ingólfsfjall**, just above Selfoss, and from there they run as one.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá

en: **Veðurstofa Íslands** gauges **5,678 km²** of catchment above its measuring station at Selfoss. Grey glacier-melt and clear spring water, welded into a single channel, with the entire Golden Circle sitting upstream of it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá

en: The channel **zig-zags along the South Iceland Seismic Zone**, following fault lines rather than gravity. Beside it lies **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**, the Great Þjórsá Lava — erupted **about 8,700 years ago** from a fissure **20 to 30 km long** in the **Veiðivötn swarm of the Bárðarbunga system**, it ran **about 130 km to the sea**, **25 cubic kilometres** of it, reaching the coast between the Þjórsá and the Ölfusá. Vísindavefur (Haraldur Sigurðsson, January 2025) calls it *"stærsta hraun sem runnið hefur á jörðinni síðan ísöldinni lauk"* — the largest lava flow that has run anywhere on Earth since the Ice Age ended.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá

en: Keep one distinction straight: **largest by volume is not the same as most powerful.** That trophy goes to **Eldgjá**. The same volcanic system also produced **Vatnaöldur in 871** and **Veiðivötn in 1477**. (The biggest thing this island ever erupted is shaped like a field. You cannot see it. That is exactly how big it is.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss

en: **The town exists because of the bridge.** **Ölfusárbrú** was consecrated on **Tuesday 8 September 1891**, and Vegagerðin's own history records it as **the first suspension bridge built in Iceland** — the first of six of that type raised here between 1891 and 1905. The municipality calls it *"þá mesta mannvirki sem Íslendingar höfðu ráðist í"*, the greatest engineering work Icelanders had ever undertaken. Trade collected at the bridgehead and **Selfoss grew up around it.** The old construction hut, **Tryggvaskáli**, is still the oldest building in town.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss

en: **The 1891 numbers.** The Alþingi found **60,000 krónur** — 40,000 as a straight grant, 20,000 as a loan to the counties of Árnes and Rangárvellir, repayable over **45 years**. **Tryggvi Gunnarsson** took the contract because nobody else would do it for that money, and Þjóðólfur reported he lost on the job. The bridge was **built in England** and shipped over ready-made, hung from **three twisted iron cables a side**, painted red, and rated to carry **144,000 pounds**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss

en: **Opening day went beautifully right up until they shut it.** Ísafold counted **a full 1,700** people on the riverbank — the largest crowd ever gathered in one place in Iceland outside the capital — and Þjóðólfur reckoned nearer **1,800**, with **just over 1,500** counted walking across in procession behind a brass band. From **just after 11 a.m.** nobody was allowed onto the bridge at all, so the **Governor of Iceland and his entire party had to be rowed across the river** — to attend the opening of the bridge.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss

en: **Then at about two in the morning on Wednesday 6 September 1944, the northern main cable snapped.** Two lorries were on the span: a big Dodge carrying **empty milk churns**, towing a second truck that had broken down on the Reykjavík run — both owned by **Kaupfélag Árnesinga**, both on milk haulage for **Mjólkurbú Flóamanna**, the dairy that had been running since December 1929. Both lorries went into the river. **Both drivers lived**; one went under with his truck and surfaced downstream. And get this bit right, because everybody gets it wrong: **the bridge did not fall.** It slumped onto the one surviving cable and hung there, and they used it as a guarded footbridge for another fifteen months.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss

en: **It had been warned about, repeatedly.** An engineering inspection that spring produced a **6-tonne limit imposed on 11 May 1944**, repeated on the radio from **29 July**, with bus passengers ordered to get out and walk across. The road director, **Geir Zoëga**, stood on the bank the following afternoon and said only: *"Jæja þá, þá er hún komin svona"* — well then, so that is how it ends. The bridge was **two days short of its 53rd birthday.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss

en: **The replacement opened at midday on Friday 21 December 1945, with no ceremony whatsoever.** A suspension bridge with an **84 m main span** plus a 50 m steel-girder approach on the south bank — **134 m in total**, a **6 m carriageway** and a metre of footway each side, the largest bridge in the country at the time. The steel had been trapped behind wartime export bans in America. By the time it opened, the war it was ordered in the middle of had been over for three months.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss

en: **The river still rearranges the town.** On **29 May 2008 at 15:45** the ground let go **twice inside about three seconds** — **Mw 5.8** beneath **Ingólfsfjall**, five kilometres north-west of here, and then **Mw 5.9** on the **Kross fault** five kilometres further west again. Veðurstofa announced **6.3** that afternoon, which is the teleseismic figure; the ground-deformation work settles the pair at a composite **Mw 6.1**. Veðurstofa's GPS station at Selfoss **moved about 20 cm to the south-east and rose 5 cm — permanently.** They **closed the bridges over the Ölfusá** as a precaution, which this river has form for. Twenty-eight people were hurt across Árnessýsla; **nobody was killed.** The town shrugged and carried on growing: **11,000 people on 1 January 2026**, up from **9,812** just two years earlier.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss

en: **Bridge number three is going up right now.** First sod cut **20 November 2024** — a **cable-stayed** bridge, **330 m long and 19 m wide**, contractor **ÞG Verk**, about **17.9 billion krónur** for the whole scheme, due **autumn 2028**, and reported on schedule as of **March 2026**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss

en: That flat-topped mountain is **Ingólfsfjall**, **551 m**, and geologically it is a **móbergsstapi** — a table mountain, built under the ice sheet in the middle of the Ice Age. Hyaloclastite with lava layers running through it, capped by a lava shield from the point where the volcano finally broke out above the meltwater. Its high point is the mound called **Inghóll**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson

en: Per the saga, **Ingólfur Arnarson** threw his carved **high-seat pillars** overboard and swore to settle wherever they washed ashore. His slaves **Vífill and Karli** found them in a bay steaming with hot springs, and he named it **Reykjavík**, "Bay of Smokes."
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson

en: **Here is the bit almost everybody gets wrong.** **Landnámabók does not say Ingólfur is buried on that mountain.** The Sturlubók text says only that he spent his **third winter *"undir Ingólfsfelli fyrir vestan Ölfusá"*** — under Ingólfsfell, west of the Ölfusá — before going on to Reykjavík. The burial in Inghóll is **munnmæli**, oral tradition, and the municipality of Ölfus labels it as exactly that on its own page. A 1964 article in **Goðasteinn** called it **þjóðtrú** and said out loud that it doubted it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson

en: The folklore is better than the history anyway. The mound is said to **open for one night every summer**, and on that night you can reach the treasure buried with him. Nobody has produced the treasure. Nobody has produced the grave either.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson

en: **He was not first here, either.** Irish monks — the **Papar** — were already in Iceland and left when the pagans arrived, and a Norseman called **Náttfari** had stayed behind years before. Ingólfur's real title is narrower: **first permanent Norse settler in the saga tradition.** He got the trophy because his descendants ended up running the parliament and writing the record.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson

en: We are on **Leið 1**, the Ring Road, only completed in **1974** for the 1,100-year settlement anniversary. Before that, reaching **Höfn** meant hundreds of extra kilometres on rough tracks.

en: Hveragerði sits on its own **high-temperature geothermal field**, at the **eastern margin of the Western Volcanic Zone** and the **western end of the South Iceland Seismic Zone**, with the **Hengill** system away to the north-east. Translation: it is steaming and it is on a fault. Fumaroles and mud pots vent **between the houses**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: **On 29 May 2008 the ground let go twice inside about three seconds.** **Mw 5.8** beneath **Ingólfsfjall**, then **Mw 5.9** on the **Kross fault** five kilometres further west — a doublet. Veðurstofa announced **6.3** that afternoon in Icelandic and **6.1** in its English release, and both are right: **6.3 is the teleseismic estimate, 6.1 is what the ground deformation adds up to.** Hveragerði's GPS station moved **199 ± 4 mm to the north-west**, and kept creeping about **30 mm more** until that August. A University of Iceland study found the damage here **averaged 5% of insured value** and was dominated by **non-structural damage and contents rather than collapse** — which is why the town is still standing and still full.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: **Rather than hide it, they built an exhibition on it.** **Skjálftinn 2008** — "The Quake" — sits inside the **Sunnumörk** shopping centre, over a fissure that runs through the building. And the best part was never meant to be an exhibit: when the centre was under construction in **2003**, an **earthquake fissure was found in the ground beneath it**, and instead of filling it in they **lit it and left it on show.** Stand on the crack. **Admission is free** — you pay only if you want a turn in the simulator, which runs at over 6.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: **The town has a birthday, and it is younger than your grandmother.** It began in **1929** on land of the farm **Vorsabær** in Ölfus: that summer the milk station went up at **Breiðumörk 26**, and the first two houses appeared — **Varmahlíð**, and a summer house at **Fagrihvammur** where **ylrækt**, growing under glass on geothermal heat, started here. A milk station, two dwellings and a greenhouse. That is the entire origin.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: **Commercial horticulture began the same year, 1929**, associated with **Sigurður Sigurðsson**; a **45 m² greenhouse went up at Fagrihvammur in 1930** for cucumbers and tomatoes. The **Garðyrkjuskóli ríkisins** at **Reykir** — the state horticultural college — turned out **its first qualified horticulturists in the spring of 1941**, and most of them walked straight out and built nurseries of their own here. The count tells it better than any adjective: **seven horticultural stations in Hveragerði by 1940, twenty by 1950.** Flowers took over in the forties and the place became **blómabærinn**, the flower town.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: **And yes, the bananas.** The horticultural college grew them **as an experiment**, never commercially, and the "Europe's largest banana plantation" line you may have read is a myth with excellent legs. Iceland is not, and never was, a banana republic.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: For scale: **about 140 people at the end of 1941**, **about 400 by 1946** — the year the district was formally constituted — and **3,342 on 1 January 2026** (Hagstofa Íslands). The **name** is far older than the town: **Hveragerði first appears in Fitjaannáll shortly before 1700**, in an account of an erupting hot spring that **shifted position during earthquakes in 1597**, and by the description of Ölfus written in **1703** the springs were already in daily use for **bathing, boiling and washing**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: Uphill behind the town is **Reykjadalur**, registered by **Náttúrufræðistofnun** as a **high-temperature geothermal area** and described by **Umhverfisstofnun** as a landscape of hot springs, pools, dykes, faults and landslides. It is the valley people walk up to sit in a warm river. Note the two are different places: the **geothermal park is in town**, Reykjadalur is the walk.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: And there is a song for this town. **SVVN**, the Icelandic producer who names his tracks after the places on this drive, has one called **Hveragerði** — so this is exactly where it goes on.

en: Right — that is me done talking. My own playlist from here into town: sixteen tracks, all Icelandic, all picked for this exact stretch of road.

en: Rícharður's Mix, The Road Home
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: Sixteen tracks, sequenced for exactly this road: quiet while you are tired, warm as the light changes, loud by the time the city shows up.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **ACT I — Silence.** You have been awake since six and the whole day is in your bones. Piano, strings, glass-cool modern classical, and a lullaby to close it. That lullaby, track three, is — heads up — technically about infanticide. We will not dwell.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **01 · Flight from the City** — *Jóhann Jóhannsson*. Opening track of *Orphée* (2016) — Jóhann's first solo album for Deutsche Grammophon, and the last solo album he ever made before he died in Berlin in February 2018. The whole record traces the Orpheus myth — death, rebirth, looking back — and was tied directly to his own move from Copenhagen to Berlin. *Flight from the City* is the literal opening of that journey out. Listen to it knowing he never made another.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **02 · Bambaló (feat. Steiney Sigurðardóttir)** — *Gabríel Ólafs*. Plot twist — that “traditional Icelandic lullaby” is actually an *Irish* folk tune that hitchhiked north centuries ago. The word *bambaló* is essentially Icelandic for “rock-a-bye.” Gabríel cut this version with cellist Steiney Sigurðardóttir for *Lullabies for Piano and Cello*. Iceland: still wearing imported clothes, still pulling it off.  [Lullaby thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **03 · Sofðu unga ástin mín** — *Hafdís Huld*. Heads up — Iceland's most beloved lullaby is, technically, *about infanticide*. The lyric is from Jóhann Sigurjónsson's 1911 play *Fjalla-Eyvindur*: outlaw's wife Halla sings it to her own baby seconds before throwing the child into a waterfall so she and her fugitive husband can keep running across the highlands. Icelandic parents have nonetheless been singing this to their toddlers ever since. Hafdís Huld cut this version on *Vögguvísur* (2012) at home — while pregnant with her own daughter Arabella. Sleep tight, kids.  [Lullaby thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **ACT II — Eyes Open.** The warmth creeps in. Laufey waltzes. **Elín Hall** sings about her dad running *toward* the lava — not a metaphor, in a country built on the stuff. **Ásgeir's** actual father writes his son a song called *The Journey Home*, and the bus suddenly knows where it is going. Then BRÍET, Friðrik Dór and Jón Jónsson, and Valdimar lift it up off the floor.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **04 · Bewitched** — *Laufey*. Title track of the 2023 album that won Laufey the Grammy for Best Traditional Pop Vocal Album in 2024. She wrote it as a “guitar voice waltz” about the moment of falling helplessly into new love after a perfect first date — then asked the **Philharmonia Orchestra** to score the inside of her head. She calls it the song that “sets the sound of the album.” One song. One orchestra. One Grammy. Done.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **05 · Tachylite** — *Elín Hall*. *Tachylite* is volcanic glass — basaltic lava that cooled too fast to crystallise. Elín Hall calls it “failed lava.” The song is a quiet tribute to her father — an **Icelandic geophysicist who works as a first responder during eruptions**. He runs *toward* the lava. She wrote a song called Failed Lava about him. Released January 2026.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **06 · Heimförin** — *Ásgeir*. *The Journey Home.* The lyrics are by **Ásgeir's dad** — Einar Georg Einarsson, a poet from the village of Laugarbakki — and most of the original Icelandic words on the 2012 debut *Dýrð í dauðaþögn* are his father's. A song called The Journey Home, written by Dad, set to music and sung by son. The album went on to become the best-selling Icelandic debut *of all time*. Family business.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **07 · In Too Deep** — *BRÍET*. Bríet's debut single — self-released in 2018 when she was eighteen. She set out to write a happy love song and changed direction mid-write; the girl in the song starts smiling and ends pulled under. The track that introduced her voice internationally.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **08 · Á Sama Tíma, Á Sama Stað** — *Friðrik Dór & Jón Jónsson*. The brothers Jónsson. (Yes — actual brothers.) The song was the official 2018 *Þjóðhátíðarlag* — the festival anthem of Þjóðhátíð on the Westman Islands, where every August Iceland packs into a lava-walled valley called Herjólfsdalur and sings whatever song the year's commissioned writer hands them. 2018: the brothers' turn. The country's biggest weekend, scored by two siblings sharing a mic.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **09 · Á Flug** — *Valdimar*. *In Flight.* Valdimar are from **Keflavík** — i.e. the literal airport town this coach just left. From their 2010 debut *Undraland*, released on Geimsteinn, the Keflavík label founded by Rúnar Júlíusson. A song about flight, made by guys you flew over.  [Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **ACT III — Bags Packed.** Reykjavík widens ahead and the volume comes up. Of Monsters and Men, then **Una Stef** singing *Like Home* — her father wrote track 39 of the other playlist. Agent Fresco blow the doors off. Reykjavík's own mystery woman finally gets a name, seventy years late. Quarashi, and then **Ingó Veðurguð** has the last word.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **10 · Tuna in a Can** — *Of Monsters and Men*. Yes — the song is actually about **canned tuna**. The image — *tuna in a can, sticky from the brine / I thought I'd gone bad, you thought I was fine* — is reportedly Nanna's nod to her **mum's tuna salad**. It became the visual anchor of the entire 2025 album *All Is Love and Pain in the Mouse Parade*; the cover is built around it as “a quilt of familial stories.” Best self-portrait-as-expired-canned-fish in modern indie pop.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **11 · Like Home** — *Una Stef*. Keep track 39 of the other playlist in mind. *Á Góðum Degi* is by **Stefán S. Stefánsson** — and Una Stef is his daughter. Two playlists, one family, and a song called *Like Home* arriving right as Reykjavík comes back into view. Neither of us planned that.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **12 · Howls** — *Agent Fresco*. Track 6 of *Destrier* (2015) — the concept album frontman Arnór Dan Arnarson wrote after **two men attacked him late one night and left him with a broken eye socket and concussion**. The whole record is grief and adrenaline. *Howls* sits at the nostalgic end — *howls of youth, when life would run with lawless legs to race the sun* — the memory of pre-violence freedom the rest of the album is trying to claw back. (A *destrier* is the medieval warhorse bred for battle.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **13 · Fröken Reykjavík** — *Friðrik Dór*. Music by **Jón Múli Árnason**, lyrics by his brother **Jónas** — the Árnason brothers wrote dozens of Iceland's most-loved mid-century standards together. For seventy-odd years nobody knew who the red-shoed woman walking down Austurstræti actually *was*. Mystery solved in 2023 — director Björn Brynjúlfur Björnsson revealed in *Vísir* that she was his mother, **Jóna Sigurjónsdóttir**. Reykjavík kept its secret for seven decades. Then it broke. Friðrik Dór cut this reworking in **2016**; his melody line wanders a fair way from Jón Múli’s original.  [Family wrote it]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **14 · Jungle Drum** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Co-written with producer Dan Carey, released as a single in March 2009. The “ay-ay-ay” scat hook took it to **No. 1 in Germany, Austria and Belgium** — Torrini's biggest chart hit by a country mile — *after* it got used in the *Germany's Next Topmodel* finale. German rockabilly band The Baseballs covered it the same year. The whole lyric is a heartbeat-as-tribal-drum metaphor. Sometimes a giant pop hit really is just *ay-ay-ay*.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **15 · Mr. Jinx** — *Quarashi*. The earworm hook is sampled from a 1973 American soul cut — **New York City's “Sanity”** — laundered through Reykjavík rap. The song itself never blew up on charts (peaked No. 43 on Radio & Records Alternative). But its second life was sync money — scoring trailers and incidental music for *Alias*, *Smallville*, NBA on TNT (2003–2005), and Madden NFL 2003. Their other *Jinx* track “Stick 'Em Up” snagged the *2 Fast 2 Furious* trailer. Iceland's quiet sync goldmine.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **16 · Takk fyrir mig** — *Ingó Veðurguð*. The last word of the day, and it was written for a party that never happened. This was **Þjóðhátíðarlagið 2020** — the official song of Vestmannaeyjar’s Þjóðhátíð, the biggest weekend in the Icelandic calendar. Ingó wrote it (his brother took a hand in part of it), and then the 2020 festival was called off under gathering restrictions. A thank-you sung to a crowd that never got to turn up. It gets its crowd on this bus instead.  [Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: It makes the power, heats half the capital, and files its own exhaust underground as gravel. It also taught Iceland that you can trigger earthquakes by being tidy.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Most power stations bury their emissions in a report. This one buries them in the rock.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Weather pivot: "The worse the weather, the better the plume — on a still cold day the steam columns are the most dramatic thing on this road."
ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: The Dragon's Breath
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Those white plumes are **steam, not smoke** — and the same plant that lights the road also **turns its own exhaust into stone**. Underneath you, permanently.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: **Hengill** is not a mountain, it is a **volcanic system** — and it sits where **three zones meet**: the **Reykjanes rift**, the **Western Volcanic Zone** and the **South Iceland Seismic Zone**. Water goes down, comes back at **reservoir temperatures of 260–320°C**, and spins turbines.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: **303 megawatts of electricity**, and the arithmetic is satisfying: **six high-pressure turbines of 45 MW plus one low-pressure turbine of 33 MW.** They arrived in stages — **two in 2006, one in 2007, two in 2008, two more in 2011** — so the plant you are looking at was assembled over five years, like flat-pack furniture for a country.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Then the quieter half. **200 MW of heat** goes **27 km down insulated pipes** to warm **more than half the capital region**, which is why Reykjavík never smells of coal. Nationally, **about 90% of the energy used to heat Icelandic homes is geothermal** — Orkustofnun's figure for **2020**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: The trick that makes it safe: the geothermal fluid down there is **hot, corrosive and full of dissolved minerals**, and **it never touches your tap.** It gives up its heat through an exchanger to clean water, and goes back underground.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: **Carbfix** is the famous bit, and the famous number needs its footnote. In **2012** a pilot dissolved **175 tonnes of CO₂ in 5,000 tonnes of water** and pumped it in at about **500 m and 35°C**. **Matter et al. (2016)** tracked it: **over 95% turned to carbonate rock in under two years.** That result belongs to *that* pilot — **not automatically to every tonne since**, at different depths, temperatures and rock.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Industrial injection is a different animal: it started on **23 June 2014**, putting the plant's own CO₂ **and H₂S** into fractured basalt at roughly **750 m and over 250°C**. By the end of **2017** that had taken down **23,200 tonnes of CO₂ and 11,800 tonnes of H₂S**. *(The line that "both gases mineralise in about two years" mixes two separate studies — do not say it.)*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: And the newest chapter is barely a year old. **ON Power opened a second capture station, Steingerður, on 19 June 2025** — about **30,000 tonnes of CO₂ a year**. Over the twelve months to **30 June 2026** Carbfix reported **99.6% of the CO₂ and 100% of the H₂S** entering the capture system being dissolved, and **cumulative mineralisation past 120,000 tonnes of CO₂ and 50,000 of H₂S**. *(Operator figures — impressive, and only one source, so say who said it.)*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Why bother with the sulphur at all? Because **H₂S stinks and is toxic**, and after the plant opened in 2006 the smell started reaching **Reykjavík** on the wrong wind — around **13,000 tonnes a year** by 2011. Iceland wrote an **ambient H₂S limit in 2010, biting in 2014**, and the cleanup followed. The rotten-egg problem is the reason the rock-making began.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Separately from all that: **Climeworks** pulls CO₂ **out of the open air** here — not out of the turbines. **Orca** started on **8 September 2021** at a nominal **4,000 tonnes a year**; **Mammoth** is nominally **36,000**. Hellisheiði supplies the power, Carbfix supplies the basalt.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: **And it is not free.** When large-scale reinjection began at **Húsmúli on 1 September 2011** at about **500 kg a second**, the ground answered immediately: **two magnitude-4 earthquakes on 15 October 2011**, around **forty events above ML 2.5**, eight between **3.0 and 4.0** — felt in **Hveragerði**, the biggest felt in **Reykjavík** — and up to **2 cm** of measured surface movement. Pushing water into a fault system moves faults. That is the honest footnote to the clean-energy story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: The pagans claimed a volcano was voting. Snorri pointed out that the ballot box was older than the religion.

en: Can a volcano vote? Around the year 1000 one appeared to try — and a chieftain took it apart with a single question, without raising his voice.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun

en: **The lava out the window has three names, and two of them are the same name.** Properly it is **Svínahraunsbruni** — two historical **ʻaʻā** flows out of the **Eldborgir just west of Lambafell**. In daily speech it is called **Svínahraun**, and so is the much older **Leitahraun** underneath it, which it ran straight over. One of those two flows is the one called **Kristnitökuhraun**, the Christianity Lava. Iceland names a thing twice and then argues about it. Entirely on brand.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun

en: It ran **around the year 1000** — Vísindavefur allows **possibly 999** — covered roughly **15 km²**, flowed **north-east** across the flats into **Þrengslin**, and **stopped about where the Ring Road runs now.** You are driving along its edge.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun

en: **Now the story, with the actual words, because this one gets told wrong everywhere.** Iceland's chieftains were at **Þingvellir**, and the two sides had just formally declared themselves **out of each other's laws** — which, in a country with one legal system and no army, is how a civil war starts.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun

en: ***Kristni saga*:** *"Þá kom maðr hlaupandi ok sagði, at jarðeldr var upp kominn í Ölfusi ok mundi hann hlaupa á bæ Þórodds goða."* A man came running and said **earth-fire had come up in Ölfus** and would run over the farm of **Þóroddur goði**. The heathens said: *"Eigi er undr í, at goðin reiðist tölum slíkum"* — no wonder the gods are angry at talk like this.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun

en: **Then Snorri goði.** *"Um hvat reiddust goðin, þá er hér brann hraunit, er nú stöndum vér á?"* — **"What were the gods angry about when the lava we are now standing on burned?"** And note exactly where he was pointing: **at the ground under his own feet, at Þingvellir.** Not at this field. He was telling the pagans that their own holy assembly ground was made of the same stuff, laid down by the same fire, long before anyone was around to be blamed for it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun

en: **Only after that** did **Hallur of Síða** buy the lawspeaking from **Þorgeir** — *hálfu hundraði silfrs*, half a hundred of silver, in Kristni saga; **three marks of silver** in Njáls saga, so the two sagas do not even agree on the bribe — and Þorgeir lay down under his cloak for a day, a night and a day.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun

en: **And here is the punchline geologists added a thousand years later.** Svínahraunsbruni is the best candidate for the lava in that account. en: A field of perfect little volcanoes, and **not one of them is real**. We dug half of them up for road gravel — and that turned out to be the reason NASA got interested.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: **They are fake volcanoes.** *Gervigígar* — properly, **rootless cones**. No conduit, no magma chamber underneath, no roots at all. The magma did not come up; it came **sideways**, through closed lava tubes just under the surface.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: **What actually happened:** lava from the shield crater **Leiti**, in the eastern **Bláfjöll** ridge, ran about **28 km** all the way down to **Elliðaárvogur** — so fluid that in places the flow is only **0.6 to 0.75 m thick.** Where it crossed wet ground, its own base crust held the water off until the weight cracked it. Water-saturated sediment then met molten lava, and the result was not a polite puff of steam but **repeated explosive mixing** — fragmentation, ash fall, ballistic ejecta — punching **back up through the flow.** Frozen mid-explosion in red scoria. The red is iron oxide. It is rust.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: **How old? Genuinely disputed, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.** **Náttúrufræðistofnun Íslands** says **5,200 years**. A University of Iceland thesis says **5,316**. **Vísindavefur** says **4,700**. **Reykjavíkurborg** says **4,500** for the same lava down in Elliðaárdalur. Four institutions, four numbers, one lava. Somewhere between four and a half and five and a half thousand years old.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: **How many cones?** The only hard count anybody ever made is **von Komorowicz's map of 1912**, which numbers **98 craters** — cone 53 was one of the biggest — plus **hornitos** on the eastern side that **are not there any more.** He thought they were real scoria cones; nobody had worked out the mechanism yet. Today the field covers about **0.8 km²** and only a handful of intact cones survive, round the edges.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: **Because we quarried the rest.** Rauðhólar was largely untouched until about **1940**, when the British occupation brought heavier machinery than this country had ever had and a war's appetite for aggregate. Red scoria made excellent road surfacing and you could shovel it **straight onto a lorry bed**. The single biggest job it fed was **building Reykjavík Airport in Vatnsmýri**. Digging ran hardest from **1940 to 1950**, and was still going in **1949** — into Hringbraut — the year the geologist **Sigurður Þórarinsson** stood up at the Natural History Society's 60th anniversary and said out loud that we were destroying it. An aerial photograph from **28 July 1954** shows how much was already gone.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: **It was then protected twice.** As a **náttúruvætti — a natural monument — in 1961**, and again as a **fólkvangur in 1974** (*Auglýsing um fólkvang í Rauðhólum* nr. **185/1974**). Every pseudocrater in Iceland now carries special protection under **náttúruverndarlög nr. 60/2013**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: **Now the Mars part, which is real, and which is not the story people tell.** Nobody trained astronauts here. What happened is that when Mars images began arriving from about **1970**, the crater clusters on them looked exactly like these — same shape, same formation conditions, same volcanism. So between **2002 and 2016**, fieldwork here funded by **NASA's Mars Data Analysis Program, Mars Fundamental Research Program and NASA Postdoctoral Program** used the **quarry faces** — the damage — to work out how a rootless cone is built on the inside, and applied it to the Red Planet. **The vandalism is the reason the science was possible.** There is nowhere else in Iceland you can look inside one of these.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: For scale, Iceland's big pseudocrater fields are **Landbrotshólar at 150 km²**, **Álftavershólar at 35**, **Mývatn at 30** and **Aðaldalur at 28**. Rauðhólar is **0.8**. It is the small one. It is also the one twenty minutes from a capital city, which is exactly why it went under a runway.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: The same lava built **Tröllabörn** west of Lækjarbotnar, and the caves **Raufarhólshellir** and **Árnahellir**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: The shallow lake beside them is **Rauðavatn**, "Red Water", and that scruffy belt of trees is the **oldest deliberate woodland in the Reykjavík area.** In **1901** about eighty shareholders founded **Skógræktarfélag Reykjavíkur**, bought **six hectares** by the lake and put the Danish forester **C. E. Flensborg** in charge of the summers. They dug **8,600 holes in 1902** and planted about **8,000 rowan** the next summer. Frost killed nearly all of it, and the fence never held — a newspaper in **1918** grumbled that the livestock *gengur þar inn og út*, in and out as they pleased. Only after the Second World War, with close to **60,000 plants**, did it finally take. The oldest mountain pines by the lake are now **over a hundred years old.** (How do you find your way out of an Icelandic forest? Stand up. This is where somebody first set out to ruin that joke, and they have been at it for a hundred and twenty-four years.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: **Ari the Wise** wrote in *Íslendingabók* that at settlement Iceland was *viði vaxið milli fjalls og fjöru* — wooded from the mountains to the shore. Today woodland covers about **1.5%** of the country.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: Behind the cones lies **Elliðavatn**, and on a low spit in it, **Þingnes**: **16–17 surface ruins, at least 18 structures**, and two nested circles nobody has ever pinned a function on. The state registers it as *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður*, the ancient Kjalarnes assembly place — **signed 25 October 1930, entered 16 November 1938.** Whether it really is the þing **Ari fróði** put on **Kjalarnes**, fourteen kilometres that way, has never been proven by anybody.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: And the electricity arc closes here: the **Elliðaár** valley below held **Reykjavík's first power station, opened in 1921** — seventeen years after **Reykdal's carpentry-shop plant** lit the nation's first bulbs in Hafnarfjörður.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: **Langjökull** means **"Long Glacier"** — Icelandic place-naming at its most ruthlessly literal, like nicknaming a tall bloke "Tall Man." It's **Iceland's second-largest ice cap** (after Vatnajökull): roughly **870–900 km²**, about **50 km long, up to 20 km wide**, holding on the order of **190 km³ of ice** up to **~580 m thick** and topping out just over **1,400 metres**. You'll be snowmobiling on more frozen water than most countries own.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: **Fire directly under the ice:** this isn't just frozen scenery — it's a **lid on two active volcanic systems**, **Prestahnúkur** and **Hveravellir**. The calm white surface you're carving across has a temper it simply hasn't used lately.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: **The waterworks of the whole Golden Circle:** Langjökull's meltwater feeds the **Hvítá** — the river that becomes **Gullfoss** — plus the **Ölfusá** system, and, via groundwater filtered through porous lava, the eerily clear **Silfra** fissure back at Þingvellir. Everything wet you've seen today drained off the glacier under your skis.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: **The timer:** Langjökull has been **losing mass steadily for decades**, and Institute of Earth Sciences modelling projects it could be **largely gone within about 150 years** on present warming — the fastest-shrinking of Iceland's big caps. Snowmobiling here is less "extreme sport," more "**visiting a patient you'll outlive.**"
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: For the fully indoors version, the **"Into the Glacier"** ice tunnel — the world's largest man-made bore into a glacier, **~500 m** long, opened **1 June 2015** from the Húsafell side — lets you walk *inside* Langjökull past ice older than the settlement of Iceland. A museum you have to dig.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: A "secret" lagoon that's **135 years old** and printed on every Golden Circle coach map. Some secret. It's the **oldest swimming pool in Iceland** — and the spot where the whole country first learned not to drown.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin

en: **Gamla Laugin** ("the Old Pool") at **Hverahólmi** by Flúðir was **built in 1891** — **Iceland's oldest surviving swimming pool**, older than the national grid, the republic, and your great-grandparents. The "Secret Lagoon" branding was bolted on 120-odd years later; the water never went anywhere.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin

en: Before it was a pool it was a **parliament**: the local Flúðir assembly met on this exact patch until **1894**. Iceland's founding instinct, again — find a warm bit of ground and hold a vote on it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin

en: In **1909** it hosted **Iceland's first formal swimming lessons** — **32 men** in the debut course, girls following by **1911** — and taught the district every summer until **1947**. In a country ringed by a lethal North Atlantic, teaching the nation to swim in a hot bath was a genuinely brilliant life-hack.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin

en: Then it was **abandoned for nearly 70 years** — the village built a modern pool and left the old one to the algae. Scrubbed up and reborn on **7 June 2014**, history intact.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin

en: The water sits at **38–40°C year-round**, sulphur-rich, kept topped up **100% by the surrounding hot springs** — including a **baby geyser, Litli Geysir**, that fires every few minutes just off the deck. The one hot tub on Earth plumbed straight into a working geyser.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin

en: The Lid On The City's Hot Water
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan

en: That dome is a **lid.** Under it sit **six steel tanks**, each **ten metres tall and twenty-three across**, each holding about **four million litres** of water at **eighty degrees** — so Reykjavík can run a bath at seven in the morning.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan

en: **Öskjuhlíð** is **61 metres** high and made of **Reykjavíkurgrágrýti** — grey basalt erupted from Mosfellsheiði late in the Ice Age, then scraped smooth by glaciers. About **ten thousand years ago it was an island.** The old shoreline round here sits **42 metres** above today's sea.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan

en: From **1913** they blasted the north face out and ran it down to the harbour on a **purpose-built railway** — one of the very few stretches of railway Iceland has ever had. **The stone became the harbour. The hole became the bowling alley.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan

en: The **Allies took this hill in 1940** and built all over it once the airfield went into Vatnsmýri in **1941.** It is now **the best-preserved military ground in Reykjavík** — pillboxes, command bunkers, trenches, blast walls, and the floors of hundreds of Nissen huts still in the trees.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan

en: The first hot-water tank went up in **1940**, more followed, two more in **1966**, and the lot was **demolished in 1986 to 87** and rebuilt. **Perlan** went on top — architect **Ingimundur Sveinsson**, opened **21 June 1991.** The steel frame does two jobs: it ties the tanks together and it is the dome.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan

en: The wood is deliberate. Planting started **after about 1950** on a council scheme, and the tallest conifers now clear **15 metres** — birch, mountain pine, Sitka spruce, Alaska poplar. In a country with almost no forest, somebody had to decide to put one here.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan

en: Why The Main Shopping Street Is Called Laundry Road
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar

en: Reykjavík's main shopping street is called **Laugavegur.** Everyone translates it as something romantic. It means **the road out to the washing pools** — and they are in that valley, and this is the road.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar

en: Out there are the **Þvottalaugarnar**, hot springs the town did its laundry in. First written down in **1672** by the physician **Þorkell Arngrímsson Vídalín**, who reckoned the water healed people. **By about 1830 nearly every household in Reykjavík was using them.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar

en: Women carried the washing out, boiled it, beat it, and carried it home wet. The town council finally voted in **1885** to build them a proper road, and it was laid in **1886.** That road is **Laugavegur.** By **1900** it was the most populous street in town with over **700 residents** — a laundry track that turned into the high street.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar

en: The name runs the other way from what people assume. The **pool** is the oldest name. **Laugardalur**, **Laugarnes**, **Laugalækur**, **Laugavegur** — all of them are named after the *laug*, not the other way about.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar

en: In **1928** they drilled the first borehole beside the pools and got **87 degree** water. In **1930** they ran a **three kilometre pipe** from there to **Austurbæjarskóli** — **Iceland's first municipal district heating.** By **1937** it warmed 58 houses.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar

en: **The same year the pipe was switched on, 1930, the laundry stopped.** The springs did not run out. They got promoted. There is a sculpture in the valley, **Þvottakonan** by **Ásmundur Sveinsson**, 1958, for the women who made the walk.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar

en: To joggers it's a postcard. To a geologist, it's a **crime scene** — ten thousand years of Iceland trying, and failing, to stay quiet.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur

en: The whole valley was redesigned when **Leiti** erupted. The crater is **Leitin**, east of **Bláfjöll**, the lava is **Leitahraun**, and it is a textbook **helluhraun** — the smooth, ropy kind you can walk on. It poured down here, hit the river and **split it in two**. Before, one river. After, two.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur

en: How long ago? Somebody dug the answer out of this valley: a radiocarbon date on **birch charcoal found underneath the lava, right here in Elliðaárdalur**, gives **about 4,600 years**. Other estimates for the same lava run up to about 5,300 — the same spread of dates that the **Rauðhólar** craters have, and for a very good reason. **Rauðhólar sit in this lava.** Same eruption, different souvenir.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur

en: Every waterfall in the valley is the river's four-and-a-half-thousand-year project to saw back down through that basalt to the sea. It is not finished.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur

en: The **Elliðaá** is one of very few **capital-city rivers anywhere with a wild Atlantic salmon run** — and there is a camera counter in it, so this is a counted number, not a boast. **1,533 fish in 2009**; **1,067 in 2003**. If you have heard "two and a half thousand salmon", that number is real but it is the wrong animal: **2,500 is a batch of smolts**, not returning adults.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur

en: Reykjavík was so taken with the river it **bought the whole thing in 1906**. Your city buys parks. We bought a river. The power station, **Elliðaárstöð, was switched on on 27 June 1921** and is still down there humming.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur

en: One kilometre of this valley has hosted a **1750s wool mill**, a **drowning pool at Skötufoss** for women convicted of "moral crimes", outlaws living in the lava tubes, **British WWII Quonset huts**, and a century-old hydro plant. And most Icelandically of all, a **burst pipe in 1998** flooded the place and washed **ten thousand years of buried history back into daylight in a single weekend.** Even the plumbing does archaeology here.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur

en: The Mountain Named After A Slave
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell

en: There is a mountain out that window **named after a slave** — and the naming is recorded in Iceland's founding text itself.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell

en: **Landnámabók** puts it in seven words: ***"við hann er kennt Vífilsfell"*** — the mountain is named for him. **Vífill** was one of **Ingólfur Arnarson's** two slaves, sent along the coast to hunt for his high-seat pillars. **Ingólfur gave Vífill his freedom.** The other one, **Karli**, said they had crossed good country only to settle an outlying headland, and walked off. **Only Vífill was freed** — and only Vífill got a mountain.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell

en: It is **655 metres**, the highest ground in Kópavogur. And that shelf halfway up is the interesting part.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell

en: **It is two mountains stacked.** The shelf is a **stapi** — a tuya — móberg built under ice and then capped with lava once the eruption melted through and the meltwater could no longer reach the vent. **The summit above it is a second, younger móberg mountain sitting on top of the first**, from a separate eruption in **probably a different ice age.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell

en: Up ahead we cross **Iceland's longest river** — a **230 km** glacial spine that the settlers argued beside and engineers turned into the country's biggest battery.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá

en: **Þjórsá** runs **230 km** to the sea, **Iceland's longest river**, draining a **7,530 km²** catchment. And it does not start where almost everyone says it does: it begins up in **Þjórsárdrög on northern Sprengisandur**, where the headstream carries the lovely name **Bergvatnskvísl**. The Hofsjökull line you will hear is a muddle — Hofsjökull and Vatnajökull feed the *catchment* that the power stations run on, which is not the same as the river's source.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá

en: By the time it reaches **Urriðafoss**, just below the bridge, it is moving about **360 cubic metres a second**. Not a river you paddle absent-mindedly.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá

en: **Urriðafoss** is **Iceland's most voluminous waterfall** — *vatnsmesti foss*, the one with the greatest average flow. It is not the tallest and it is not the most powerful; **Dettifoss** up north is the *aflmesti*, the most powerful. The two get swapped so reliably that the University of Iceland has had to correct it in print. Low, wide and unphotogenic beats tall and famous, if the metric is water.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá

en: Every winter the river builds an ice jam here with its own name, the **Urriðafosshrönn** — ice and slush packing in until Iceland's most voluminous waterfall is simply not visible, buried under its own river. Landsvirkjun surveyed it in the winter of 2002–03; the numbers are in their report and not in my mouth.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá

en: It does more electrical work than any river in Iceland. The classic cascade on the **Þjórsá–Tungnaá** system is **six stations** — Búrfell, Sultartangi, Hrauneyjafoss, Vatnsfell, Sigalda and Búðarháls, the last of those only since **2014**. Landsvirkjun now counts **seven**, because Búrfell got a second station, and the proposed **Hvammur** would be the eighth. The original **Búrfell came online on 16 September 1969**, and the reason a country of 380,000 people generates this much electricity is spelled **aluminium**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá

en: People have wanted **Urriðafoss** itself since **1927**, when the poet **Einar Benediktsson's** company **Titan** was granted permission for a **160,000-horsepower** station here and never turned a sod. The modern version is **Urriðafossvirkjun** — **140 MW**, about **1,037 GWh a year** — and on **17 February 2026** Alþingi left it in **biðflokkur**, the hold category, with the committee specifically recommending against moving it to the use category. A hundred years of wanting, and the river is still winning on points.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá

en: Midstream sits the island of **Árnes**, and the district is still called **Árnessýsla** after an assembly nobody can now locate. Alþingi's own research material says the scholars are split: **no assembly booths have ever been identified on the island**, while **thirty to forty** booth-like structures are recorded at **Búði**, on the north bank, where a spring assembly serving **three goðorð** ran until **963**. A whole county named after a meeting, and we have lost the room.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá

en: About the name. **Landnámabók** says the settler **Þórarinn Þorkelsson** sailed into the mouth with a **bull's head on his prow**, giving *Þjórsá*, the bull river — **Árnastofnun** records the traditional reading as **Bolafljót**. But **Þórhallur Vilmundarson** argued the original was ***Þjótsá***, from the verb for roaring, pointing at the farm on the bank still called **Þjótandi**, "the one that roars". A river named either for a cow's head or for the noise it makes. Iceland has never settled it.

en: Carved into the soft sandstone beside the **Ytri-Rangá** is a cluster of **man-made caves**, some with simple **crosses** and **stone benches** cut into the wall.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🕳️ Hella

en: A popular theory ties them to the **Papar** — the Irish monks that **Íslendingabók** and **Landnámabók** both say were in Iceland *before* the Norse, and who left the moment longships appeared. Tempting. But honestly: the dating is **disputed**, and **no archaeology has confirmed a pre-Norse origin** for these caves. Treat it as suggestive, not settled. The caves are real, the crosses are real, the monks are a maybe.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🕳️ Hella

en: The town itself is a newcomer by comparison. **Hella dates from 1927**, when a trader who had been working out of **Rauðalækur** bought a small plot out of the land of the farm **Helluvað**, right by the bridge over the Ytri-Rangá, and opened a general store — and a slaughterhouse. Nothing anchors a settlement like being able to buy your groceries and butcher your lamb in one stop.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🕳️ Hella

en: And the farm's name is the town's name. **Helluvað** gave **Hella** — so a place famous for holes in the rock is named after the flat slab of rock at the ford.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🕳️ Hella

en: In **2022** this river was **the top-producing salmon fishery in the whole of Iceland** — **5,112 fish.** And before the 1970s it had **essentially no salmon in it at all.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss

en: The **Ytri-Rangá** is a **60 km spring-fed river** rising in Rangárbotnar north of Hekla, running at about **50 cubic metres a second** and barely changing — the springs come out at **4 to 6 degrees** all year, so it does not flood in summer and it does not freeze.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss

en: **And that is exactly why it had no salmon.** The bed is too fine, the water too cold, and salmon fry could never get a grip. **These were trout rivers.** Then people started releasing smolts by the hundred thousand.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss

en: In **1982** they cut a **fish ladder** into this waterfall, and another into Árbæjarfoss upstream in **1985.** Both carry **fish counters**, and the one here is the river's census point. In **2024** it logged **6,400 salmon** going up, from which the river reckoned about **twelve thousand** came in off the sea.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss

en: The state fisheries institute is careful enough about it that **when it publishes Iceland's wild salmon figure, it subtracts these rivers first.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss

en: The falls also mark a line in the ground. The old **interglacial shield lavas** that make up all the flat farmland north of here **stop right at Ægissíðufoss.** Everything past it is younger.
