en: What did a "McMansion" look like for a powerful Icelandic chieftain **800 years ago**? It came with **its own escape tunnel**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏡 Keldur

en: **Keldur** is, in *Morgunblaðið*'s exact formulation, **the oldest turf farm in the country — and part of it is the oldest house in the country.** Not the oldest ruin. The oldest house. The National Museum traces the hall to the **late 1100s**, framed while the sagas were still being lived rather than written, and **Bautasteinn** calls it the largest preserved turf farm in the whole south.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏡 Keldur

en: It was a seat of the **Oddaverjar**, the clan the sagas call the **"Kings of the South"**, and it stands square in **Njáls saga** country — its first inhabitant, **Ingjaldur Höskuldsson**, is named in the saga itself.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏡 Keldur

en: The thick turf walls were not decoration, they were **climate technology**: keeping people, animals and food alive through long wet winters on an island with almost no timber to spare.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏡 Keldur

en: And then the good bit. A hidden **underground tunnel** runs from the hall down toward a stream. **Matthías Þórðarson published it in 1932** under the title *Forn jarðgöng fundin á Keldum* — "ancient tunnel found at Keldur" — and archaeologists went back to it again in **1998**. It is not romantic and it is not a secret passage for lovers. It is an **escape route**, in case somebody came in the night to **burn the house down with everyone asleep inside**. In this neighbourhood that was not paranoia. Ask Njáll.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏡 Keldur

en: Here is a detail worth the bus's time: the man who dug that tunnel out, **Matthías Þórðarson**, also spent years digging at **Bergþórshvoll**, looking for the burning itself. One archaeologist, two ends of the same story — the fire, and the way out of it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏡 Keldur

en: You cannot see any of this from the road. Keldur sits about **eleven kilometres inland up road 264**, behind a ridge, which is precisely why it survived. It is owned by **Þjóðminjasafn Íslands** and open to visitors from **1 June to 31 August** — and it is still a working farm, with a farmer living on it.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur / 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur

en: **Hvolsvöllur** is the last full-service fuel stop before Vík, planted in the heart of **Brennu-Njáls saga** country — Iceland's **longest, bloodiest, most carefully built** family saga. The farms and low hills around you are its stage.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur / 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur

en: Written **late in the 1200s** but set around **the year 1000**, its set-piece is the **brenna** — the burning of **Njáll**, his wife **Bergþóra** and their sons at **Bergþórshvoll**, on the flat land just east of here, which the saga's own chronology puts around **1011**. *Game of Thrones*, except half the cast also had to be home for the haymaking.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur / 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur

en: And here is the part that makes it more than a story. **People went and dug it up.** **Sigurður Vigfússon** excavated Bergþórshvoll in **1883 and 1885**; the national antiquarian **Matthías Þórðarson** went back in **1927**, again in **1931**, and the work ran on to **1951** — seventy years of Icelanders looking for one fire. **They did find a burnt layer**, right at the bottom of the occupation deposits, from buildings that had plainly burned, its edges curled up against the walls. What nobody has ever been able to say is that it was **his** fire.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur / 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur

en: Odder still: **Bergþórshvoll is not in Landnámabók at all** — it was not a settlement farm. But Landnáma **twice mentions Njáll's burning as something everybody already knew about.** The event outran the address.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur / 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur

en: In town: the **Saga Centre**, with a **replica Viking hall**, a model of **Þingvellir around the year 1000**, and the long **Njáls saga tapestry**, stitched by locals and visitors — a medieval soap opera in coloured thread, still being sewn.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur / 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur

en: Next door, the **LAVA Centre** opened in **2017**, and it was put here on purpose: it sits between **four active volcanic systems** — Hekla, Katla, Eyjafjallajökull and the Westman Islands, all inside 50 km — with a live seismograph reading the ground under your feet. A museum wired to the next eruption.

en: Puffins, Ports and Plumes

en: In **1973** a brand-new volcano opened at the edge of a working fishing town — and the town **fought it with a fire hose and a dredger, and ended up with a better harbour than it started with.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar

en: **Just before two in the morning on 23 January 1973**, a fissure tore open on the eastern side of **Heimaey**. Icelandic accounts give it as **1,600 metres with 30 to 40 vents**; the **USGS** says it opened to about **two kilometres, right across the island from shore to shore**, with submarine activity at both ends. Out of it came a volcano that had not existed the day before: **Eldfell**, "Fire Mountain", which grew to roughly the height of **Helgafell** standing next to it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar

en: **The town was 5,273 people** — that is the census count of **1 December 1972**, seven weeks earlier. **Nearly all of them were off the island and safely on the mainland within six hours.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar

en: **The reason it worked is that the fishing fleet was in port.** Iceland has **no army**; the evacuation was run by the people who happened to own boats. The explanation everybody gives — **including me** — is that a storm the day before had kept the fleet in. Be straight about it: **the fleet being in port is documented; the storm is the story that goes with it.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar

en: **It did not stop for five and a half months.** The eruption **was not declared over until 3 July 1973.** For the whole of that spring Heimaey was a disaster zone, a building site and an active volcano at the same time, and people went to work in it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar

en: **The damage, counted by early May:** about **300 buildings engulfed by lava or gutted by fire**, and another **60 to 70 homes buried completely by tephra**. Iceland's own Pompeii — and some of those houses have since been **dug back out** and left open at the **Eldheimar** museum.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar

en: **Then the part nobody believes.** On **6 February** the **Vestmannaeyjar fire brigade** started spraying seawater at the lava front with hoses — about **100 litres a second**, which against a lava flow is a rounding error. On **1 March** the dredger **Sandey** arrived with **56-centimetre steel pipe** and pushed about **400 litres a second**. American equipment landed on **26 March**. By the time the pumps stopped on **10 July** they had put roughly **eight million cubic yards of North Atlantic seawater** onto the flow, through **43 pumps** and **more than nineteen miles — thirty kilometres — of pipe, three-quarters of it plastic.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar

en: **And it worked.** The tongue of lava that had almost closed the harbour entrance **stopped where they cooled it**, and the USGS is blunt about what happened next: it **is now acting as a breakwater, protecting the harbour from storms.** The volcano tried to shut the port. The port came out **better sheltered than before.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar

en: The lava and tephra also added **nearly a square mile** of new ground — **about 20% more island** than they started with.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar

en: **On the deaths, be straight, because it is genuinely contested.** **Icelandic institutional sources record no deaths from the eruption.** **The USGS records one fatality — a man overcome by gas inside a building** — with several others partially affected. Those two accounts have **never been reconciled**, and I am not going to reconcile them for you out of a bus window. What I will say is that **the lurid version some guides tell, a looter overcome in a pharmacy basement, is not documented in any source I would stand behind.** A town of **5,273** got out from under an erupting fissure with, at the very most, one death. **That is the fact. It does not need decorating.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar

en: Today **4,518 people** live out there — **1 January 2026** — and the ferry from **Landeyjahöfn**, open since the summer of **2010**, takes **just over thirty minutes**, against **three hours** by the old route.

en: The **Markarfljót** in front of you rises under **Torfajökull**, up in the highlands — not off the two ice caps everyone assumes. *Heima er bezt* puts it at about **75 km** from source to sea. Then again, ask how long it is and you have picked a fight: it is a **braided** river, and Iceland's national map data carries **190 separate channels** all called Markarfljót, adding up to well over 200 km of water. It does not have a course. It has a committee.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi

en: What **Eyjafjallajökull** and **Mýrdalsjökull** do is feed it lower down — two ice caps sitting on live volcanoes — which is why it occasionally stops being a river and becomes a **jökulhlaup**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi

en: **2010, and the bit everybody gets wrong.** You will hear that engineers deliberately cut the Ring Road embankment to save the bridge. What *Morgunblaðið* reported at the time is better: **the swollen river broke its own gap** in the flood dyke east of Markarfljót, and that is what took the load off the bridge. The deliberate version is a real Icelandic technique — at **Skeiðará in 1996** they cut **five gaps** in the embankment and planned to cut the road itself in two places — but here, the river did its own engineering and the engineers let it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi

en: Tucked into the far slopes is **Hlíðarendi**, home of **Gunnar**, the finest fighter in **Njáls saga** — the saga claims he could leap his own height in full armour, backwards as well as forwards, which is the kind of thing sagas claim.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi

en: Sentenced to exile, Gunnar rode out, glanced back and said the line every Icelander knows: ***"Fögur er hlíðin"*** — fair is the hillside — and I will not go away. That one look cost him everything. He turned back, stayed, and was killed defending his farm.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi

en: And the ending is worse than that. Besieged, his bowstring cut, he asked his wife **Hallgerður** for two locks of her hair to twist a new one. She refused — payback for a slap years before — and let him die. A thousand years on, it is still the most quoted argument in Icelandic literature.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi

en: We've barely left town and we've already **driven off the map** — this flat land used to be the **bottom of the Atlantic Ocean**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains

en: It looks like "just flat fields", but you are crossing a giant **flood-deposit fan**, built grain by grain by glacial rivers charging out of the highlands — chiefly the **Markarfljót**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains

en: The name gives it away. **Landeyjar means "land islands"** — the grassy patches that stood up out of the marsh and sand back when the water still owned everything around them. Waves once rolled over where this road runs, and the sea came right up to that **cliff line** inland. Then the land rose, the rivers kept dumping sand, and the coastline **marched south, kilometre by kilometre**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains

en: So the cliffs you can see used to be beach, and the beach is now several kilometres further out. Iceland does not have a coastline so much as a rolling negotiation.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains

en: This "empty" plain is also **Njáls saga's stage**. **Bergþórshvoll** — where Njáll and his family were burned alive, around **1011** in the saga's own reckoning — sits out here among the hayfields. Flat, quiet, and a thousand years ago the address of Iceland's most famous house fire. People have dug for it, more than once, and found a burnt layer.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains

en: The Cloud That Stopped Europe
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: In **2010**, this innocent-looking glacier volcano shut down **air travel for millions** who couldn't even say its name.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: It does not look like much: a tidy white lid over green fields. **Veðurstofa Íslands** describes what is actually under there — a cone **about 1,666 metres** high, the volcano itself **25 km long and 15 km wide**, mostly buried in ice, with a **crater about 2.5 km across**. It has been a fairly active volcano for the last **8,000 years**, and its magma runs **all the way from basalt to rhyolite** — which is exactly why it can produce fine, glassy ash instead of tidy lava.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: By volcanic standards **2010 was small**: a **VEI 4**, only about **0.27 km³** of ash. But it fired a **plume 8–9 km high** straight into the **jet stream**, and those glassy particles turn jet engines into **expensive sandblasters**. A small volcano in exactly the wrong place, pointing at exactly the wrong wind.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: The result was the **worst aviation shutdown in Europe since the Second World War** — **104,000 flights cancelled over eight days, 15 to 22 April**, about **48% of expected European traffic**, roughly **10 million passengers** who simply could not fly, and the airspace of some **20 countries** closed. Europe discovered that volcanoes do not read timetables.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: The first hit, though, was local. As meltwater poured off the ice, **500 to 800 people were evacuated overnight** from the farms below, and the ash fell thick enough to turn day into night. At **Þorvaldseyri**, right at the foot, they **milked the cows in respirator masks** and scraped ash off the roofs — and then built a visitor centre, because if a volcano is going to rewrite your year you may as well sell the story back.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: And the question every single group asks: **did it set off Katla next door?** Here is the honest answer. The two sit **25 km apart**. Eyjafjallajökull erupted in **1821–1823**, in **1612–1613** and **probably in 920**, and you will very often hear that Katla followed each time — but **Veðurstofa's own page lists those eruptions and does not make that claim**. What is certain is that in **2010 Katla stayed shut**. Treat this mountain as a warning light, not a trigger.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: A rock that **forgot to leave** when the rest of the mountain eroded away — and became a barn, a film set, and an elf hotel.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn

en: **Drangurinn** stands alone in the field like a stubborn leftover: a block of **móberg**, palagonite tuff, the same subglacial-eruption rock that built **Pétursey** further along this coast, left standing when the softer cliff around it weathered away. It is about **300 metres from the farmhouse**, in the home field of **Drangshlíð**, under the **Eyjafjöll** cliffs — which is why it looks dropped there rather than grown there.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn

en: The saga version is more fun. **Grettir the Strong**, Iceland's great troublemaking outlaw, is said to have torn it out of the cliff above and thrown it down here, leaving a notch in the ridge behind. Once you have heard that, the notch stops looking like erosion and starts looking like a **missing tooth**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn

en: Locals did not waste a rock this size. They **built turf barns and cowsheds straight up against it**, and the folklore — **Jón Árnason's** collection — says **elves live inside**, that they quietly mind the farmers' cows, and that at calving time they will even **milk them**. The most useful neighbours in Iceland, if you believe it, and rent-free stabling if you do not.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn

en: Here is the part that should make the coach laugh: **people have been stopping for this rock for a century.** *Lesbók Morgunblaðsins*, in **1928**, wrote that few things catch a passing traveller's eye like the Drangur at Drangshlíð. Ninety-odd years of buses slowing down for the same stone, and it has not moved an inch.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn

en: It later turned up as a location in the Viking film ***Hrafninn flýgur*** — "When the Raven Flies". Even the movies knew a dramatic rock when they saw one.

en: The Living Climate Graph
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull

en: This is where the glacier stops being "a nice view from the bus" and turns into a **giant, melting history book.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull

en: A gravel path pulls you toward **Sólheimajökull**, an outlet tongue of **Mýrdalsjökull** — Iceland's **fourth-largest ice cap**, and the lid on **Katla**. You are standing on the drainpipe of a buried volcano.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull

en: Up close the ice isn't white. It's streaked with **black ash bands** from **Katla** and **Eyjafjallajökull**, like a sooty paintbrush dragged across it. Each dark line is a bad year for somebody's washing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull

en: In front sits a **blue-green lagoon** with small icebergs in it. The colour is **glacial flour** — rock ground so fine the water turns to liquid stone-dust. That lagoon is **new**. It is here because the ice is not.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull

en: Here is the part nobody makes up, because it is measured. **Somebody has walked out to this ice with a tape measure every year since 1930**, and the numbers are public. Over that whole record the front has pulled back **just under two kilometres — 1,995 metres.** Over the last ten years it has averaged **about 50 metres a year**; the most recent measured year, **2023 to 2024, was 43 metres.** The worst single year on record is **134 metres**, and it has happened **twice** — in **2007–08** and again in **2017–18**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull

en: And here is the bit that gets left out. **It is not a straight line down.** Between **1969 and 1995 this glacier ADVANCED in 23 years out of 29**, putting on **440 metres** — a quarter of a century of growing, in the middle of the record. That is why the measurements matter more than the slogan: real data has a reversal in it, and it still ends where this one ends.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull

en: Signs along the path mark where the front used to reach — "here… and here… and here." You have just walked **decades of retreat in a few minutes**, and the walk keeps getting longer.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull

en: The Ghost in the Sand
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck

en: Somewhere out there in the black void is a silver ghost that **Justin Bieber made world-famous** — and that half the internet gets the name of wrong.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck

en: Everyone calls it a "DC-3". It isn't. It is a **US Navy Super DC-3 — a Douglas R4D-8 / C-117D** — same family, the cousin who went to the gym. It has worn the wrong name for fifty years and has long since stopped correcting anybody.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck

en: On **21 November 1973** it was flying **Höfn to Keflavík** when **ice choked both carburettors** over the **Vatnajökull** ice cap and both engines quit. The tourist version — that it "ran out of fuel" — is wrong. It iced up, and became, in the crew's own description, a massively overweight glider.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck

en: The pilot turned **south for the coast** and put it down on the black sand. **All seven crew walked away.** The Navy stripped out the useful parts and left the bare hull sitting there, which is how you end up with an aeroplane as a landmark.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck

en: For decades it was a quiet local curiosity. Then came a **Bieber video in 2015**, the Bollywood hit *Dilwale*, and Instagram, and that was that. **Cars were banned in 2016**, so now you walk a **4 km track each way** across old ocean floor in order to touch a plane with no wings.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck

en: ⚠️ And that walk deserves respect. **Eight kilometres round trip across open sandur with no shelter of any kind** — not a tree, not a rock, not a wall — and no vehicle coming to get you. The weather out there can change while you are still walking out. It is a proper expedition dressed up as a photo stop.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck

en: The Island That Got Left Behind
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey

en: A **288-metre lump of frozen explosion** that used to be a real island — submarine volcano, sailors' landmark, and a cave with a chapel, a shieling and a monster in it. **Most mountains never have a CV that long.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey

en: **Pétursey** is **móberg** — the ash-and-rubble palagonite rock you get when a volcano **erupts under water or ice**. Hot magma met cold sea, shattered mid-blast, and cemented into these steep walls. Same recipe as nearby **Drangurinn**. **Landmælingar Íslands** puts the summit crags at **288 metres**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey

en: It was not always a mountain in a field. **Its old name was Háey — "the high island"** — and Iceland's national place-name record says so outright: *Pétursey var nefnd Háey eða Eyjan há í gömlum ritum.* The Atlantic really did go all the way round it, and sailors steered by it, until **Katla's black sand filled the gap and stranded it inland.** The island is still here. The sea moved out.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey

en: At the foot on the north side is **Eyjarhellir**, a cave big enough to echo, and the official place-name record for it reads like a short story. There are **ancient man-made marks** inside. Its side chamber is called **Stúkan** — the chapel stall — and was held to be **an old chapel**, until a landslide closed the door on it. **Loðmundur**, the settler at Sólheimar, is said to have kept his **shieling** in there. And the record ends by wondering whether **papar** — Irish monks, here before the Norse — lived in it, and whether the marks in Stúkan are theirs.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey

en: It also had a tenant nobody wanted. An **óvættur**, a malevolent thing, lived in Eyjarhellir and was seen before **blizzards and fatal accidents**. It was last seen around **1900**, in the shape of a dog that **grew until it was a troll reaching halfway up the mountain.** Horses refused to pass the cave mouth. A second-sighted farmer named **Indriði** reckoned the creature spent its time fighting the **water-demon of Klifandi** — and that this was the only reason Klifandi had not washed Pétursey's fields away. Which it has, partly, anyway. Even the monster was only doing an adequate job.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey

en: The name travelled. A line-fishing boat called **Pétursey** was lost in **March 1941** on passage to Scotland, and was reported sunk. This coast names its boats after its landmarks, and the war took some of them back.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey

en: The cliffs still work as a **seabird colony** — fulmars and **puffins** wheeling round it as though it never stopped being an island. Two farms sit at the base: **Eystri-** and **Vestri-Pétursey.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey

en: The Architect's Roots
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja

en: This tiny country church is the **DNA** of some of Iceland's most famous modern buildings.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja

en: This modest church was built by the master carpenter **Samúel Jónsson** — by all accounts a prolific and well-respected house-builder — one of those simple, sturdy rural churches put up to shrug off wind, rain and ash.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja

en: His son, **Guðjón Samúelsson**, was born **16 April 1887** and became **húsameistari ríkisins**, the state architect, **from 1915 until he died on 25 April 1950**. Thirty-five years designing the country. The University of Iceland made him an **honorary doctor of philosophy in June 1940**, which is not a thing that usually happens to carpenters' sons from Mýrdalur.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja

en: His **Hallgrímskirkja** — the basalt-column church on the Reykjavík hill — took **forty-one years to build** and was **consecrated in 1986**. Guðjón had been dead for **thirty-six** of those years. He drew the most recognisable building in Iceland and never saw it standing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja

en: Look at this roof, then picture that one. You can feel these small rural churches — built plain, built to last, built for weather — echoing in the capital's skyline. Iceland's grandest church is a farm chapel that went to architecture school.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja

en: The Door Hole
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey

en: Ahead on the right is the **front door of the South Coast** — a headland with a hole so big a pilot once flew a plane **clean through it. Three times, because once is an accident.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey

en: **Dýrhólaey** means "door-hill island", and Iceland's own conservation service describes it precisely: a **120-metre móbergsstapi** — a tuff tuya — **formed in an eruption in the sea**, taking its name from the **arch rock** that from either side looks like an enormous doorway cut in a sheer cliff. Half of it is tuff, **Háey**; half is basalt, **Lágey**. And despite the *-ey*, the "island" on the end of its name, **it is firmly attached to the mainland.** It has been misnamed for a thousand years and nobody has bothered to fix it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey

en: Sailors were less romantic. They called the hole **Portlandið** — or just **Húllið**, the hull.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey

en: On top sits a castle-like lighthouse, one of the most powerful lights on this coast, **built in 1927**. It is there because this headland is the first thing a ship coming out of the Atlantic sees, and the last thing it wants to hit.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey

en: From up there you can read the whole **Katla Corridor** in one turn of the head — the sandur behind, the **Reynisdrangar** needles ahead, and the Atlantic hurling itself at the basalt. It is a **seabird city**: Dýrhólaey has been a **friðland — a protected nature reserve — since 1978**, all **1.51 km²** of it, and the official reason is not the view, it is the **birds**. Parts close in the nesting season for the puffins, there is a **ranger here all year**, and the rules are the birds' rules.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey

en: It was long called the **southernmost point of the mainland** — until **Katla's 1918 flood built Kötlutangi**, which took the title off it for several decades, before the sea carried that sand west again. The volcano moved the goalposts; the Atlantic moved them back.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey

en: And in **October 1993**, pilot **Arngrímur Jóhannsson** and MP **Árni Johnsen** flew a light aircraft through the arch. *Morgunblaðið* ran it as "the first aeroplane through Dyrhólaey". Three passes — because if you only do it once, people will say you meant to miss.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey

en: Black sand. A basalt pipe-organ. Sea stacks offshore. **Iceland's most beautiful beach — and its most dangerous. Never turn your back on these waves.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar

en: ⚠️ **Before anything else.** The Icelandic word is **laumualda** — a "sneaking wave". It runs far higher up the beach than the sea in front of you suggests, the water is freezing, and the undertow pulls. **At least five people have been killed by this surf since 2007**, the most recent of them reported in June 2022; a **warning-light system** went up that same summer. Stay high on the dry sand, keep off the wet, and do not turn your back on the water for a photograph. The beach takes about **half a million visitors a year** and has no opinion about any of them.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar

en: Under your feet: fine **black volcanic sand** — basalt that met the sea, shattered, and got ground down to grains. **No shells, no coral, just pulverised volcano.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar

en: To one side, **Hálsanefshellir** — the shallow cave with its pipe-organ wall of **hexagonal columns** under the **Garðar** cliff. That is **stuðlaberg**: lava that cooled so slowly it contracted and cracked into near-perfect six-sided pillars. Same trick as the Giant's Causeway, better acoustics.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar

en: Out in the surf stand the **Reynisdrangar** sea stacks, the last hard bones of an old headland the sea otherwise chewed away — the "stack" at the end of the crack-cave-arch-stack sequence, and you can see every stage of it from where you stand.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar

en: In the legend they are **two night-trolls and a ship**, caught by the sunrise mid-theft and turned to stone. Icelandic trolls are strictly nocturnal; daylight is their kryptonite. They have been standing there mid-heist for a few thousand years, which is the longest anyone has ever been caught in the act.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar

en: Above, the **Reynisfjall** cliffs fill with nesting seabirds in summer — **puffins, fulmars and guillemots**. Bring the zoom as well as the wide angle.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar

en: The biggest threat on the South Coast doesn't look like a threat — it's a **white ice cap, peaceful and silent.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: Under that ice sits **Katla**, and she is not a tidy cone. **Veðurstofa Íslands** puts the system at **about 80 km long**, reaching **around 1,500 m**, with an **ice-filled caldera** and fissure swarms running **northeast towards Síðujökull**. The caldera is not the neat ten-kilometre circle you will read online — that came from a proposed shape in a 1973 paper. The Icelandic geoscience journal **Jökull** describes something elongated, roughly **100 km²**. Either way: the mountain you cannot see is bigger than the mountains you can.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: The lid is **Mýrdalsjökull**, Iceland's **fourth-largest ice cap** — **520 km² when it was surveyed in 2019** — sitting on the furnace like several hundred metres of insulation. Being subglacial is the entire danger. She doesn't just throw ash; she **flash-melts a glacier into a flood.** Veðurstofa is blunt about it: without the ice on top, these would probably just be lava eruptions.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: She is the **fourth most active volcanic system in Iceland**, with **at least 21 eruptions in the last 1,100 years**. The last one to break through the ice was **1918**. From the settlement to 1918 the **average gap between eruptions was about 50 years**; Jökull's commonly cited range is **every 40 to 80**. It is now **108 years**. Do that sum on a bus and watch the faces change.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: An eruption under ice makes a **jökulhlaup**, and the estimates for Katla's peak discharge run to around **300,000 cubic metres a second** — an estimate, not a gauged reading, because nobody has ever stood downstream with a flow meter and lived to publish. Historically those floods came down **Mýrdalssandur**; in prehistory they also came down **Markarfljót**. The town of **Vík** has drilled for this for decades.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: **12 October 1918** is the date that rearranged the map. The flood carried so much sediment to the sea that it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km** — a saga headland that once stood by open water is now stranded **inland**. A volcano that does land reclamation.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: Even asleep she exhales. A **2018 study in Geophysical Research Letters** — Ilyinskaya and colleagues, flying instruments over the ice in **2016 and 2017** — measured **12 to 24 kilotonnes of CO₂ a day** coming off Katla, which would make her one of the largest measured carbon sources among the world's *non-erupting* volcanoes, perhaps **4% of the global total**. Nobody has repeated the measurement since, so treat it as a photograph of two summers, not a live feed.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: And the family has a bigger member. The **Eldgjá** eruption, on the same system's fissure swarm, **began around 939 CE** and produced **about 20 km³ of lava and tephra** — Veðurstofa's own figure. For scale, the **Holuhraun eruption of 2014–15**, which most of us watched on the news, made about **1.5 km³**. Eldgjá was over thirteen times that.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: Over this hill is Vík: one small village, **a lot of black sand**, and a volcano that once shoved the coastline forward like it was rearranging furniture.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal

en: Vík is Iceland's **southernmost mainland village**, strung along the beach with **Víkurkirkja** parked safely up on the hill — the official *run here if Katla wakes* point. There is **no natural harbour** anywhere along this coast, so historically this was a place you **rowed boats out through the surf from an open shore.** Yes. On purpose. For fish.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal

en: It is not the sleepy outpost it used to be. **740 people in the village and 1,004 in Mýrdalshreppur on 1 January 2026** — and the district was **451 in 2012**. It has **more than doubled in fourteen years**, which for an Icelandic village is a population explosion conducted entirely by tour bus.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal

en: Here is a thing worth getting right, because you will hear both numbers. Vík is, in **Veðurstofa's own wording, the warmest weather station in the country *ásamt Vestmannaeyjakaupstað*** — "along with Vestmannaeyjar". Over the standard period **1971–2000 its annual mean is 5.3 °C**. Over the station's **last two decades, 1991–2013, it is 5.9 °C**. Both figures are real; they are simply different slices of time, and the gap between them is the warming. Reykjavík did the same thing over the same window, **4.3 °C up to 5.1 °C**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal

en: "Warmest" is doing heroic work in that sentence, by the way. The warmest year in Vík's entire record is **6.7 °C, in 2003**, the coldest is **4.1 °C in 1979**, and the lowest temperature ever logged there is **−16.9 °C on 1 April 1968** — an April Fool's joke delivered with a thermometer.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal

en: It is also properly, professionally wet: **2,317 mm a year across 1971–2000**, against Reykjavík's **822 mm**. That is **2.8 times** the capital's rainfall, and Vík's own wettest year was **2,973 mm in 2007**. Still not the champion — **Kvísker**, out east under Öræfajökull, averages **3,457 mm** and took **4,630.4 mm in 2002**, with **293.3 mm falling in a single January day**. When Kvísker has a wet year, it does not do it quietly.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal

en: In **1918 Katla** erupted under the ice and sent a **jökulhlaup** to the sea so vast it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km**, burying everything under fresh sand. **Hjörleifshöfði** — a saga headland that once stood by open sea — is now stranded **inland**, the gap quietly filled by a century of Katla's black homework.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal

en: That massive rock is a **1,100-year-old crime scene** — and the address of Iceland's most famous ghost.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði

en: **Hjörleifshöfði** is a **222-metre móberg headland** — Landmælingar Íslands' own survey figure — named for **Hjörleifur Hróðmarsson**, sworn **blood-brother of Ingólfur Arnarson, Iceland's first settler**. The two sailed here together around **874** and then split. Ingólfur let the gods choose, following his high-seat pillars to Reykjavík. Hjörleifur, who **refused to sacrifice to any god at all**, parked at the first headland he came to. **His burial mound still crowns the summit.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði

en: Come the spring, says *Landnámabók*, he had **one ox** — so he had his **enslaved Irishmen drag the plough** instead. They killed the ox and **blamed a bear**. Iceland **has no bears.** The newcomers simply did not know that yet, and when they scattered across the sand to hunt an animal that does not exist here, the thralls **ambushed them one by one**, Hjörleifur included, and fled with the women and the boats to the islands offshore.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði

en: Ingólfur found the bodies, tracked the killers out to those islands and killed every one of them. *Landnámabók* has him stand over his blood-brother and say, in effect, that it is a sad end for a good man to die at the hands of slaves — and that this is what comes of refusing to sacrifice. Even the eulogy is a told-you-so.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði

en: And the islands kept the name. They are the **Vestmannaeyjar**, the **"Isles of the West Men"** — *vestmenn* being the Norse word for the **Gaels of Ireland and the Hebrides**. The archipelago out there is **named after the enslaved men who did the killing.** The postcard version of free, self-made Viking farmers is missing a chapter.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði

en: The ghost arrives **three centuries later**. **Katla**, a fearsome housekeeper at the nearby monastery of **Þykkvabæjarklaustur**, owned **a pair of breeches that never tired**. The shepherd **Barði** borrowed them; she **drowned him in the whey vat**. As the whey sank and the body came closer to showing, she walked out onto **Mýrdalsjökull** and threw herself into the chasm still called **Kötlugjá — "Katla's rift"**. Soon afterwards a **flood burst out of the ice**. **The volcano is named after her**, and every eruption since has been blamed on her temper.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði

en: Like Pétursey back down the road, this cape **was once an island** — now tethered to Iceland by miles of Katla's black sand. At its foot sits **Kötluklettur**, "Katla's Rock", in case anyone was in danger of forgetting whose neighbourhood this is.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði

en: The waterfall that **looks like a fantasy backdrop** and sounds like someone left a giant tap on **since the Ice Age**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss

en: The **Skógá** river skips the rapids and walks straight off the old sea-cliff — **about 60 metres down and 25 metres wide** — free-falling into a deep pool before racing across the sandur to the Atlantic. At the base you have to **shout to be heard**, which is why most videos from here are people silently pointing at it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss

en: This cliff is the **coastline of thousands of years ago**, and it is textbook waterfall geology: hard cap-rock over soft, undercut until it collapses, so the fall eats its way **upstream** and leaves a gorge behind it. Then the land lifted, the rivers dumped black sand, and the real shore marched several kilometres south. **Skógafoss never moved. The sea did.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss

en: The metal staircase on the right is your free fitness test. At the top begins the **Fimmvörðuháls** trail, which climbs between **Eyjafjallajökull and Mýrdalsjökull** — the same gap the 2010 eruption cracked open to start with.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss

en: And there is treasure in it. **Landnámabók** names **Þrasi Þórólfsson inn gamli** as the settler at Skógar — folklore shifts him a little east to Þrasastaðir, so even his address is disputed — and the story says he hid a **chest of gold behind the falls**. Someone eventually got a hand to it, hooked the **iron ring** on the chest, and pulled. The ring came off. The chest did not. That is the whole legend and it is, frankly, the most Icelandic ending available.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss

en: **Seljalandsfoss** drops off Iceland's old sea-cliff, fed by the **Seljalandsá** running down off **Eyjafjallajökull**. *Morgunblaðið* puts it at **62 metres**; you will also see 60 quoted. What nobody mentions is that it is the **first and lowest fall on the river** — there are more of them upstream, and not one coach stops for any of them.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Seljalandsfoss / 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi

en: A natural recess lets you walk **all the way behind the curtain** in summer. Wet, slippery rock, so: good boots, a waterproof, and **one hand free**. In ice the path closes, and the barrier means it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Seljalandsfoss / 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi

en: The cliff itself is an **old sea cliff from just after the Ice Age**, when the Atlantic came right to the foot of the **Eyjafjöll**. Rivers then filled the lowlands and the coast is now several kilometres south — the same drowned-then-stranded shoreline as Skógafoss down the road. **The sea left. The waterfalls stayed.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Seljalandsfoss / 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi

en: A short walk north, **Gljúfrabúi** — "the canyon-dweller" — hides in a narrow mossy gorge with only its top showing. It is on a different river: the **Gljúfurá**, also called **Hamragarðaá**, which runs down beside the Seljalandsá. To meet it you **wade up the stream**, and **wet feet are non-negotiable**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Seljalandsfoss / 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi

en: **Rútshellir** is one of the **largest man-made caves in Iceland** — an arched hall roughly **20 m long and 2.5 m high**, hacked from the soft cliff of **Drangshlíðarfjall**, about **3 km west of Skógafoss.** Long claimed as Iceland's **oldest surviving man-made dwelling.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Skógafoss / Rútshellir

en: The legend: a brute named **Rútur** — troll, looter or bad chieftain, take your pick — lived here, and his **slaves carved a hole under his sleeping ledge and speared him from below** as he slept. Even dead he terrified them: one killer, **Björn**, bolted to the mountain **Bjarnarfell**, which still carries his name.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Skógafoss / Rútshellir

en: It's in the record, not just the poetry — logged in **Árni Magnússon's land register (1714)** and the travel book of **1756**. A **cross carved in the ceiling** has people guessing at Irish monks before the Norse — unproven, so serve it as “some think.”
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Skógafoss / Rútshellir

en: Weirdest chapter: in **1936 Himmler's Ahnenerbe** — the SS pseudo-science unit — searched here convinced they'd find an ancient Nordic temple. They found a barn.

en: **Laufskálavarða** is a low **lava ridge on the east edge of Mýrdalssandur**, by the river **Kúðafljót** — carpeted in **stone cairns.** The custom: anyone crossing this deadly black desert **for the first time** piled a cairn for a **safe journey**, and centuries of first-timers built the field you see.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Laufskálavarða

en: The danger was real — **Mýrdalssandur is Katla's flood path**, swept by **jökulhlaups** without warning, so a little supernatural insurance made sense.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Laufskálavarða

en: The name comes from **Laufskálar**, a big settlement-era farm here — tradition gives it **24 doors on iron hinges** — buried by **an early Katla eruption.** (You'll see a “894” date on the signs; the maths doesn't work, so just call it an early Katla eruption.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Laufskálavarða

en: Don't add to it: visitors are now **asked not to build new cairns** — the field is protected heritage, not a DIY project.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Laufskálavarða

en: The Fires of 1783
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: That soft green moss you can't stop photographing? It's the lid on the **deadliest eruption in Iceland's history** — the one that nearly ended the country.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: In **June 1783** the **Lakagígar** fissure tore open — a **27 km rift of more than 140 vents** — and erupted for **eight months** (the **Skaftáreldar**, “Skaftá Fires”), laying down **14.7 km³ of lava across ~600 km².** That makes it **the second-largest lava flood in historical time, behind Eldgjá** and its **~20 km³** — larger still, but **8,700 years before anyone was here to see it**, is **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**. You're driving across the runner-up.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: And yet the lava barely killed anyone — the **gas** did. The fissure breathed out **~122 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide** plus a fluorine fog that poisoned the grass, and the famine that followed has a name of its own: the **Móðuharðindin, “Mist Hardships.”** The haze even crossed **Europe**, wrecking harvests as far as France.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: The green fuzz is **grámosi**, woolly fringe moss — **decades to grow, one boot-print to wreck.** Admire it through the window.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: The **Skaftáreldar** began on **8 June 1783** and did not stop until **7 February 1784** — eight months to the day, near enough.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: It did not spread politely across country, it went down the rivers: on **11 June** the **Skaftá** simply stopped, and on **3 August** the **Hverfisfljót** went the same way. Two rivers deleted, by something arriving down their own beds.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: Landgræðslan measures that moss mat at an average **38 centimetres** thick, which is also why nothing else grows here — **well over two centuries on**, vascular plants are still sparse, because the mat smothers seeds before they germinate.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: The arithmetic of the **Móðuharðindin**: roughly **10,000 dead — about a fifth of all Icelanders** — the population down from just under **50,000** to just under **40,000** by the end of **1786**, with **smallpox** taking another **1,500** and **earthquakes in August 1784** flattening about **400 farms**.

en: The haze formed a continuous cloud across the whole northern hemisphere, **30 to 90 degrees of latitude**, depositing **over a tonne of sulphuric acid per square kilometre**. Europe called it the dry fog and spent that summer wondering where it came from.

en: The national figure hides the local one. **Vatnajökulsþjóðgarður** puts the livestock loss at **around three quarters of every animal in the country** — and in the worst-hit districts, the ones we have just driven through, **about 40% of the people died.** (One in five is the headline. en: Tradition (via *Landnámabók*) says the **Papar** — Irish monks — were here **before the Norse**, and the ground was so blessed no heathen could settle. In **1186** the Benedictines made it official: **Kirkjubæjar convent**, a nunnery that ran until the **Reformation in 1550.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: The place-names still gossip about the nuns: **Systrafoss** (“the sisters' falls”), lake **Systravatn**, and **Systrastapi** — the rock where, the darker tale goes, two sisters were burned for sin and only later cleared.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: Nearby is **Kirkjugólf**, the “church floor”: a patch of **columnar basalt** worn flat so it looks like a tiled cathedral floor. Nobody laid it — **the volcano did the tiling.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: And this is where **Rev. Jón Steingrímsson** delivered his **Eldmessa — the “Fire Sermon” — on 20 July 1783**, preaching as the Laki lava bore down. It halted at the edge of the parish. He kept preaching.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: The convent was founded by **Þorlákur helgi**, Bishop of Skálholt and later Iceland's patron saint, and its first abbess was **Halldóra**, about whom the record says almost nothing at all.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: Behind the two-sisters legend sits one documented case: in **1343** a nun of this house — the sources cannot agree whether **Katrín or Kristín** — was **burned at the stake** for heresy and for having given herself to the devil in writing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: She is an outlier twice over. Iceland's actual burning age was the **17th century** — the **first burning for witchcraft** was **1625** and the last **1685** — and of roughly **25 Icelanders** ever burned about **23** were for witchcraft and the overwhelming majority were **men**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: **Kirkjugólf** is not weathered flat, it is decapitated — *jökul- og brimsorfið stuðlaberg*, columns planed off by a glacier and scoured by the sea. Protected **náttúruvætti since 1987**, with a **10-metre** exclusion zone and a **50-metre** buffer, so walk to it and do not stand on it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: **Séra Jón Steingrímsson**, **1728–1791**, is the **eldklerkur**, the fire priest, and the reason we know any of this in detail — he wrote the eruption down almost day by day. He also buried a great many of the parish he had held together, once the famine arrived.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: Two footnotes the story usually loses. The charges against the nun in **1343** were not only heresy and having given herself to the devil in writing — she was also accused of having **misused the body of Christ.** And what the ground shows at the Fire Sermon is a lava front that **stalled**, held up by the terrain and by its own cooling crust. Both things are true at once, and Icelanders have never felt any pressing need to choose between them.

en: **Fjaðrárgljúfur** (“feather-river canyon”) is **about 1.5 km long and up to 100 m deep** — those are the figures in its own protection order — a snaking gorge with mossy green **palagonite (móberg)** walls.

en: Two ages, don't mix them up: the **rock is about 2 million years old** (Ice-Age palagonite), but the **cutting began about 10,000 years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age**, when meltwater from a retreating glacier sawed straight down through the soft rock — **and it is still going on today.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Fjaðrárgljúfur

en: The **Fjaðrá** river still does the digging, one grain at a time. That serpentine shape is just water taking the lazy route — and turning it into art.

en: In **2015 Justin Bieber** filmed *I'll Show You* wading through it; Instagram did the rest. So many boots trampled the moss that the site now **closes periodically to recover.** Two million years of rock, nearly worn flat by one music video.

en: It is not finished. The protection notice states plainly that the cutting **is still ongoing**, and **100 metres** in **10,000 years** works out at roughly **a centimetre a year** — a hundred metres of rock removed at about the rate your fingernails grow.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Fjaðrárgljúfur

en: “Closes periodically” has hard dates. It shut in **February 2019** for waterlogged ground and reopened **31 May 2019**; then the notice went out on **5 April 2023** and the gate shut the next morning, at **09:00 on 6 April 2023**, under the emergency power in **Article 25a of the Nature Conservation Act no. 60/2013**, reopening **20 April 2023** after two weeks of gravel being carried in and laid. That gravel is what you are standing on.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Fjaðrárgljúfur

en: It was finally protected on **11 May 2024** by **Auglýsing nr. 555/2024**, covering **0.15 km²** — **fifteen hectares**. A patch you could walk across in ten minutes needed a legal instrument of its own.

en: That wall is **Lómagnúpur**, and it comes up before the sandur does: **Núpsstaður at route km 263.1, Lómagnúpur at 265.5**, both on the **left, north of the road**, while **Skeiðarársandur proper does not begin until km 268.6.** In **chapter 133 of Brennu-Njáls saga** the cliff swings open like a door and a man in a goatskin cloak walks out with an iron staff, names **Flosi's** men one by one, calls himself **Járngrímur**, and says he is bound for the **Alþingi** to clear the juries, then the courts, then the battlefield.

en: The dream at **Lómagnúpur** is a death list, read out in order. **Járngrímur** names **Grímur the Red**, **Árni Kolsson**, **Eyjólfur Bölverksson**, **Ljótur son of Hallur of Síða**, the **Sigfússynir**, then **Lambi**, **Móðólfur** and **Glúmur**, and last of all **Gunnar Lambason** and **Kolur Þorsteinsson.** Flosi had been shaken awake at **Svínafell** by **Glúmur Hildisson** and told the whole thing to **Ketill úr Mörk** — whose reading took one word, *feigir*, doomed, and whose advice took one sentence. Tell nobody.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Lómagnúpur & Núpsstaður

en: Tucked under that cliff at **Núpsstaður** is a **bænhús**, a one-farm prayer house — a timber box **6.15 by 2.50 metres** inside a turf shell, **no pulpit, no font, unpainted throughout**, church dated **1657** and the standing timber to about **1850**. It has been in the care of **Þjóðminjasafn Íslands since 1930.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Lómagnúpur & Núpsstaður

en: The paperwork on the **Núpsstaður bænhús** is the best of it. **Minjastofnun** lists it as a **friðlýst kirkja** with the designer recorded, with admirable Icelandic honesty, as **Ókunnur** — unknown. The turf shell is **about 9 m long and 7.5 m wide**; side walls and the back of the chancel are **stacked turf and stone up to window height**, and the roof is **krossreist** and laid with turf. Inside: a **flagstone floor** in the nave with a bench along each wall, a chancel raised **two steps**, an altar under a small window, and **no altar rail.**

en: **Skeiðarársandur** runs to **about 760 km² on Náttúrufræðistofnun's register — one of the great sandur plains anywhere**: black sand and braided rivers, dumped grain by grain by the glaciers pouring off **Vatnajökull.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: For centuries this was **the gap in the ring**: unbridgeable rivers that could flood without warning. The **Ring Road (Route 1) wasn't finished until 1974**, when the Skeiðará bridge finally welded the country into one loop.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: Then on **4 November 1996** the **Gjálp/Grímsvötn** eruption melted the ice cap and loosed a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood — peaking near **40,000–50,000 m³ a second, briefly rivalling the Amazon.** It **tore a 24-metre section out of Skeiðarárbrú**, twisting steel girders like wire.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: Those **mangled girders now stand as a roadside monument** — Iceland's polite way of saying “we rebuilt it, but don't get comfortable.”
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: The piece that closed the loop was **Skeiðarárbrú**, started **1972** and finished in **July 1974** at **904 metres** — the **longest bridge in Iceland**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: For scale on **1996**: the **Ölfusá at Selfoss** averages **400 cubic metres a second**, so the flood was running at roughly **125 times** that, carrying icebergs the size of vans. Total damage came in around **1.5 billion krónur** at 2007 prices.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: Rebuilding was quick and quietly humiliating: the span went back up at **880 metres** instead of **904**, and in **2017** it was retired altogether — the national record went backwards to **Borgarfjarðarbrúin at 520 metres**, because the river the big one was built for wandered off. (A national record trimmed by a river that could not be bothered to use the bridge.)

en: The measured sequence for **Vatnajökull itself** is brutal: **8,723 km² around 1890**, **8,087 km² in 2000**, **7,745 km² in 2014**. And for **all of Iceland's glaciers together** — not just this one — the cover has gone from **12% of the country 130 years ago to about 10% by 2014**, thinning by roughly **a metre a year.**

en: Icelandic research puts the endpoint plainly — on current trends the country's glaciers will be **largely gone within two centuries**. The tongues along this road have already pulled back **around 4 kilometres** since measurements began in the **1930s**.

en: **Öræfajökull** in **1362** produced the **largest explosive eruption in Iceland's recorded history** — about **10 cubic kilometres** of tephra, ash on roughly **75%** of the country, **30 to 40 centimetres** deep locally, out of a caldera of **about 12 km²**. It has erupted once since, in **1727**.

en: Before **1362** the glacier was **Knappafellsjökull** and the district was **Litla-Hérað**, the Little District. en: Everything you will ever read says this church was built in **1884.** Both the bodies that actually own and protect it — **Þjóðminjasafn Íslands** and **Minjastofnun** — say the build ran **1883 to 1885.** The joiner was **Páll Pálsson** from **Hörgsdalur.** So it is not a Viking church, it is Victorian, and it is younger than the Eiffel Tower.

en: Look at how it is put together, because it is three different buildings at once: a **timber frame** inside, **long walls of stacked stone with no mortar**, and a roof of **stone slabs with turf laid over the top.** Most turf buildings are turf walls. en: That is the pattern along this whole coast, and it is worth naming: people here do not abandon a place, they **move it upslope and carry on.**

en: The Country Doctor Who Worked Out How Glaciers Move

en: In **1794** a country doctor stood in front of a glacier tongue and worked out something nobody in Europe had: **glaciers flow.** They are not frozen still. **They move like something thick and half-melted** — and he was about a century early.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson

en: **Sveinn Pálsson**, **1762–1840.** He took a **natural-sciences degree in Copenhagen in the spring of 1791** — the first person in Denmark to sit that exam — and went home meaning to come back and finish the medical half. He never did finish it. He doctored anyway, for the rest of his life.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson

en: In **1799** a new medical district was created covering **Árnessýsla, Rangárvallasýsla, Vestur-Skaftafellssýsla and the Westman Islands.** He took it up in **1800**, moved to **Suður-Vík in Mýrdalur in 1809** — the village we are driving into — and stayed there until he died in **1840.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson

en: The glaciers were his own time, not the job. At **Kvíárjökull in 1794** he looked at the curved cracks running across the ice and wrote that it had moved *"hálfbráðinn eða sem þykkt seigfljótandi efni"* — **half-melted, like a thick viscous substance.** That is the modern answer: ice deforms under its own weight and creeps downhill.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson

en: Europe never got to read it. His ***Ferðabók*** and the glacier treatise ***Jöklaritið*** **stayed in manuscript and were not printed until 1945**, translated by **Jón Eyþórsson, Pálmi Hannesson and Steindór Steindórsson**; the English edition came in **2004.** By 1945 the credit for glacier flow had long gone elsewhere.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson

en: And be accurate about the one guides get wrong: **he was not Iceland's first doctor.** That was his father-in-law, **Bjarni Pálsson**, the first *landlæknir*. Sveinn stood in as acting *landlæknir* himself, briefly, in **1803–04.**

en: The numbers, because they're the whole show down here: **5,770 metres long** — roughly **63 blue whales stacked nose-to-tail**, because Iceland loves its whales — and **3,750 of them run under the sea**. Deepest point: **165 metres below sea level**, with up to **40 metres of water** over the roof. If you're claustrophobic, just pretend you're in a very damp IKEA car park.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🕳️ Hvalfjörður Tunnel

en: Blasting started from both ends in 1996, the crews met in the middle, and it opened *ahead of schedule* on **11 July 1998** — the same year *Titanic* won Best Picture. Coincidence? Probably. Cost: **4,630 million krónur** at 1996 prices… or one slightly used volcano.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🕳️ Hvalfjörður Tunnel

en: Before the tunnel, driving round the fjord took **an hour**. Now: about **7 minutes** — enough time to recite the Icelandic alphabet (*good luck*), explain why Björk's swan dress was *art*, and question your life choices as you descend into literal darkness. One single tube, by the way — because why build two when you can play chicken with oncoming traffic?
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🕳️ Hvalfjörður Tunnel

en: Designed for 5,000 vehicles a day; now about **8,800** use it like a drive-thru for fermented shark, and the toll went in **2018**. There's serious talk of a second tube — imagine two straws in a milkshake, but the milkshake is made of basalt.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🕳️ Hvalfjörður Tunnel

en: How does a fjord get named "Whale fjord"? Officially: whales. In the folklore: **one specific whale** — with a red head, a grudge, and a body count.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: The folklore — filed as folklore, from Jón Árnason's collection: a man refused to acknowledge his child by an elf-woman, and was turned into an evil whale with a red head — **Rauðhöfði**. He smashed **nineteen boats** before two priests conjured him up the fjord — thereafter **Hvalfjörður** — and into the lake above — thereafter **Hvalvatn**. Whale bones "are said" to have been found up there. *Said.*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: The waterfall he was forced up: **Glymur**, named for the din. **198 metres**, long held to be Iceland's highest — a rival was measured taller in 2011, never confirmed. Glymur is contesting the ruling.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: The island: **Geirshólmi**. Harðar saga puts **180 outlaws** on it, until the local farmers lured them ashore and killed them at **Þyrilsnes** — dated **986**. Hörður's wife **Helga** swam for it with her two boys; the sound is still called **Helgusund**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: The digging: **1881**, an archaeologist opens the grave-mound — *"nothing there."* The island: **no trace of any building**. A hundred and eighty men, zero evidence. The honest version — and the better story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: Then the 20th century: from **1940** the fjord hid Allied convoys — and Geirshólmi, island of outlaws, spent the war as a **gunnery target**. Aggro level: maximum. Postcard-serenity: also maximum. Very Hvalfjörður.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: A Whale Bone at 85 Metres, and Two Irish Brothers
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⛰️ Akrafjall

en: There is a **whale bone in that mountain, 85 metres above the sea**. Nobody carried it up there. The sea delivered.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⛰️ Akrafjall

en: Twelve to thirteen thousand years ago, in the **Bølling** warm spell, the land was still pressed flat under the weight of the ice sheet and the sea stood correspondingly high — high enough to cut a **wave-cut notch into Akrafjall at 105–125 metres** above today's sea level. And a **whale bone has been found at 85 metres** up the mountain. That's a beach line and its residents, parked the height of a church spire above the modern shore.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⛰️ Akrafjall

en: Same rock as Esja: the lavas here erupted between about **4.5 and 3 million years ago**, one continuous basalt sheet with the mountain across the water — until glaciers cut **Hvalfjörður out of the middle of it, 2.5–3 million years ago**. Esja and Akrafjall aren't neighbours; they're the two halves of the sandwich the ice ate.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⛰️ Akrafjall

en: Hidden bonus: the **Gilbert/Gauss magnetic reversal** — the Earth's field flipping over, **3.6 million years ago** — is recorded in the mountain at about **350 metres elevation**. A compass error, archived in basalt.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⛰️ Akrafjall

en: The people: written tradition — Landnámabók, so tradition, not archaeology — says that shortly after **880** two brothers came **from Ireland**: **Þormóður and Ketill, sons of Bresi**, Irish-born, Norwegian descent. They claimed all of Akranes and drove out the family already living there. Þormóður farmed at **Innri-Hólmur**, the last farm before the tunnel; where Ketill settled, the sources disagree — even Akranes's own town history says "uncertain." A thousand years on, and we still haven't sorted the brothers' addresses.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⛰️ Akrafjall

en: The clue they left is in the names: **Akranes, Akrafjall, Akrakot, Garðar** — a cluster of grain-field place names, cited as evidence the Irish brothers actually grew corn here. The map remembers the harvest.

en: The town in the saga is **Digranes**. **Skallagrímur** — Egill's father — took the land "between mountain and shore," named his farm **Borg** and the fjord **Borgarfjörður**; his man **Grani** got the land at Digranes and built **Granastaðir** — which, by the local reading, makes Grani's household the first inhabitants of what is now Borgarnes. Skallagrímur's own farm, **Borg á Mýrum**, is still there — church and farm, visible north-west of town. A settlement claim you can check from the car park.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes / 🪦 Borgarnes

en: **Kveldúlfur's coffin.** Egill's grandfather died at sea on the voyage out — and ordered his crew to put him overboard *in a coffin*, telling his son to settle wherever it washed ashore. They later found the cove where the coffin landed, carried it onto the ness, and piled stones over it. Local tradition points at **Kveldúlfshöfði**, just south of town — with the honest hedge that it's "not fully clear" where the coffin actually beached. Either way: this family's estate agent was a dead man in a floating box.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes / 🪦 Borgarnes

en: **Brák.** Skallagrímur, mid-berserk rage during a ball game, seized the boy Egill — and the woman who stepped in was Egill's foster-mother, **Þorgerður brák**. He chased her to the outer end of Digranes; she leapt from the cliff and swam for it; he hurled a great stone that struck her between the shoulders, "and neither came up again." The sound below the old town is still called **Brákarsund**. A servant woman, drowned a thousand years ago — and her name is on the water and half the street signs. Iceland picks its heroes carefully.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes / 🪦 Borgarnes

en: The town itself, in one breath: first house built **1857** by a Scot called **James Ritchie** — no relation, probably — for canning salmon; trading licence **1867** after 212 locals signed the petition. Population when Ritchie arrived: effectively zero. Now: the saga capital of the west.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes / 🪦 Borgarnes

en: **Skallagrímur's mound.** When his turn came, his body was taken out through a **hole broken in the house wall**, rowed out at high tide, and buried on the point of the ness **with his horse, his weapons and his smith's tools**. Years later Egill reopened the mound and laid his drowned son **Böðvar** beside him — the scene in the 1970 bronze relief in **Skallagrímsgarður**, two minutes' walk from here. The mound is a protected monument. It has been dug into, more than once. **Nothing — no bones, no artefacts — has ever been found in it.** That's the honest version, and it's a better story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes / 🪦 Borgarnes

en: If the graves whet the appetite: the **Settlement Centre** down by the harbour opened on **13 May 2006** and tells this exact saga. And one closing twist — **Snorri Sturluson**, the man widely believed to have *written* Egils saga, married the heiress of Borg and lived there from **1201**. The suspected author, living on the story's home farm. Write what you know.

en: Why does this peninsula have volcanoes at all? The plate boundary **left six million years ago** — packed up, moved to Reykjanes — and Snæfellsnes **kept erupting anyway**. Most recently in the **10th century**. Some things don't take the hint.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🌋 Iceland's First Rift Zone

en: The whole ridge ahead is **Iceland's first rift zone** — the original crack, running through Snæfellsnes and north into Húnaflói. It stopped rifting about **6 million years ago**, and the spreading jumped south-east to **Reykjanes**, where all the recent fireworks are.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🌋 Iceland's First Rift Zone

en: And then the peninsula ignored its own retirement. Volcanism restarted, and today Snæfellsnes carries **three volcanic systems**: **Ljósufjöll** in the east, little **Lýsuskarð** in the middle (**30 km by 5** — the runt of the litter), and **Snæfellsjökull** at the tip.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🌋 Iceland's First Rift Zone

en: The eastern system is a rebel twice over: nearly every Icelandic volcanic system runs SW–NE, but this one runs **SE–NW** — at right angles to the active rift's fissures. (Iceland's spatial planning, ladies and gentlemen.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🌋 Iceland's First Rift Zone

en: The last eruption in any of the three: **the 10th century**, in the Ljósufjöll system. That's Settlement-era — there were farmers here watching it.

en: The **Ljósufjöll system** runs nearly **90 km** WNW–ESE, and its lavas have travelled **at least 15 km** from the mountains — as far as the mouth of Hvammsfjörður on the far side. One system, most of the horizon.

en: The ridge itself is mostly **móberg** — hyaloclastite. During ice ages it erupted *under* the glacier and built ridges of consolidated volcanic glass; between ice ages the lavas ran down the valleys. Same volcano, two completely different products, depending on whether there was a lid on.

en: Some of it is uncomfortably fresh: **Hólmshraun** in Hítardalur may have flowed **shortly before the settlement**, and its dated neighbours run about **2,600** and **3,600 years old**. In geology terms, the paint's still wet.

en: Now the history. **1148**, Hítardalur, up that valley on the right: Bishop **Magnús Einarsson** of Skálholt was at a feast when the building burned. The annals put the toll at **roughly eighty people**, the bishop among them — the deadliest fire in Icelandic history, and it happened at dinner.

en: **Eldborg** is an oval crater, about **200 m long and 50 m deep**, sitting mid-lava **38 km north of Borgarnes**. It's the textbook shape for this system: eruptions here open on a short fissure, then focus down into one big dome-shaped crater. The fissure is the draft; the crater is the final edit.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🌋 Eldborg

en: The Environment Agency records **two eruptions** here — the later one "most likely during the Settlement Age." That's the official wording, and we'll keep it: the honest answer to "when exactly?" is that nobody's published a firm date. Possibly the first settlers got a show.

en: Its lava, **Eldborgarhraun**, covers about **32 km²**, and the crater rim reaches **100 m above sea level** — with birch woodland around the base, which is rarer in a lava field than you'd hope.

en: Nobody carved these columns. Cooling rock shrinks, shrinking rock cracks, and the hexagon wins because it's the roundest shape that still fills a plane with no gaps.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: It's the same maths as a beehive. The bees do it in wax in a summer; the basalt did it in stone over years — and neither of them ever took a geometry class.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg
