ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: Who stacked all those pillars? Nobody. That wall on the right did it to itself — and the reason it's **hexagons** is the same reason bees build hexagons: **geometry only offers so many options**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: **Gerðuberg** is a belt of columnar basalt — *stuðlaberg* — running between two farms, with the slopes below it coming right down to the road. The columns look quarried, dressed, and stacked by a contractor with a level. They weren't. No hands involved.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: Here's the mechanism, properly: basaltic melt is fully **solid at about 1,000 °C** — but it's still cooling after that, and cooling rock **contracts**. Shrinking solid rock has to crack. The cracks organise into columns, usually **six-sided**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: And they're hexagons because the hexagon is the shape **closest to a circle that still tiles a plane with no gaps**. Triangles and squares tile but aren't remotely circular; octagons are nicely round but leave gaps. The hexagon is the compromise candidate — and in geology, as in politics, the compromise candidate wins.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: The columns always grow **perpendicular to the cooling surface** — and up close they carry horizontal "chisel marks," **1–2 cm** per groove, each one a record of a single cracking increment. The rock kept its own worksheet.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: For a sense of the timescale: on Heimaey, a **40-metre-thick** lava took about **ten years** to cool and crack all the way through. A wall like this wasn't built in a day; it wasn't even *cooled* in a decade.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: As for how tall Gerðuberg is exactly — I'd love to give you a number, but there's no official measurement published, and on this bus we don't invent figures, we just point at the wall.

en: The Quiet Leg Over the Spine
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið

en: The road under you is exactly as old as **Wikipedia** — both launched in **2001** — and the flat-topped mountains beside it were built **under an ice sheet**. Brand-new tarmac, Ice Age scenery, no middle ground.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið

en: **Road 56 — Vatnaleið**, "the lakes route" — is very nearly the newest thing you will touch all day, and the Road Administration wrote the date down. **Friday 2 November 2001**: the transport minister **Sturla Böðvarsson** cut the ribbon, helped by the director of roads, **Helgi Hallgrímsson**. That same day the old **Kerlingarskarð** pass was retired after generations of hauling traffic over the peninsula's spine.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið

en: It was not a foregone conclusion either. Through **1999** there was a proper planning fight over whether to build this route at all or simply rebuild Kerlingarskarð, and it went as far as a **ruling from the planning authority**. Somebody won an argument, and the argument is the road you are sitting on.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið

en: The numbers are the point of it: **16.4 km** of new road topping out at **230 m**, against Kerlingarskarð's **311 m** — and only **3 km** of it above 200 metres, where the old road had **ten**. **We replaced the pass, not the mountains.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið

en: Those flat-topped mountains flanking the road are **móberg** — the fought-a-glacier-and-lost rock, now on both sides of you. The whole spine of Snæfellsnes is built of it, and the ice sheet that made it left ten thousand years ago and never came back for its work.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið

en: **Baulárvallavatn** sits just west of the road, one of the lakes that gave the route its name. And down in the bogs at the south end of **Sátudalur**, two streams rise almost side by side and then immediately fall out with each other: **Rauðusteinalækur** runs south into Baulárvallavatn and eventually reaches the sea as Straumfjarðará, while **Fossá** runs north. Same bog, opposite coasts.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið

en: The Waterfall Iceland Never Bothered to Name
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: Icelandic farmers named **everything**. Seventy-nine separate features on this one abandoned farm — every gully, every boulder, the rock where the hidden people sang. They did not name the waterfall. And the name on your map today? Somebody in tourism made it up.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: Start with the river, because the internet gets this wrong constantly. This is **Fossá** — literally *"waterfall river."* It is **not** Straumfjarðará. Straumfjarðará rises in Baulárvallavatn, back the way we came, and runs the opposite direction to the sea at Straumfjörður. Different river, different catchment, different ocean-facing coast.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: **Landmælingar Íslands**, the National Land Survey, has this fall in its database. Mapped, plotted, classified as *foss*. The name field is **blank**. Náttúrufræðistofnun holds the same point, also blank.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: So I went looking. **Zero** hits for "Selvallafoss" in Árnastofnun's national place-name archive. **Zero** in the national mapping database — the only "Selval-" name in the whole country is the lake. **Zero** across the entire Icelandic newspaper corpus, which runs back well over two hundred years. "Selvallavatn" gets 71 hits. The waterfall gets none.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: Meanwhile the place-name survey of the farm above us lists **Steinkarl**, **Nóngjá**, **Krummaklettar**, **Stóriklettur** — *"where the hidden people sang."* Seventy-nine names. They named a rock for its singing elves and left the waterfall alone.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: I think the old answer was just simpler than ours: the river was **already** called *the waterfall river*. Naming the waterfall on the waterfall river is like opening a restaurant called Restaurant.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: And no — **nobody has ever officially measured its height.** No figure in the national survey, none in the natural history institute, none in *Íslenskir fossar*, the standard reference on Icelandic waterfalls, which records two other falls in this district and skips this one. Every number you'll find online was typed by somebody with a website and a deadline. I'd rather give you nothing than give you a number I can't stand behind.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: One last thing while we're demolishing: **sel** does not mean sheep, and it does not mean seal. A *sel* is a **shieling** — the summer dairy station where the milking animals went up the valley. **Selvellir** means *"the shieling flats."* In the **1700s** the farm Horn was split in two, and the new half was built on Horn's old shieling ground. The farm went empty in the **1920s** and never came back.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: The Lake With No Way Out
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: Water pours into this lake all day long. **Nothing flows out of it.** Not a stream, not a trickle, nothing above ground. Somewhere under that lava the whole lake is quietly draining away — and nobody has ever proved where it goes.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: **Selvallavatn** sits at **62 metres** above sea level in a hollow between Berserkjahraun and the mountain wall. Fossá runs in on the east, small becks run in on the south. And that is the entire hydrological story, because there is **no outflow above ground.** None.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: The man who wrote down the place-names here was **Lárus Halldórsson**, born on the farm above us in **1920**. Going back over the survey he added a feature the earlier recorder had missed: **Rás** — a swallow-hole at the lava's edge *"where the water is sucked in a whirlpool down into the lava."* Then he added one careful sentence: **perhaps that is the answer to the riddle of Selvallavatn's outflow.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: *Perhaps.* He left it open. And as far as I can find, in the eighty-odd years since, **nobody has closed it.** No dye trace, no survey, no paper. A lake disappearing into a lava field, and the last word on it is a farmer's son saying "maybe."
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: It hasn't always been Selvallavatn either. The old name in the record is **Svínavatn** — *pig lake.* Less romantic, and it clearly lost the marketing meeting.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: There's **brown trout and Arctic charr** in it — the trout run a solid **three to six pounds**, and on summer evenings shoals of small charr work along the lava edge. In a dry spell the water level can drop by **a metre and a half**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: How big is it? Genuinely nobody agrees. The standard Icelandic reference says **0.85 km²**. The national mapping database maps the shoreline at **0.30 km²**. That is a factor of nearly three, on a lake you can see the whole of from here, and I am not going to pretend I can settle it. **Maximum depth: never surveyed at all.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: The lay-by you are standing on isn't an accident, by the way. When Vatnaleið was built, an **architect** was brought in to design this viewpoint — and in **2003** the whole road took **Vegagerðin's first-ever award** for construction and finish, with the jury singling out this spot. Congratulations. You are standing on an award-winning lay-by.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: The Severance Package Was a Bath
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🪨 Berserkjahraun

en: Iceland's first recorded construction contract: clear a road through this lava and marry the farmer's daughter. **The contractors finished the job. They should have read the fine print.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🪨 Berserkjahraun

en: Erupted about **4,000 years ago** from a row of **scoria cones of the Ljósufjöll volcanic system** — **Rauðakúla, Gráakúla, Smáhraunakúla and Kothraunskúla** — rough **aa lava** that crawled to the sea at **Bjarnarhöfn** and **Hraunsfjörður** and has been gathering moss ever since.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🪨 Berserkjahraun

en: **Eyrbyggja Saga** supplies the labour dispute: two **Swedish berserkers** were promised a farmer's daughter if they could clear a path through the lava. **They succeeded** — whereupon their master **Víga-Styrr** had them killed, **unarmed, in the bath**, and buried in the lava.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🪨 Berserkjahraun

en: The path — **Berserkjagata** — is **still clearly visible** a thousand years on, and there is a stone cairn beside it the saga calls their grave. Careful here: the antiquarian **Sigurður Vigfússon** only **examined** it (1889 survey, published **1893**), and a local farmer **re-stacked it** in the mid-20th century. **Minjastofnun records no excavation and no bones.** The road is the evidence. The grave is the story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🪨 Berserkjahraun

en: The Man Who Refused to Settle
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: The man who took that land was called **Björn the Easterner** — and he got the name because he **refused to settle in the west.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: *Landnámabók* is blunt about it. Björn, son of **Ketill flatnefur**, was driven off the family's Norwegian estates by **King Haraldur hárfagri**, went west over the sea, *"og vildi þar ekki staðfestast"* — **and would not settle there.** So they named him for the direction he wouldn't stop facing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: He took the land between **Hraunsfjörður** and **Stafá**, kept a magnificent household — and **died unbaptised**, the only one of Ketill's children who never took the faith. No churchyard: a heathen mound by **Borgarlækur**. When an archaeologist went looking for it in **1900**, he found the stream had eaten both the mound and the farm. Nothing left to look at.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: The genealogy is the gift: Björn → Óttar → Helgi → **Ósvífur hinn spaki** → **Guðrún Ósvífursdóttir**. **The most famous woman in the Icelandic sagas is his great-great-granddaughter.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: **The church is 1856–58** and is **the last of its kind standing.** One builder from Grundarfjörður put up three towered churches on this peninsula in the 1850s — Helgafell, Skarð and this one. **The other two are gone.** This one lost its tower around 1900 and survived precisely because nobody thought it worth replacing. Seven metres by four and a half, inside.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: And the shark. **Everything you have heard about how it is made is wrong.** The Greenland shark **has no urinary system**, so urea builds up in the flesh and breaks down to **ammonia** — that is the toxin. **Nobody urinates on it.** Vísindavefur calls that idea *"mikill misskilningur."* At Bjarnarhöfn it ferments **six to eight weeks in slatted wooden boxes**, then hangs **six to eight weeks more** in the drying shed. Not buried in gravel, not any more.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: In **2023 Matís** — the national food research institute — noted that **almost no scientific work had ever been done on how Icelanders make their national dish.** A thousand years of it, and the first proper study was a master's thesis, done with this farm.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: The Mountain You Walk Into When You Die
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: There is a mountain out there that people believed they went **into** when they died — and one autumn evening a shepherd stood on the hill and watched **the north side open up.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: **Þórólfur Mostrarskegg** held it so sacred that **no one was to look at it unwashed**, and nothing on it — beast or man — was to be harmed. *"Það var trúa þeirra Þórólfs frænda, að þeir dæi allir í fjallið"* — **he and his kin believed they would all die into the mountain.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: *Eyrbyggja saga*, chapter 11: a shepherd north of Helgafell **saw the mountain open**, saw great fires inside, and **heard Þorsteinn þorskabítur being welcomed in and told to sit in the high seat facing his father.** Next morning men rode in from Höskuldsey with the news. **Þorsteinn had drowned that day.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: **Snorri goði** — remember him — farmed there **thirty-one years**, and when he had a problem he walked up it: *"Þau ráð hafa síst að engu orðið er þar hafa ráðin verið"* — **"the plans laid up there have least often come to nothing."** It is where he and Víga-Styrr sat the day they decided what to do about the berserkers.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: He is also **the man who ended the argument at the conversion.** When a messenger reported lava flowing and the heathens cried that the gods were angry, Snorri asked: *"Um hvað reiddust goðin þá, er hér brann hraunið, er nú stöndum vér á?"* — **"What were the gods angry about, then, when the lava we are standing on was burning?"** That is *Kristni saga*, and it is the same man from this hillside.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: **Be careful with the three wishes.** Walk in silence from Guðrún's grave, don't look back, don't tell anyone — every guidebook prints it. **The earliest written record of it is 1955.** The Icelandic living-heritage register says so plainly. It is real folklore and it is **younger than rock and roll.** It appears nowhere in Eyrbyggja or Laxdæla.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: And the grave itself: the State's own protection register calls it **"leiði Guðrúnar Ósvífursdóttur, svo nefnt"** — **the *so-called* grave.** The one man who dug there, **W. G. Collingwood in 1897**, never gave the lecture he promised and never handed the finds in. **Nobody actually knows where she lies.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: The herring came back after a long absence. They **began wintering in southern Breiðafjörður in 2006**, having been gone since roughly **1940**. By **2008** Hafrannsóknastofnun measured **800,000 to 900,000 tonnes** in the bay. **The day before it happened, close to 300,000 tonnes of live herring were sitting in this one fjord.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🌊 Kolgrafarfjörður

en: **13–14 December 2012: around 25–30,000 tonnes died.** Then **1 February 2013: another 22,000.** Cause — **oxygen depletion**. Prolonged calm, cold weather, and simply too much fish in too small a space. And once December's dead began to rot, **the decomposition ate the remaining oxygen**, which is why it happened again six weeks later.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🌊 Kolgrafarfjörður

en: **Now the correction, because everyone blames the bridge.** Verkfræðistofan Vatnaskil reported for Vegagerðin on **21 October 2015**: **the causeway was not the cause.** It may marginally worsen oxygen levels during a huge influx in bad conditions, but the effect is **negligible** against what the herring themselves did — and **worse conditions have occurred since with no die-off.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🌊 Kolgrafarfjörður

en: The aftermath was biblical. Thousands of tonnes of rotting fat coated the shore. Birds came in tens of thousands — gulls, shags, cormorants, gannets, eiders, ravens — **and a large part of Iceland's entire white-tailed eagle population.**

en: Keep the chronology straight, because guests always ask about burnings. Iceland's actual witch-hunt was the **17th century** — the first burning for witchcraft was **1625**, the last **1685.** Of roughly **25 Icelanders** ever burned, the overwhelming majority were **men.**

en: And the ending is *us*: **Snorri goði** sent a priest, yes — but the real remedy was a **door-court**. Every revenant formally **summoned, charged, tried and sentenced** at the door of the house. en: What's more dangerous than being the richest man in Iceland? **Standing between English merchants and their cod.** In 1467, right here, the King of Denmark's own governor found out.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: **Björn Þorleifsson the Rich** — head of the Skarð family, one of the wealthiest houses in Iceland — sailed for Copenhagen in **1456**, got seized by Scots at Orkney on the way, and came out of the whole mess ennobled: **King Christian I** gave him a coat of arms — a **white bear on a blue field** — and made him ***hirðstjóri***, governor of Iceland, **for life**. "For life" turned out to be the operative clause.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: In **1466** the king banned the English from trading in Iceland. The English ignored him — they had a trading post here and cod is cod. In **1467**, English merchants killed Björn at Rif. What he was doing here, nobody wrote down; later sources say his son had been seized and he came to free him. His death sat inside a real Anglo-Danish trade war, settled by treaty in **1473**. Icelandic historians file the whole era under *Ten Cod Wars, 1415–1976* — this was an early round.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: Now the folklore layer, and I'll label it: the **axe-mark on Björnssteinn**, the body **cut in seven pieces and sent to his widow in barrels**, and her answer — **"Do not weep for farmer Björn — gather men instead."** Every one of those details was **first written down more than a century after the event**, in the late 1500s, with what the scholars politely call a strong folk-tale colouring. The record gives us one line; folklore wrote the screenplay.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: His widow, **Ólöf the Rich Loftsdóttir**, needs no embroidery anyway: the king's own letter to the King of France calls her *mulier spectabilis* — "a distinguished woman." Royal correspondence rated her before the barrels ever entered the story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: This wetland holds **17,000 nests** of arctic tern — the **biggest single colony in Iceland**, by a distance, and big enough to qualify as **internationally important**. For scale: the runner-up colonies on this peninsula are Arnarstapi at **850** nests and Kvíabryggja at **500**. That's not first place. That's a different league.

en: The commute: some of these birds winter at the **edge of Antarctica** and fly here to breed — pole-ish to pole-ish, twice a year, every year, on a wingspan you could cover with a tea towel.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🐦 The Tern Capital

en: By **12 August** the breeding season is mostly done — which is the only reason we can stand this close in peace. In June, the *kría* runs an air force here, and trespassers get personally escorted out by the head. The rule stands anyway: **stay out of the marked colony area.** They've earned the fence.

en: One more thing about these particular birds — they weigh **about 110 grams** and they fly **pole to pole**. That commute is the longest migration of any animal on Earth, and it is being done by something lighter than a mobile phone.

en: On the hill: **Ingjaldshóll**. Church built **1903** — one of Iceland's oldest concrete churches — with tradition claiming the site back to the early 1300s. Also the farm where **Eggert Ólafsson** grew up, where the **1754 glacier climb** set out. Told you the name would come back.

en: The story you may have read: "Columbus wintered at Ingjaldshóll in 1477." What Columbus actually left us: one note — in February 1477 he sailed **"one hundred leagues beyond" Thule**. That's it. **He never said he went ashore**, and Iceland's own record is silent.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / ⛪ Hellissandur, Ingjaldshóll & the Columbus Story

en: Where the wintering story really comes from: **fiction** — a short story by the Danish author **Sophus Bauditz**, serialised in the emigrant paper *Heimskringla* in **Winnipeg from 1889**, then translated "back" into Icelandic. One scholar's verdict, and it's the phrase to keep: **"fiction historicized."** The parish-hall painting (1998) is a 20th-century picture of a 19th-century short story.

en: Time to meet the landlord of this whole coast. **Bárður Snæfellsás** — giants on his father's side, trolls in the family, raised by a creature living inside a mountain — and the first thing the saga has him do on arrival here is **take a bath**.

en: The saga gives Bárður a CV like no other settler's: his father **Dumbur** was descended from **giants**, with **troll stock** in the line; his mother **Mjöll** was human. Half-troll, half-giant, part human — the saga is genuinely specific about the mix, and so are we.

en: From age ten he was fostered by **Dofri**, a *bergbúi* — a mountain-dweller, a being that lives *in* the mountain — who taught him genealogy, fighting skill, and "magic and ancient lore." At thirteen he married Dofri's daughter. A conventional childhood, by the standards of nobody.

en: Arriving on Snæfellsnes, says the saga, he came to a pond, took off all his clothes and **washed at its edge** — and the pond is called **Bárðarlaug**, "Bárður's bath," to this day. en: Basalt columns are supposed to stand up straight. Half of the ones on this coast are **lying flat on their sides** — and the rock is following the rules by doing it.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🐦 The Arnarstapi Cliffs

en: The clefts along this shore are the **Stapagjár** — columnar basalt, *stuðlaberg*, running **both vertical and horizontal**. Same maths as Gerðuberg this morning — columns grow perpendicular to whatever cooled them — except half of these cooled sideways. Read the angle and the rock tells you which way the heat left.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🐦 The Arnarstapi Cliffs

en: The ledges hold about **10,000 pairs of kittiwakes** — just under **2% of Iceland's entire population** of the species — plus roughly **12,500 pairs of arctic terns**. Now the hard number: kittiwakes here **fell 55% in one year**, 2017 to 2018. Not "declining somewhat." Fifty-five per cent. Someone counted the nests, twice.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🐦 The Arnarstapi Cliffs

en: While you're walking, look **out**, not just down: **orcas, harbour porpoises and minke whales** are regularly seen off this coast. No promises — they haven't read the itinerary.

en: This little cove was once the **seat of government for western Iceland**. Then somebody took the government building apart, put it on a boat, and **shipped it away**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: Arnarstapi was one of the harbours of the **Danish monopoly trade** — the *einokunarverslun* — and the landing here was reckoned **one of the best "under the Glacier."** Where the trade sat, power sat: this became the residence of the **amtmaður**, the district governor.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: The house itself went up **1774–87**, built by the Royal Trading Company for its trade manager **Hans Hjaltalín** — one of the very few Icelanders ever to hold such a post under the monopoly. Trade was freed in **1787**, he bought the business and the house; he went bankrupt around **1820**; and from **1821** it housed the governor of the West Amt. One building, three careers.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: Then the move: in **1849–50** the house was **taken down and carried away by sea** to Vogur á Mýrum — and moved *again* around 1983, to Korpúlfsstaðir, for storage. (We don't demolish good timber. We forward it.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: What's left is what matters now: the small-boat harbour, **rebuilt in 2002**, is today **the only harbour on the whole south side of Snæfellsnes** — motorboats since about 1933, and it still fishes year-round. The governor left; the fish didn't.

en: How does a small parish on a lava field get its church back? One widow. **Steinunn Sveinsdóttir** filed the paperwork with the church authorities, put up her own money, and **rebuilt it herself** — and the black church on that lava is hers.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: The black church is **Búðakirkja**. First church on the site: **1703**, built by Bent Lárusson. The one you're looking at is the widow's: **Steinunn Sveinsdóttir** applied to the church authorities for permission, then led and paid for the rebuild herself — **rebuilt in the late 1840s, consecrated in 1851**. (The archives offer three build dates; the consecration is solid, so that's the one we stand on.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: Legend has it Bent Lárusson appeared to Steinunn **in a dream** and asked her to do it. That's the story as recorded — told as legend, kept as legend. She died a few years later and lies in this churchyard, gravestone still standing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: The church has been **legally protected since 1 January 1990**, was moved within the churchyard in one piece in **1984**, and today belongs to the National Museum. A museum piece that still holds services — Iceland doesn't really do "retired," see also: this entire peninsula.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: Under it, **Búðahraun**: lava from the **88 m** crater Búðaklettur, about **5,000–8,000 years old**, and its beach sand is **nearly pure olivine** — the lava carries yellow-green olivine crystals, and the sea has milled the rock down to its minerals. Green-gold sand, next to a black church.

en: The lava is also the county's botanical garden: **over 130 plant species**, including **11 of Iceland's 16 fern species**, in a nature reserve since **1977**. Somebody counted the ferns. Eleven. They're probably still out there, counting.

en: **03 · Ísland farsælda frón** — *Karlakór Reykjavíkur*. The melody Icelanders actually sing is the wrong one. Helgi Helgason's tune gets the credit — but the version everyone knows is centuries older, a Lydian-mode chant from medieval manuscripts that got married to Jónas Hallgrímsson's 1835 lyric long after the wedding bells. A 600-year-old tune wearing 19th-century words.

en: **06 · Æskuminning** — *Alfreð Clausen*. 1953. Iceland's first-ever ballad recorded with a full orchestra, Carl Billich on the baton. Walked it into the SKT dance-song competition the year before — and *lost*. The audience promptly overruled the judges and handed it the people's prize. Iceland figuring out who runs music: the people. Always the people.

en: **10 · Sveitin milli sanda** — *Elly Vilhjálms*. There are no lyrics. None. Elly sings the entire thing on one open vowel — wordless, weightless, pure *Aaaaaa*. It started life as the score to a 1962 Ósvaldur Knudsen documentary; Magnús Blöndal Jóhannsson never bothered to add words and nobody ever asked.

en: **11 · Vor í Vaglaskógi** — *Vilhjálmur Vilhjálmsson*. Akureyri, February 1966. Two lovers go camping in Vaglaskógur — a 300-hectare birch forest in Fnjóskadalur — and Iceland gets its forever-song. The hook line every Icelander mouths on first beat: *Draumar þess rætast, sem gistir Vaglaskóg* — “the dreams of those who sleep in Vaglaskógur come true.” Kaleo dragged it onto the global stage in 2016. The forest has not stopped collecting tourists since.

en: **13 · If you knew** — *Thor's Hammer*. Recorded on Parlophone — *the Beatles' label* — in London, 1966. The “Umbarumbamba” EP that houses it now goes for thousands at auction; among 60s garage-rock collectors it's the white whale, the holy grail, the EP they'll remortgage their flat for.

en: **14 · Tætum og tryllum** — *Stuðmenn*. From the soundtrack of *Með allt á hreinu* (1982) — Iceland's biggest film of all time. 120,000 tickets. In a country of 230,000. Half the country watched it. Half the dialogue was improvised on the day, and the rival on-screen girl-band “Gærurnar” was actually Grýlurnar (skip ahead to track 19) — meaning the battle of the bands was real on screen *and* in the bar afterwards.

The lyric is twelve seconds of pocket-sized natural history: a curlew on the marsh, a golden plover singing “bí-bí-bí,” and that's it — that's spring, officially clocked in by the *lóa*.

en: The pale flats are **Löngufjörur** — "the Long Beaches" — running from Hítarnes in the east all the way west to Búðir. en: **01 · Sofðu unga ástin mín** — *Hafdís Huld*. Heads up — Iceland's most beloved lullaby is, technically, *about infanticide*. The lyric is from Jóhann Sigurjónsson's 1911 play *Fjalla-Eyvindur*: outlaw's wife Halla sings it to her own baby seconds before throwing the child into a waterfall so she and her fugitive husband can keep running across the highlands. Icelandic parents have nonetheless been singing this to their toddlers ever since. Hafdís Huld cut this version on *Vögguvísur* (2012) at home — while pregnant with her own daughter Arabella. Sleep tight, kids.  [Lullaby thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **02 · Flight from the City** — *Jóhann Jóhannsson*. Opening track of *Orphée* (2016) — Jóhann's first solo album for Deutsche Grammophon, and the last solo album he ever made before he died in Berlin in February 2018. The whole record traces the Orpheus myth — death, rebirth, looking back — and was tied directly to his own move from Copenhagen to Berlin. *Flight from the City* is the literal opening of that journey out. Listen to it knowing he never made another.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **03 · Bambaló (feat. Steiney Sigurðardóttir)** — *Gabríel Ólafs*. Plot twist — that “traditional Icelandic lullaby” is actually an *Irish* folk tune that hitchhiked north centuries ago. The word *bambaló* is essentially Icelandic for “rock-a-bye.” Gabríel cut this version with cellist Steiney Sigurðardóttir for *Lullabies for Piano and Cello*. Iceland: still wearing imported clothes, still pulling it off.  [Lullaby thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **05 · Twice** — *Little Dragon*. The piano line you're hearing wasn't supposed to be a Little Dragon song. It was written for a *children's collage book*. Yukimi Nagano walked into the studio, heard drummer Erik Bodin's friend's kids'-book melody, and started scribbling lyrics on the spot. It became Little Dragon's debut single (2007) and got them signed to Peacefrog. Robert Glasper Experiment later covered it. Bedtime story to indie classic, in one studio drop-by.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **06 · Pretty Face** — *Sóley*. Track 2 of Sóley's 2011 debut *We Sink*. The lyric obsesses over the narrator's own reflection in someone else's eyes — validation, identity, choosing to disappear into a dream rather than stay. Listen for the eerie under-hum; that's the song quietly unraveling around you.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **07 · Tachylite** — *Elín Hall*. *Tachylite* is volcanic glass — basaltic lava that cooled too fast to crystallise. Elín Hall calls it “failed lava.” The song is a quiet tribute to her father — an **Icelandic geophysicist who works as a first responder during eruptions**. He runs *toward* the lava. She wrote a song called Failed Lava about him. Released January 2026.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **08 · Heimförin** — *Ásgeir*. *The Journey Home.* The lyrics are by **Ásgeir's dad** — Einar Georg Einarsson, a poet from the village of Laugarbakki — and most of the original Icelandic words on the 2012 debut *Dýrð í dauðaþögn* are his father's. A song called The Journey Home, written by Dad, set to music and sung by son. The album went on to become the best-selling Icelandic debut *of all time*. Family business.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **09 · In Too Deep** — *BRÍET*. Bríet's debut single — self-released in 2018 when she was eighteen. She set out to write a happy love song and changed direction mid-write; the girl in the song starts smiling and ends pulled under. The track that introduced her voice internationally.

en: **10 · Á Sama Tíma, Á Sama Stað** — *Friðrik Dór & Jón Jónsson*. The brothers Jónsson. (Yes — actual brothers.) The song was the official 2018 *Þjóðhátíðarlag* — the festival anthem of Þjóðhátíð on the Westman Islands, where every August Iceland packs into a lava-walled valley called Herjólfsdalur and sings whatever song the year's commissioned writer hands them. 2018: the brothers' turn. The country's biggest weekend, scored by two siblings sharing a mic.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **11 · Á Flug** — *Valdimar*. *In Flight.* Valdimar are from **Keflavík** — i.e. the literal airport town this coach just left. From their 2010 debut *Undraland*, released on Geimsteinn, the Keflavík label founded by Rúnar Júlíusson. A song about flight, made by guys you flew over.  [Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **12 · Tuna in a Can** — *Of Monsters and Men*. Yes — the song is actually about **canned tuna**. The image — *tuna in a can, sticky from the brine / I thought I'd gone bad, you thought I was fine* — is reportedly Nanna's nod to her **mum's tuna salad**. It became the visual anchor of the entire 2025 album *All Is Love and Pain in the Mouse Parade*; the cover is built around it as “a quilt of familial stories.” Best self-portrait-as-expired-canned-fish in modern indie pop.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **13 · Coming Home** — *Sjonni's Friends*. Sjonni Brink wrote the music. **His wife Þórunn Erna Clausen wrote the lyrics.** So in effect, this is her words sung back to her. He was due to perform it in Iceland's Eurovision semi-final on 29 January 2011 — and died of a brain aneurysm on **17 January 2011, age 36**. Twelve days before the show. Six of his musician friends formed *Vinir Sjonna* / Sjonni's Friends to perform it in his place at Eurovision in Düsseldorf, finishing 20th with 61 points. The song's message — *never know when your time's up, so live and love hard* — was written before he died. Then performed after.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **14 · Howls** — *Agent Fresco*. Track 6 of *Destrier* (2015) — the concept album frontman Arnór Dan Arnarson wrote after **two men attacked him late one night and left him with a broken eye socket and concussion**. The whole record is grief and adrenaline. *Howls* sits at the nostalgic end — *howls of youth, when life would run with lawless legs to race the sun* — the memory of pre-violence freedom the rest of the album is trying to claw back. (A *destrier* is the medieval warhorse bred for battle.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **15 · Fröken Reykjavík** — *Ríó Tríó / Stórsveit Reykjavíkur*. Music by **Jón Múli Árnason**, lyrics by his brother **Jónas** — the Árnason brothers wrote dozens of Iceland's most-loved mid-century standards together. For seventy-odd years nobody knew who the red-shoed woman walking down Austurstræti actually *was*. Mystery solved in 2023 — director Björn Brynjúlfur Björnsson revealed in *Vísir* that she was his mother, **Jóna Sigurjónsdóttir**. Reykjavík kept its secret for seven decades. Then it broke.  [Family wrote it]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **16 · Jungle Drum** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Co-written with producer Dan Carey, released as a single in March 2009. The “ay-ay-ay” scat hook took it to **No. 1 in Germany, Austria and Belgium** — Torrini's biggest chart hit by a country mile — *after* it got used in the *Germany's Next Topmodel* finale. German rockabilly band The Baseballs covered it the same year. The whole lyric is a heartbeat-as-tribal-drum metaphor. Sometimes a giant pop hit really is just *ay-ay-ay*.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **17 · Mr. Jinx** — *Quarashi*. The earworm hook is sampled from a 1973 American soul cut — **New York City's “Sanity”** — laundered through Reykjavík rap. The song itself never blew up on charts (peaked No. 43 on Radio & Records Alternative). But its second life was sync money — scoring trailers and incidental music for *Alias*, *Smallville*, NBA on TNT (2003–2005), and Madden NFL 2003. Their other *Jinx* track “Stick 'Em Up” snagged the *2 Fast 2 Furious* trailer. Iceland's quiet sync goldmine.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **18 · Takk fyrir mig** — *Ingó Veðurguð*. The last word of the day, and it was written for a party that never happened. This was **Þjóðhátíðarlagið 2020** — the official song of Vestmannaeyjar’s Þjóðhátíð, the biggest weekend in the Icelandic calendar. Ingó wrote it (his brother took a hand in part of it), and then the 2020 festival was called off under gathering restrictions. A thank-you sung to a crowd that never got to turn up. It gets its crowd on this bus instead.  [Homecoming]

en: It begins with a wedding threat. Ingólfur and his sworn brother **Leifur** went raiding with the three sons of **Atli jarl hinn mjóvi** of Gaular, and at the feast **Hólmsteinn** announced he would marry **Helga Arnardóttir** — *“eða öngva konu ella”*, **or no woman at all.** Helga was **Ingólfur's sister and Leifur's wife.** (You can see where this is heading.) **Two of the three brothers died** in the fighting, the pair **forfeited their lands**, and they sailed for Iceland not as pioneers but as men with nothing left.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar

en: Leifur earned his nickname the hard way. Raiding in Ireland he broke into an underground chamber, found a man holding a sword in the dark and killed him for it — *“síðan var hann kallaður Hjörleifur.”* **Sword-Leifur** (*hjör* is sword). On that same raid he took **ten slaves**, five of them named: **Dufþakur**, Geirröður, Skjaldbjörn, Halldór and Drafdittur. **He picked up his name and his killers off the same beach.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar

en: Then the ox. They made land the same season and wintered apart — Ingólfur east at **Ingólfshöfði**, Hjörleifur at the headland on the south coast — and come spring he wanted to sow: *“hann átti einn uxa”*, **he had one ox** and ten men to pull against it. Dufþakur's plan was clean. **Kill the ox, blame a forest bear**, and take the Norsemen one at a time as they scatter to hunt an animal that does not exist in Iceland. *“Þá settu þrælarnir að sérhverjum þeirra og myrtu þá alla.”*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar

en: Ingólfur came west — *“Eftir það fór Ingólfur vestur til Hjörleifshöfða”* — stood over the body, and blamed **the gods**: *“Lítið lagðist hér fyrir góðan dreng, er þrælar skyldu að bana verða, og sé eg svo hverjum verða, ef eigi vill blóta”* — **little came to this brave man, that slaves should be his death, and so I see it goes for every man who will not sacrifice.** Ten enslaved men, one ox, and his conclusion was **insufficient piety.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar

en: He found them at **Eið** — *“Fundu þá þar sem Eið heitir í eyjunum”* — and they were **eating.** That is the low sand neck between **Heimaklettur** and **Stóra-Klif**, and the islanders have their own name for it: **Þrælaeiði, the Slaves' Isthmus.** Heimaslóð is blunt about why — *“þrælar Hjörleifs hafi komið þar að landi, og einhverjir þeirra líklega drepnir þar af Ingólfi Arnarsyni.”* **Ten men murdered their owner, rowed open ocean, made land — and stopped for a meal.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar

en: *“Ingólfur drap þá alla.”* **He killed them all.** **Dufþakur** went off the cliff at the place still called **Dufþaksskor**, on the north face of **Heimaklettur** — the **279-metre** mountain we sail underneath on the way into the harbour.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar

en: Then the sentence that names the map: *“Vestmannaeyjar heita þar síðan, er þrælarnir voru drepnir, því að þeir voru Vestmenn”* — the islands have been called Vestmannaeyjar ever since, **because the slaves were West Men.** Irish and Hebridean Gaels. What is out there today: **14 to 18 islands**, depending on how small a rock you are willing to promote, plus about **30 skerries and sea stacks** — and only **Heimaey** is inhabited, **4,518 people** as of **1 January 2026**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar

en: And here is the one thing I cannot give you: **a year.** **Landnámabók puts no date on any of it** — not the killing, not the pursuit, not the naming — and the book was written **roughly three hundred years after the events**, in the twelfth century, about the ninth. Vísindavefurinn's own historian **Helgi Þorláksson** rejects the literary Ingólfur outright and calls it *“samkomulagsatriði”*, **a matter of agreement**, that the first settler lived in Reykjavík and was called Ingólfur. The one firm date came out of a volcano: *“menn voru á ferð í Reykjavík þegar fyrir 871 ± 2”* — people were already moving about Reykjavík before **871, plus or minus two.** That is the **landnámslag**, the settlement ash layer, dated against ice cores. **The saga gives me names, numbers and a meal. The only thing it will not give me is a year — and for that I have to ask a volcano.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar

en: This harbour has no bay, no headland and no natural shelter. It was built on an open black beach that the sea has been trying to fill in ever since.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn (ferry terminal) / ⚓ Landeyjahöfn

en: Before **2010** these islands were three hours from anywhere. The ferry ran out of **Þorlákshöfn** — about **2 hours 45 minutes** on the water, and a drive at the far end on top of that. Landeyjahöfn cut the crossing to about **35 minutes** and took Reykjavík to Heimaey from about four hours down to two. The first ship came in on **20 July 2010**, scheduled service the next morning. For **4,518 islanders** that is not a convenience. **That is the difference between living offshore and living up the road.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn (ferry terminal) / ⚓ Landeyjahöfn

en: The catch is that they built it on a beach that moves. No bay, no headland, nothing to hide behind — black sand and the open North Atlantic. Roughly **400,000 cubic metres of sand a year** travels east past this spot, most of it handed over by the **Markarfljót**, the glacial river you crossed on the way here. The glacier grinds the rock, the river carries it down, and the sea posts it straight through the harbour mouth. So a dredger has to dig it back out — and the dredger needs **five calm days in a row**, which an Icelandic winter does not hand out. (Ask nicely all you like.) **This harbour is downstream of a glacier, and the glacier does not negotiate.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn (ferry terminal) / ⚓ Landeyjahöfn

en: When it shuts, the ship does not stop — it simply goes to **Þorlákshöfn** instead, which turns a **35-minute** hop into **2 hours 45 minutes** on the water plus a drive at both ends, and on the worst days it does not sail at all. Every hospital appointment in Reykjavík, every lorry of fresh fish, every away match and every funeral gets re-planned around a wave forecast. **Ask an islander about this harbour and you will not get a neutral answer.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn (ferry terminal) / ⚓ Landeyjahöfn

en: Out there is an island younger than the Beatles. Nobody is allowed to set foot on it, and that is precisely the point.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey

en: It started **18 km south-west of the island we're heading for**. Early on the morning of **14 November 1963** the sea out there began to smoke — the eruption had been climbing through **about 130 metres of water** for days before anybody noticed — and by **15 November**, one day later, there was an island. It did not stop until **5 June 1967**: **three and a half years**, one of the longest eruptions in Iceland's recorded history — and the longest unbroken one. They named it for **Surtur**, the fire giant who rides up from the south at the end of the world with a burning sword. (Understated, the Norse.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey

en: It has been shrinking every day since the fire went out. Surtsey came out of the sea at about **2.7 km²** and stood **171 metres** high. By **2006** the waves had chewed it back to roughly **1.4 km²** — close to half of it gone in forty years. The loose ash and tuff goes first, now at something like **a hectare a year**, and underneath sits a hard basalt core. The arithmetic says that in **another 160 years or so** the core is all that will be left. **You are looking at an island with an expiry date.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey

en: Iceland worked out what it had before the eruption had even finished. Umhverfisstofnun's own phrase for the place is *náttúruleg rannsóknarstofa* — **a natural laboratory.** The word for what they are watching is *landnám*, **colonisation** — the very same word Icelanders use for the settlement of Iceland itself. Sterile rock, day zero, and every arrival since logged *án áhrifa mannsins*, **without the influence of man.** That record has now run unbroken for **more than sixty years.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey

en: They locked it in **1965**, while it was still erupting — not afterwards, during. The stated reason was to stop people importing life on a boot sole: *til að forðast aðflutning lífvera af mannavöldum*, **to avoid the arrival of organisms by human agency.** The reserve was widened to **65 km²** in **2006**, taking in the whole volcano and the sea around it, and **UNESCO listed it in 2008.** Landing needs a permit. **You are not getting one, and neither am I.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey

en: The first colonist was too small to see. Diatoms were found on the new rock in **August 1964**, nine months in. The first insect turned up even earlier, in **May 1964** — the volcano was still going. The first flowering plant waited until **1965**: *fjörukál*, **sea rocket**, arriving the only way anything arrives out there, as a seed on the current. Sea first, then wind, then birds. **The order of arrival is not a guess here. It is a logbook.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey

en: Then, in **1970**, something nested. Three years after the fire went out, researchers found *tvö hreiður teistu og eitt fýlshreiður* — **two black guillemot nests and one fulmar nest.** Three nests, on an entire island. **Thirteen bird species** have bred there since, and this is the turn in the story: a bird is not a visitor. **A bird is a delivery service**, carrying seed in its gut and fertiliser in its rear.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey

en: The gulls did the rest, and they did it with droppings. In **1986** the lesser black-backed gull, *sílamáfur*, bred on Surtsey for the first time; by **1990** there were close to **200 breeding pairs.** Vísindavefurinn is blunt about what followed — the gull has had by far the greatest effect on the island's vegetation, both by spreading seed and *ekki síður með driti sínu*, **no less by its droppings.** Vascular plants went from **21 species in 1985 to 43 by 1995**, and **60 by 2003**, plus roughly **300 species of small invertebrate.** **A colony of gulls built the soil, and the soil built everything else.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey

en: We are sailing into this harbour through a gap between a cliff that is 40,000 years old and a lava wall that did not exist when your parents were born.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur

en: The cliff on your right is older than everything else you will see today. That is **Heimaklettur**, **279 metres**, the tallest of the **Norðurklettar**, the North Rocks. It is **móberg of around 40,000 years** — the ash-and-rubble stone you get when a volcano erupts under ice or under the sea and the water quenches the lava before it can flow. Its northern summit, **Hákollar**, tops out at **283 metres** and is **the highest point in the whole archipelago.** The town below it is the newcomer.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur

en: **Dufþaksskor** — the ledge named for Dufþakur, the ringleader from the story I gave you on the mainland — is on the side you cannot see from here, on the **north face**, turned away from the harbour and out towards the open sea. Note carefully: it is local scholarship that fixes the spot, **not *Landnámabók***, so take it as tradition rather than gospel. But it is very precise tradition. **The islanders know exactly which crack in the rock they mean.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur

en: Beside it runs **Dufþekja**, the green slope — *ákaflega flá og brött*, **extremely sloping and steep** — and men fell off it with grim regularity. The belief was that **twenty people had to perish there before it would be finished**, the same number as in **Jökulsá á Sólheimasandi**, the glacial river out on the black sand of the south coast. The two places were said to *kallast á* about their dead, **to call to one another.** Dufþakur was counted the first. **The final tally is put at twenty-one or twenty-two.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur

en: Nobody went up there for the view. Dufþekja was *mikið fýlapláss* — **a great fulmar place** — and before that a source of *hvönn*, angelica, and of roots dug out of the turf. Men climbed that face because a fulmar chick is dinner and angelica is medicine, and on an island with no forest and no fields there was no other way to get either. **Every single death on that slope was an economic decision that went wrong.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur

en: The names are written down, which is what stops this being folklore. **Jón Árnason** of Vilborgarstaðir, about **70**, fell on **24 August 1823.** **Jón Ólafsson** of Elínarhús, **28**, on **20 July 1825.** **Hannes Sæmundsson** of Nýibær, **26**, on **21 July 1858** while digging roots — and his body washed ashore at **Kross in Landeyjar**, on the flat mainland shore you sailed from. Then the last: **Ísleifur Jónsson** of Hlaðbær, about **20**, caught by falling rock in the **earthquake of 26 August 1896** and dead of his injuries on **31 August.** After that, they said, the slope was satisfied.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur

en: Now the wall on your left, which did not exist in 1972. That is **1973 lava** from **Eldfell.** Before the eruption this harbour lay open to the south-east and took a beating in every winter gale. The flow crept down, stopped **just short of sealing the entrance**, and left behind a breakwater no engineer could have got funded. The islanders lost **417 houses** and **gained one of the best harbours in the country.** Nobody here calls that a fair trade. **Nobody here denies the harbour is better, either.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur

en: Both halves of the founding story are on one side of this rail. Off to your right is **Eið**, the low green neck where Ingólfur found the ten of them sitting down to a meal — and above the neck, on the **north face of Heimaklettur**, is **Dufþaksskor**, where the chase ended. The supper and the fall in a single look, without turning your head, **and about eleven and a half centuries sit between them and the concrete under your feet.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur

en: Everyone on this boat has seen a photo of that rock. Almost everything written about it online is wrong, including its name.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named

en: Start with the name, because the name is wrong. The internet calls it **Elephant Rock** and hands you a confident Icelandic original: **Halldórsskora.** So go and look Halldórsskora up. It sits at entry **358** in the old Vestmannaeyjar place-name register, and the entry reads, in full: *“hér er grastó og lömbum beitt þar á vetrum”* — **here is a grassy ledge, and lambs were pastured there in winter.** Not a cliff. Not an elephant. **A different mountain altogether.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named

en: **What you are actually looking at has no Icelandic name at all.** It is part of the **Norðurklettar**, the oldest exposed rock on Heimaey at roughly **40,000 years** — the same subglacial **móberg** as Heimaklettur, ash and rubble welded together under ice or sea. And while we are correcting things: the widely repeated claim that this is **columnar basalt** is **not supported by any Icelandic geological source.** Móberg does not form columns. **It does exactly this — soft, layered, and carved by weather into a face.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named

en: **Eleven centuries, and nobody once thought elephant.** Islanders named the ledges, the clefts, the hollows, the bird-cliffs and every patch of winter grazing on these mountains, because they had to climb them and work them. They looked straight at that head and that trunk for a thousand years and saw **rock they could not graze.** **The elephant needed an outsider with a camera.** It is a shape you can only see if you have no job to do on it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named

en: The register is the joke in itself. It was compiled by **Gísli Lárusson**, and it is exhaustive to the point of comedy. Entry **358** is **Halldórsskora**, the grazing ledge. Entry **359** is **Halldórsskorukórar** — **the little grassy hollows next to Halldórsskora.** They named the ledge, and then they went back and named the dents beside the ledge. **Hundreds of entries, every one of them earned by somebody who had to climb it, cut it, graze it or fall off it.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named

en: And the mountain is the young part of this. Vísindavefurinn traces the **Vestmannaeyjar volcanic system back 70,000 to 100,000 years**, sitting on sea floor that is **ten million** years old, under **700 m** of marine sediment full of shell fossils. So: **Surtsey is from 1963. The elephant is 40,000. The floor beneath both of them is ten million.** Three orders of magnitude in one view, and only one of them has a name in English.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named

en: The elephant is a fashion, and fashions are dateable. Not one Icelandic source records the resemblance — no folk tale, no place name, no entry in Gísli Lárusson's register. It appears with the aerial photograph and the phone camera. **We can date almost every other name on this coastline to within a century. The most famous one we cannot date at all, because it has no history — only a feed.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named

en: Practical note, so you do not spend the rest of the day hunting for it. **You will not get the face from this deck, and you will not get it from the road either.** It sits on the seaward side of **Ystiklettur**, turned away from the harbour, and from the land it is about **641 m across a ridge** — both further and rougher than that number sounds. That is exactly why **every photograph you know of that rock was taken from a boat.** It is not one angle among several. It is the only angle there is. If you want the shot, you want the sea, and that is a separate morning.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named

en: **Margrét Hermanns-Auðardóttir** put a trowel into this valley in **1971** and did not stop until **1980**, turning up **eight houses** across roughly **1,300 m².** Then she published a date and the room went cold. The oldest layers, she argued, sit *underneath* the **landnámslag** — the pale settlement ash of **871** that every archaeological trench in Iceland is measured against. If she is right, somebody was living in this bowl **before Ingólfur ever saw Reykjavík.** It is not accepted: **Orri Vésteinsson** calls the claim *“as yet lacking proper documentation and cannot be verified.”* But notice what nobody disputes — **the eight houses are real.** Only the date is heretical.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🏡 Herjólfsdalur

en: The turf farm in front of you went up in **October 2005**, a longhouse and an animal house rebuilt from the dig's own ground plans, and it is meant to be the farm of **Herjólfur Bárðarson.** And even *he* is contested. *Hauksbók* says *“Herjólfur Bárðarson, bróðir Hallgríms Sviðbálka, byggði fyrst Vestmannaeyjar”* — **Herjólfur built here first.** *Sturlubók* gives the credit to his son **Ormur.** The argument is not between the sagas and the archaeology. **It is inside one book, between two copies of it.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🏡 Herjólfsdalur

en: One letter is doing an enormous amount of work here. *Sturlubók* actually calls him *“Ormur ánauðgi, son Bárðar Bárekssonar”* — **Ormur the enslaved.** **Sigfús M. Johnsen** reads that as a scribe's slip for *auðgi*, **the wealthy**, and then reconciles the two manuscripts by letting both be true in sequence: **Herjólfur settled the valley, and his son Ormur inherited it**, farmed at **Ormsstaðir** and ended up owning **every island in the group.** One wobbling vowel is the difference between the richest man in the archipelago and somebody else's property.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🏡 Herjólfsdalur

en: Then a raven, a rockfall, and the daughter who walked out. Herjólfur had a daughter, **Vilborg**, and she is why this valley has a sequel. The crag of **Molda** came down on the farm — and the story says a bird got there first: *“sagði hrafn Vilborgu við skriðunni og bjargaði þannig lífi hennar”*, **a raven told Vilborg of the landslide and so saved her life.** The record tags it *“sögunni samkvæmt”*, **according to the story** — which is the polite Icelandic way of saying do not build a thesis on this.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🏡 Herjólfsdalur

en: She had already fallen out with him over water. Herjólfur, by the local account, **charged people to draw from his spring**, and Vilborg handed it out free in the evenings. (Iceland's first pricing dispute, settled by geology.) When the rockfall settled the argument she built her own farm at **Vilborgarstaðir**, beside a pool she named **Vilpa**, and laid down a rule — *“skyldi engum verða meint af vatni úr Vilpu”*, **no one was to be denied water from Vilpa**, however unlovely it looked. **Hold on to Vilborgarstaðir.** That is where the islanders held their assembly, and the ruling I will give you at the horse gully was made there.

en: Once a year this quiet green bowl holds more people than live on the island. Three times more.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🎪 Þjóðhátíð

en: It began on **Sunday 2 August 1874** — the thousandth anniversary of the settlement, and the year the Danish king finally handed Iceland a constitution. Districts the length of the country threw a millennium festival that summer, and then **everyone else let it lapse. The islanders picked it back up** — held **annually since 1901**, and missed only twice, for the war years of **1914 and 1915.** More than a hundred and fifty summers after that first one it is still going, in this bowl, on that grass.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🎪 Þjóðhátíð

en: About **400 people** walked in around midday — *“reistu tjöld við suðurhlið tjarnarinnar og hlóðu veisluborð úr torfi og grjóti”*, **pitched tents on the south side of the pond and built a banquet table out of turf and stone.** **Þorsteinn Jónsson** gave the toast to the king, **nine cannon shots** were fired off the hillside, and they danced under open sky until midnight. **Parts of that turf table are still there in the western end of the valley.** You can put a hand on the foundations of the whole thing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🎪 Þjóðhátíð

en: Attendance now runs **15,000 to 18,000** against a resident population of **4,518** — three times the island, in this bowl, with a **10-metre bonfire built from about 3,000 wooden pallets** burning on **Fjósaklettur.** The only time it ever left here was after **1973**, when the valley lay under pumice and the festival decamped south to **Breiðabakki**, **not returning until 1977.** The 1973 edition was one evening, a small fire, and almost nobody present but the clean-up crews. **They held it anyway. That is the entire character of the place in one sentence.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🎪 Þjóðhátíð

en: Since **1933** this festival has commissioned itself a brand-new song every single year. The first was *Setjumst að sumbli.* **Oddgeir Kristjánsson** wrote the tunes almost single-handedly for the first decades, and after his death the job was passed around the island's composers rather than dropped. That is **more than ninety consecutive commissions** for one weekend in one valley. (Try asking your local town council for that.) **No other event in Iceland has asked that much of its own songwriters.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🎪 Þjóðhátíð

en: The moment everyone actually comes for is younger than the eruption: *“Árið 1977 fór fyrst fram brekkusöngur á þjóðhátíð undir stjórn Árna Johnsens”* — **the hillside singing was held for the first time in 1977, led by Árni Johnsen.** The entire slope sits down in the dark and sings, accompanied by very little except itself. People assume it is medieval. **It is younger than the lava in the harbour.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🎪 Þjóðhátíð

en: Then it all goes. The white town — the streets, the stage, the tents, the eighteen thousand people — *“hverfur svo nánast sporlaust fjórum dögum síðar”*, **disappears almost without a trace four days later.** A settlement the size of Akureyri's town centre goes up and comes down inside a week, every year, and leaves grass. **What you are standing in is the festival's off-season, and the emptiness is the achievement.**

en: The Horse Gully
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur → Stórhöfði / 🐴 Kaplagjóta

en: Iceland had a horse problem and no way to eat its way out of it. This gully is what they did instead.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur → Stórhöfði / 🐴 Kaplagjóta

en: **Kaplagjóta is a long cleft on the south side of Dalfjall**, the **150-metre** ridge you have just come out from under, running east and roughly parallel to the festival valley. *Kapall* is the old word for a horse — and specifically for a spent one, a nag. So: **horse-gully.** **The name is not decoration. It is a job description.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur → Stórhöfði / 🐴 Kaplagjóta

en: **Iceland converted around the year 1000 and gave up horsemeat as part of the deal.** For centuries afterwards eating it was forbidden, which left the country holding an animal it could neither ride, work nor eat once the animal was finished. On an island with a hard edge and no spare grass, that arithmetic has one answer: *“Gjótan dregur nafn sitt af því að hestum var varpað þar niður til þess að farga þeim”* — **the gully takes its name from horses being thrown down it in order to destroy them.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur → Stórhöfði / 🐴 Kaplagjóta

en: It was policy rather than cruelty, and the paperwork survives. At the **Vilborgarstaðaþing of 1528** — the assembly held at **Vilborg's farm**, the one whose founding I gave you back in the valley — it was ruled that *“ekki skyldu vera fleiri en 16 hross í Heimaey”*, **no more than 16 horses on the whole of Heimaey.** The king's agent could kill or confiscate anything over the ceiling, and owners were given **14 days** to move the surplus off the island. **After a fortnight, the gully did the administration.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur → Stórhöfði / 🐴 Kaplagjóta

en: **Sixteen. For an entire island.** That is the whole weight of the ruling: grazing on Heimaey was finite, and a horse you can neither ride, work nor eat is a mouth taking grass off the sheep that feed you. So the assembly did the sums, set a hard ceiling, gave it teeth in the shape of the king's agent, and attached a **14-day** fuse. **This is a medieval community legislating its own carrying capacity — and enforcing it over a cliff.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur → Stórhöfði / 🐴 Kaplagjóta

en: Above us are the grassy ledges called **Tíkartær**, and they have a tenant. A small boy — badly treated at home, by the local account, and sent up there against his will to take puffins — went over the edge and died. They say he is still at it, *“steypa sér kollhnís fram af Tíkartónum ofan í Kaplagjótu”*, **turning a somersault off the Tíkartær ledges down into Kaplagjóta**, over and over, for ever. And the record is careful to add one thing about him. **He never harmed anyone.** (Even the ghosts here are well behaved.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur → Stórhöfði / 🐴 Kaplagjóta

en: Now the correction, because you will read the wrong version on your phone tonight. A great deal of the internet tells you this gully is where **Ingólfur killed the Irish slaves.** **It is not.** That happened at **Dufþaksskor** and **Dufþekja** on **Heimaklettur**, the cliff we sailed under on the way in, at the other end of the island. Two grim holes in the ground, **seven centuries apart**, and one lazy conflation copied from site to site ever since. **Kaplagjóta has nothing to do with Dufþakur. It has to do with horses.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur → Stórhöfði / 🐴 Kaplagjóta

en: And this was not even the only one. Heimaey ran a second disposal site at **Kaplapyttir** on **Stórhöfði** — the headland we are driving to right now. An island this size kept **two** designated places to get rid of a horse, which tells you the **16**-animal cap was not a piece of theory that sat in a book. **You will be standing at the other one inside the hour.**

ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði

en: **Stórhöfði** is **122 m** high, the southernmost tip of Heimaey, thrown up in a **submarine eruption about 6,000 years ago** and then tethered to the rest of the island by a thin low neck called **Aur** — **Brimurð** on the east side of it, **Vík** and **Klauf** on the west. Stand on that neck and there is open Atlantic on both sides of you at once. The **lighthouse went up in 1906**, and the wind set about it immediately. Six thousand years on, it is still arguing with the sea.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði

en: And the horse pits are here too. **Kaplapyttir**, the island's second disposal site, is on this headland — the other end of the arrangement I gave you at Kaplagjóta. **Sixteen horses allowed on an entire island, and two separate places to put the seventeenth.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði

en: **17 September 1921, and it has not missed a day since.** The lighthouse keeper **Jónathan Jónsson** started taking readings alongside the lamp. **Three times a day at first** — kl. 8, 14 and 21 — then five or six a day **from 1922**, **seven from 1941**, and **eight since 1952**, at 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24. **Not a day missed in over a century.** The **annual mean wind speed is 11 m/s**, **13.2 in January** and **8 in July**, and wind has been clocked here at **130 knots, about 67 m/s.** In **2005** the **World Meteorological Organization** accredited the station to its strictest international standard, one of only three in Iceland alongside **Keflavík** and **Akureyri.** A century of unbroken data off a rock this exposed is a genuinely rare object.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði

en: **One family has been reading this weather for over a hundred years.** **Jónathan Jónsson** kept the light from **1910 to 1935.** His son **Sigurður V. Jónathansson** took it from **1935 until his death in 1966.** His son **Óskar J. Sigurðsson** held it from **1966 to 2007.** His son **Pálmi Freyr Sigurðsson** has it now. **Four generations, one headland, one unbroken record.** That is exactly why the data off this rock is worth so much — nobody moved house, so nothing was ever interrupted.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði

en: Be accurate if a guest pushes back: **Stórhöfði does not hold Iceland's wind records**, and that is the single most repeated error told about this place. **Skálafell** holds the ten-minute mean at **62.5 m/s**, set on **20 January 1998.** **Gagnheiði** holds the gust at **74.5 m/s**, set on **16 January 1995.** What Stórhöfði holds is not the peak. It is the **relentlessness** — a mean of **11 m/s** year in and year out, roughly **four genuinely calm days a year**, and **86 fog days**, more than anywhere else in the country. Anywhere in Iceland can have one appalling afternoon. This place has had a century of them.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði

en: What that wind actually does to things: windblown sand off the beaches scoured the lighthouse glass so badly that **the light itself became useless** — and the fix was not engineering but botany, planting sand grasses on the slopes below to hold the ground down. Waves of up to **30 m** have been measured off this headland. Annual rainfall runs about **1,556 mm** on the **1961–2000** mean, and most of it arrives sideways. (Umbrellas here are a spectator sport.) When somebody tells you Iceland has weather rather than climate, this is the address they have in mind.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði

en: **Óskar J. Sigurðsson** ringed seabirds off this headland from **1953 to 2014** — **91,695 individual birds** across some **40 species**, mostly puffins, then fulmars and snow buntings. By **1997** *Guinness World Records* had entered him as the person who had ringed more birds than anyone else on earth. He was not a scientist on a grant and he had no field station. He was the lighthouse keeper, and this is what he did between observations.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði

en: **This is the densest puffin ground in the archipelago.** Vestmannaeyjar as a whole holds **840,375 breeding pairs** — about **41.5% of every puffin in Iceland.** The burrows are packed into the grass slopes below you like a housing estate, which is more or less what they are. And the colony is in trouble: numbers have fallen by more than **3% a year since 1998**, and in **2018** the puffin went onto Iceland's Red List as **Critically Endangered.** Islanders hunted these birds for food for centuries. Now they count them instead, which is a harder job and pays worse.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði

en: In late August the pufflings get it catastrophically wrong. The **pysjur** leave the burrows after dark and navigate towards the brightest thing on the horizon, which for several million years was the moon on the water and is now a fishing town with street lighting. They come down in gardens, in car parks, in the middle of the main street. Since **2003** the **Pysjueftirlitið** — the puffling patrol — has organised the island's children to go out at night with cardboard boxes, collect them, **weigh them, measure a wing**, and then carry them to the cliff edge and throw them at the sea. About **a quarter are ringed** on the way past. **This is a town where primary-school children do seabird fieldwork as an evening activity, and think nothing of it.**
