en: **Eldfell did not exist on the evening of 22 January 1973.** Every stone under your boots arrived in the small hours that followed, which puts this mountain's birthday inside living memory. **For thirty-seven years this was the youngest mountain in Iceland — until Fimmvörðuháls in 2010.** It is still the youngest with a town at the foot of it. Published heights run anywhere from **200 to 220 m** — which is not sloppiness, it is the honest answer for a cone whose scree is still settling. The red colour is iron oxidising in the scoria. **The mountain is, quite literally, rusting.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell

en: **Nobody was warned.** Iceland had recorded **small earthquakes of around magnitude 3 in the two days before**, and their unusual depth pointed to magma rather than ordinary faulting — but no announcement was made. **A magnitude 3.0 struck at 01:40, and the fissure opened in the small hours that followed — the accounts differ by a few minutes and nobody has ever pinned it exactly.** Two islanders happened to be out walking near midnight and watched it happen: *«Jörðin hreinlega opnaðist og eldtungur skutust upp á yfirborðið»* — **the earth simply opened and tongues of fire shot up to the surface.** The fissure tore open **east of Kirkjubær**, one of the island's oldest farm sites, along the edge of the settled ground. **Evacuation began within thirty minutes.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell

en: **A 1,600-metre fissure with 30 to 40 vents**, and it opened along the eastern edge of a working fishing town of **5,273 people** — the count taken on **1 December 1972**, seven weeks before. It did not stop for **five and a half months**; the eruption was not declared over until **3 July 1973.** For the whole of that spring Heimaey was a disaster zone, a building site and an active volcano at the same time, and people went to work in it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell

en: The arithmetic of the damage, and the arithmetic of the gain. Out of **1,350 houses** on the island, **417 were buried outright** and roughly **400 more were damaged.** Meanwhile the island itself got bigger — **11.2 km² before, 13.44 km² after**, a gain of about **2.2 km²** from roughly **0.25 km³** of erupted material. The town lost around a third of its buildings and gained a fifth of its surface area. **Nobody here calls that a fair trade.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell

en: They fought the lava with the sea, and won. By **4 February** the flow was pouring into the harbour mouth with such force that the harbour was **closed to all traffic from 4 to 20 February.** The front was advancing about **200 m a day**, straight at the entrance channel — and the harbour is the reason the town exists. The physicist **Þorbjörn Sigurgeirsson**, who had watched Surtsey do much the same thing a decade earlier, proposed the only idea available: *«að stýra hrauninu með því að dæla á það sjó»* — **steer the lava by pumping sea water onto it.** For the dates I am leaning on the islands' own eruption chronicle, which is a community record rather than an institution, so take it as the islanders' own: **the cooling trials starting on 6 February, the dredger Hákur brought in on 13 March, and the American pumps landing on 28 March.** By **30 March** the volume was up by a further **50%.** The front chilled, crusted and turned aside. **The harbour survived.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell

en: And here is what pumping seawater onto lava actually does, because it is not what it sounds like. Þorbjörn's own figures, as translated in **USGS Open-File Report 97-724**: each cubic metre of water cools about **0.7 m³ of lava**, and a single stationary jet at **100 litres a second**, held on one spot for days, will chill about **a hectare** of flow. *“A solid layer of lava about 1 m thick will form in 24 hours.”* Boreholes drilled afterwards found the cooling had driven **13 to 15 metres down** after roughly two weeks of pumping. So you are not putting the eruption out and you are not freezing the flow. **You aren't cooling the lava — you're building a dam out of it, and the still-molten inside has to go round.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell

en: Nothing was wasted, which is very Icelandic. Before **1973** the island had a chronic shortage of fill material — you could not build anything here without tearing up somewhere else to get gravel. The eruption solved that overnight. The ash carted off the streets went, among other places, into **lengthening Heimaey's airport runway**, an extension Icelandic sources say would otherwise simply not have been possible. The new lava gave the town ground for housing, for sports pitches and for the road you came in on.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell

en: Then they sent the volcano a bill. With the eruption over, the islanders flattened a large area in the middle of the new lava field, drilled holes down into it and poured water in — *«holur boraðar og vatn leitt þar ofan í til þess að hita upp hús»*, **holes drilled, and water led down into them to heat houses.** The **hraunhitaveitan**, the lava district-heating utility, ran the town's hot water off the residual heat of the thing that had just tried to bury it. It worked for roughly **ten years** before the heat faded, and then they went back to electricity. **Part of the cost of the eruption was paid, quite literally, by the eruption.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell

en: And then they had a row about what to call it. The **örnefnanefnd**, the Place-Name Committee, announced **Eldfell** on **24 April 1973** after sifting more than **twenty suggestions.** The geologist **Sigurður Þórarinsson**, the country's leading volcanologist, went public against it in a letter dated **23 January 1974** — a year to the day after the eruption began: *«Eldfell þýðir jú ekkert annað en vulkan, eldfjall»*, **Eldfell means nothing other than volcano.** He wanted **Kirkjufell**, after **Kirkjubær**, the ancient farm beside which the fissure had opened. He lost. **The mountain Iceland named in 1973 is, in effect, called Volcano.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell

ctx: the point of the block — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

en: Most towns that lose 417 houses to a volcano become a ruin. This one became a fishing port with a very good harbour and an excellent museum.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

en: The Town That Refused to Stay Evacuated
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

en: Five thousand people left this town in one night. Nobody made them come back. Most of them came back anyway.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

en: **One night, and the whole town was gone.** On **23 January 1973** this island held a little over five thousand people — **the December count was 5,273, and Hagstofa's year-end register said 5,303.** Both are right, taken four weeks apart. **A magnitude 3.0 struck at 01:40, and the fissure opened in the small hours that followed — the accounts differ by a few minutes and nobody has ever pinned it exactly.** The first boat left the harbour at about **02:30**, inside the hour, and by breakfast almost everybody was standing on the quay at Þorlákshöfn with whatever they had picked up on the way out of the door. Only **200 to 300** stayed behind, and they stayed to work: firefighters, harbour crews, and the men who would spend the next five months digging their own town back out.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

en: **The luckiest storm in Icelandic history.** The only reason that worked is that the entire fishing fleet happened to be tied up alongside. A hard south-easterly had blown all through the previous day and **only dropped at about ten o'clock that evening**, a few hours before the ground opened. On any ordinary January night those boats would have been out on the grounds, twenty miles away. Instead they were in the harbour, fuelled and crewed, and they carried **between 4,300 and 4,500 people** to the mainland in roughly **four hours.** Set that against a population of five thousand-odd and you are short by about **500** — and those went out **by air from the airfield through the morning**, which is the part the boat story always leaves out. One **300-tonne** boat, *Gjafar* **VE 300** under skipper **Rafn Kristjánsson**, took **430 people** in a single crossing — *«fólk var í borðsal, í göngum, klefum aftur í og fram í»*, **people were in the mess, in the passageways, in the cabins fore and aft.** **Not one person was hurt.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

en: The clean-up was brutal arithmetic. Roughly **800,000 tonnes** of ash and pumice had to come off the streets and off the roofs, and the roofs were the urgent part — wet ash is heavy enough to bring down a house the lava never touched. Crews worked at it right through the spring and the summer. The moment the islanders themselves point to is **6 September 1973**, the day **the street lights came back on.** Not the harbour, not the fish plant, not the shop. The street lights — **because that is when a buried town starts to look like a town again after dark.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

en: And then, without anybody ordering them to, they came back. There was no compulsion, no guarantee the mountain had finished, and no sensible reason to be first. **About 1,200 were home by mid-September 1973.** Over **2,000 by November.** They moved into a town that was still half-buried, still smelled of sulphur, and was still warm underfoot when you walked across the new ground. The eruption had been over for barely two months.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

en: But not all of them, and this is the part worth saying plainly. **Hagstofa Íslands**, the national statistics office, counted **5,303** people here at the end of **1972.** At the end of **1973** it was **4,906.** At the end of **1974** it bottomed out at **4,396** — **907 fewer** than before the eruption. Half a century on, the island has still never got back to its **1972** figure. The town survived. **Around a sixth of the people who made it never came home, and every family here can name one of them.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

en: Why they came back is tied up at the end of this street. This is the **only harbour on the entire south coast of Iceland** between **Þorlákshöfn** and **Höfn í Hornafirði** — everything in between is surf and black sand with nowhere to put a boat. That is why there is a town here at all, and it is why the fight to save the harbour mouth in February 1973 was a fight for the town's existence rather than its convenience. Today it runs **just under two kilometres of quay** — Siglingastofnun's figure is **1,978 m** — with an entrance dredged to **9.5 m.** The vessel count I would stand behind is a **2005** snapshot: **78 registered vessels** working out of **58 companies.** The islanders' own formulation is blunt — **the harbour is the precondition for settlement in the islands.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

en: And what you are having lunch in: an island of **4,518 people** (**1 January 2026**), a harbour the eruption accidentally improved, and a working fish town that happens to have a volcano at the end of the road. What strikes visitors is the complete absence of memorial solemnity. **1973** is not treated here as a tragedy to be observed. It is treated as a thing that happened, was dealt with, and has since been turned into a museum, a set of walking paths and a very good view.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey

ctx: the point of the block — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

ctx: the spoken close — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: The House at Gerðisbraut 10
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: This museum is built around one house. A family walked out of it in the middle of the night in 1973 carrying a bottle for the baby, and it stayed buried for over forty years.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: The house you are standing in is **Gerðisbraut 10.** It belonged to **Gerður Sigurðardóttir** and **Guðni Ólafsson**, and they lived here with **three young children** — the youngest **only a few weeks old.** This was never a monument or a landmark or a site of any historical significance. It was a family's kitchen, a family's sitting room and a family's bedrooms, and on the night of **23 January 1973** they had minutes to decide what mattered.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: **What they took with them was a bottle for the baby.** That is the entire inventory. In the dark, with the eastern sky lit up and the ground shaking under the floor, **Gerður** and **Guðni** walked out of this house carrying an infant, two other children and **a feeding bottle.** Nothing else. Everything around you now is what they left standing where it stood. They never lived here again. Nobody did. And roughly **five thousand** other people made a version of that same decision within about an hour of one another, almost all of them on the same assumption — **that they would be back in a week to collect the rest.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: It stayed buried for **more than forty years.** Ash and pumice sealed the house where it stood, at the foot of the cone that produced them. The digging began in the summer of **2005** under the working name ***Pompei norðursins*** — **the Pompeii of the North.** When **Gerðisbraut 10** came back up, the decision was taken not to move it, not to restore it and not to tidy it. The museum was built **over the house, where the house is.** **You are standing inside the actual room.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: And it was not the only house they dug out. The **Pompei norðursins** excavation went street by street through ground nobody had walked on since **1973.** **Suðurvegur 25** came up first. **Suðurvegur 16** was uncovered on **7 July 2006** and **Suðurvegur 18** on **25 July 2006**, and the work reached into **Búastaðabraut**, **Gerðisbraut** and the ground around **Helgafellsbraut.** These are real streets with real house numbers, and for more than four decades the only measurable thing about them was the depth of pumice on top.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: One house, standing in for four hundred. **The museum's own text says almost 400 homes and businesses. The islands' eruption chronicle puts it at 417 buried outright.** Either way, **roughly a third of every building on Heimaey.** You cannot exhibit that. What you can do is excavate one entirely ordinary home, leave the crushed roof and the buckled walls exactly as the pumice left them, and let one family's rooms carry the weight of all the others. **That is the whole curatorial decision behind this building, and it is why people who came in expecting a geology museum tend to come out quiet.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: **Eldheimar opened on 23 May 2014.** RÚV carried it that day under the headline *Gosminjasafnið Eldheimar opnað í Eyjum.* You will also see the museum's own phrase, **forty years after the eruption**, which rounds you back to 2013 — but that is a turn of speech, not a second opening date. **Inside a building whose whole purpose is to get one night exactly right, it is worth being exact about its own.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: Upstairs is the other eruption. The **Surtsey exhibition** opened on **14 November 2014** — deliberately, the anniversary of the day in **1963** that Surtsey broke the surface. Two eruptions, one roof, and they mean opposite things to the people who live here. **Surtsey made new land where there had been none, and nobody lost anything. Eldfell made new land too, and it took 417 homes to do it.** The islanders live with both, and they do not confuse them.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: Be straight with people about the death toll, because it is genuinely contested. **Icelandic institutional sources record no deaths from the eruption.** International volcanology — **the USGS** and **Oregon State** among them — records **one death, from volcanic gas** that pooled in a low-lying space. Those two accounts have never been reconciled, and I am not going to reconcile them for you on a Tuesday afternoon. What I will say is that the lurid version some guides tell, a looter overcome in a pharmacy basement, **is not documented in any source I would stand behind.** A town of **5,273** people evacuated from under an erupting fissure with, at the very most, one fatality. **That is the fact. It does not need decorating.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

en: A fort that failed, a raid that took half the island, and a church given as a gift a thousand years after the event it commemorates. All in about forty metres.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: Iceland's oldest purpose-built fort is mostly famous for the one day it did not work.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: The Fort That Was Not Finished In Time
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: The islanders built a fort to stop pirates. In 1627 the pirates arrived, looked at it, and simply landed somewhere else.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: Built for the wrong enemy, and then left to rot. **Kornhólsskans** — nobody calls it that, everyone says **Skansinn**, from the Danish *skanse*, a redoubt — went up in **1586** on the orders of the Danish crown, to protect the royal trade monopoly against **English privateers.** The king sent a naval officer, **Hans Holst**, with the men, the tools and the guns. The islanders were made to do the labour **unpaid**, and were given free provisions in lieu of wages. (A packed lunch, essentially.) By around **1600** the English threat had faded and Denmark stopped maintaining the place. **That decision is the hinge of everything that follows.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: **16 July 1627.** Three ships out of **Algiers**, roughly **300 men.** They had already been working the Icelandic coast for a fortnight and had taken **110 captives between 5 and 13 July** before they ever reached here. They tried to put men ashore at **Kópavík** and found it too awkward, so they went round and landed at a spit that has been called **Ræningjatangi** — **Raiders' Point** — ever since. The fort had cannon and it had men with powder. It was also **unfinished and a generation neglected**, and the raiders simply declined to sail past it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: The Danish trader here was **Lauritz Bagge**, and his last act before he ran is the good bit. He looked at three shiploads of armed men, did the arithmetic, and got his family into a rowing boat for the mainland — but not before making certain the raiders got nothing usable out of him. His captain went out to the trading ship, **bored holes in her hull and cut her moorings** so she would either drift ashore or go down. Bagge himself went to the guns: *«kaupmaður gekk svo frá fallbyssunum, að þær skyldu eigi nytjast ræningjunum, ef þær féllu í þeirra hendur»* — **the merchant left the cannon in such a state that they would be of no use to the raiders, if they fell into their hands.** He could not save the islanders. **He could at least deny the enemy the artillery.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: They killed about **36 people** and carried off **242 islanders** to be **sold at auction in Algiers.** Around **200 got away by hiding** — in the fish-drying caves at **Fiskhellar**, in **Hundraðmannahellir**, the Cave of a Hundred Men above Herjólfsdalur, and behind **Sængurkonusteinn**, the Childbed Woman's Stone, where tradition holds a woman nursing an infant was found and, for once, spared. Add those three numbers and you have a community of barely **500 souls.** **242 of them gone in a single day is not a raid. It is the removal of a generation.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: They sent one man back to ask for money. **Ólafur Egilsson** was the elderly priest of the islands. He was taken with the rest, then released in Algiers almost immediately for one specific purpose — **to travel to Denmark and Iceland and raise the ransom for everybody else.** He crossed Europe on foot and by ship and reached home on **6 July 1628**, not quite a year after he had been dragged off this shore, carrying the news of exactly who was still alive and what each of them was priced at. He also wrote it down. His ***Reisubók*** is one of the strangest documents in Icelandic literature — **a captivity narrative composed by the hostage who was sent home to fundraise for the other hostages.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: The ransom took the better part of a decade. Money was collected across **Iceland, Denmark and Norway**, and in the end about **35 Icelanders** were bought back, roughly **27 of them islanders**, home after some **nine years.** Among them was **Guðríður Símonardóttir**, whom Iceland has never stopped calling **Tyrkja-Gudda.** In the autumn of **1636** the freed captives were held in **Copenhagen** to have their Lutheran faith refreshed before they were let home, and the student assigned to teach them was a young man called **Hallgrímur Pétursson.** She was about **sixteen years older** than he was. They came back to Iceland in the spring of **1637** and married. He went on to write the ***Passíusálmar***, printed at **Hólar in 1666** and reprinted **more than ninety times** since — the most read book of verse in the language. **It comes out of this beach.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: Iceland's answer to 1627 was drill. The fort was rebuilt properly and Denmark sent **a military instructor** to run the defence of the islands, and **every able-bodied man** was required to turn out for weekly weapons practice. From **1639** the gunner at Skansinn was **Jón Ólafsson Indíafari** — 'the India-farer' — who had sailed for the Danish crown as far as India, come home injured, and now sat on a rock in the North Atlantic waiting for ships that never came back. **The raid never repeated. The drills carried on for generations anyway.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn

en: Then **1973** rearranged the whole scene. The lava came through here as well and changed the ground, the shoreline and the view completely — what you are looking at is a reconstruction standing on the original site. And there is a great deal packed into about forty metres: **Landlyst**, just here, went up in **1847** and is among the oldest houses in Iceland, with Iceland's **first maternity hospital** built beside it in **1849**; the **water tank** dates from **1931**; and **Klemensarkirkja**, the Norwegian **stave church**, was given to Iceland by **Norway** for the thousandth anniversary of the conversion and consecrated on **30 July 2000**, presented by **King Harald.** **A fort, a maternity ward, a water tank and a Viking-age church, all standing on ground that is itself only fifty years old.**

en: Born as **Meeks Field**, a US Army bomber base thrown up in **1942–43** and named after pilot **George Everett Meeks**, killed in Iceland on active service. First plane down **23 March 1943**. Its job: the **Battle of the Atlantic** — keeping German U-boats off the North Atlantic convoy lanes.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Keflavíkurflugvöllur → Njarðvík / ✈️ Keflavíkurflugvöllur

en: None of it happens without the **British invasion first** — **Operation Fork**, **10 May 1940**: **746 Royal Marines** waded ashore in Reykjavík and Hafnarfjörður to grab neutral Iceland before Germany could. Iceland formally protested the invasion, then rented them the land. The **US took over in July 1941.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Keflavíkurflugvöllur → Njarðvík / ✈️ Keflavíkurflugvöllur

en: The **1946 Keflavík Agreement** handed the field back to Iceland; the Americans returned in **1951** under NATO and didn't leave until **2006**. Until the civilian terminal — named after **Leifur Eiríksson** — opened in **April 1987**, holidaymakers cleared **military checkpoints** to board a flight.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Keflavíkurflugvöllur → Njarðvík / ✈️ Keflavíkurflugvöllur

en: Iceland is a **double engine**: a spreading **plate boundary** sitting on a stationary **mantle hotspot.** The oldest rock anywhere in Iceland is only **fifteen or sixteen million years** old — and out here on Reykjanes it's a tiny fraction of that. en: Iceland became a **founding NATO member in 1949** — no standing army then, none now. In **1951** it signed a US Defence Agreement, planting the permanent **Iceland Defence Force** here. Peak in the 1980s: ~**3,000 US personnel**, ~**5,000 with families.**

en: The whole point was **geography.** Iceland straddles the **GIUK Gap** — the Greenland–Iceland–UK chokepoint every Soviet sub had to squeeze through to reach the open Atlantic. **P-3 Orion** patrol planes flew that gap on a loop for the entire Cold War.

en: Last US forces left **30 September 2006.** Since **2016**, with Russian activity climbing again, NATO has quietly moved back in — you can furlough a base, but not its coordinates.

en: The same base armed Iceland's cheekiest win: the **three Cod Wars** with Britain (**1958–61, 1972–73, 1975–76**). The threat was blunt — accept our fishing limits, or we leave NATO and close the gap. The Royal Navy actually **rammed** Icelandic boats in the third one. Iceland won **all three.**

en: ***Keflavík* = Driftwood Bay** — named for timber washed up from the Atlantic, genuine treasure on a **treeless** coast. Settled in the Viking Age, a documented **fishing station from at least the 12th century**, and for centuries one of Iceland's top **cod ports** — English, Hanseatic and Danish traders all worked it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Keflavíkurflugvöllur → Njarðvík / 🏘️ Keflavík

en: What a **cod port** actually meant: **stockfish** — cod split and wind-dried on these headlands, keeping for years without a grain of salt, and worth a fortune in Catholic Europe with all those meat-free days to feed. Through the **1400s** English merchants effectively owned the trade off this coast. Then Hamburg's **Hanseatic** men muscled in, and the two sides spent the best part of a century licensing, seizing and occasionally shooting at one another over dried fish, until the Danish crown lost patience and shut the lot behind a **royal trade monopoly in 1602.** (Iceland's first hostile takeover. Nobody sent a memo.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Keflavíkurflugvöllur → Njarðvík / 🏘️ Keflavík

en: Then in **1941** the US military arrived, and from **1942** built the airport as an Atlantic refuelling stop — accidentally inventing the modern town in the process.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Keflavíkurflugvöllur → Njarðvík / 🏘️ Keflavík

en: And that is what ended the fishery's reign here — not a bad season, but a better payslip. Work on the base, and later at the terminal, was steady, year-round and indoors, which no boat has ever managed. The fleet is still here and still lands fish. It simply stopped being the only employer in town.

en: The lava out both windows looked so alien that **NASA used Iceland as astronaut training ground.** During the **Apollo programme (1965–67)**, **32 astronauts** — **Neil Armstrong** among them — trained on Icelandic rock.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌑 Route 41

en: The heavy fieldwork was at **Askja** in the highlands, but the Reykjanes flows you're passing are the same **young basalt.** Volcanologist **Sigurður Þórarinsson** guided the crews; Armstrong later called the Icelandic terrain one of the closest Earth matches to the lunar surface.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌑 Route 41

en: The two lava types here — **pahoehoe** (smooth, ropy) and **aa** (rough, jagged) — are the same textures mapped on the Moon and Mars. In **2023** the **NASA Artemis** astronauts came back to the same fields to train for humanity's return to the Moon.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌑 Route 41

en: Reading the age of it is easy once you know the trick: nothing grows on it. The jet-black, plant-free fields are the new ones. These older flows, **east of the new ones** toward Hafnarfjörður, are ~**700–1,000 years old** — medieval — and still look like last week's, because Iceland has almost **no weathering**: no acid rain, no baking heat, no forest to break the rock down. Cold, clean Atlantic air preserves lava almost perfectly. (Nothing tidies up here. It just sits there looking new for a thousand years, like a show home.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌑 Route 41

en: And a fair bit of it is hollow. **Lava tubes** form where the surface crusts over while molten rock keeps running underneath, then drains away and leaves the pipe behind. The whole pile is hundreds of metres thick — but the hollow tubes are just under the crust, sometimes only a metre or two below the wheels. (You are, in a modest way, driving on a ceiling.)

en: ***Svartsengi* = Black Meadow**, for the scorched ground it stands on. **Geothermal water from 1976, electricity from 1978 — the first plant anywhere to make both from the same well field.** That first turbine was a modest **1 MW**, quietly running the pumps for its own boreholes.

en: It drills **1,000–2,000 m** down to water at **240°C**, and now makes **85 MW of electricity** and **190 MW of heat.** The **seventh generating unit came on line on 1 December 2025**, replacing units three and four. That heat is piped across the **Suðurnes**, a region now well over **30,000** people. The **Blue Lagoon** was never planned — just mineral-rich wastewater pooling in the lava next door.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / ⚡ Svartsengi

en: In **2024**, the eruptions sent lava straight at it. The plant was evacuated and defended with **earthen barriers up to 6 m high**, bulldozed into place in days. The lava stopped short. It's still running today.

en: The **Reykjanes Fires** are a recurring cycle: the peninsula sleeps for centuries, then wakes for decades of eruptions across several systems, then sleeps again. The last full cycle ran ~**950–1240 CE** and laid most of the lava we've driven on.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires

en: After **1240 it went quiet for ~800 years** — then on **19 March 2021** a fissure split open at **Fagradalsfjall** and the Fires restarted. That first show ran six months; **50,000+** people hiked out to watch a volcano like it was a gig.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires

en: Then **Meradalir (2022)** and **Litli-Hrútur** ("Little Ram", **2023**), before the action jumped north to the **Sundhnúkur crater row** by Grindavík: **nine eruptions there between December 2023 and August 2025** — **twelve on the peninsula since 2021.** The last ended **early August 2025.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires

en: As of **2026** there is **no active eruption** — the **longest pause yet** — but magma is still pooling under **Svartsengi**, and the Met Office (**Veðurstofan**) rates a fresh eruption the **most likely near-term outcome.** Their hazard map runs a six-level colour scale, green through yellow and orange to red, across zones **A to F.** Grindavík is zone A, and it currently sits at **yellow — *nokkur hætta*, some hazard.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires

en: That first eruption ran **six months to the day** — **19 March to 18 September 2021** — and left about **150 million cubic metres** of lava over **4.8 km²**, averaging **more than 30 metres thick**, peaking in May and June at around **12 cubic metres a second.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires

en: Under Svartsengi right now there is **about 28 million cubic metres** of magma on the Met Office's assessment — and that assessment runs out on **30 September**, which tells you how fast this moves. The ground is still rising at roughly **2 cm a month**, which makes today's quiet the pause between two eruptions rather than the end of anything.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires

en: **Could it go off while we're here?** Honestly — it could. There's about **twenty-eight million cubic metres** of magma under Svartsengi and the Met Office's own assessment says an eruption is the **most likely next event.** Here's the part that matters: when it moves, it moves **sideways first**, and that gives somewhere between **twenty minutes and four hours** of warning. Iceland has evacuated this ground **nine times** and has **not lost a single person to lava.** If it happens today, we'll know before it reaches the surface, and we'll be somewhere else.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires

en: Krýsuvík did the same job last time round. The **Krýsuvíkureldar of 1151 to 1188** laid down **Ögmundarhraun**, **Mávahlíðahraun** and **Kapelluhraun**, and then the system shut for **eight centuries** and has not opened since.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires

en: The 2021 fissure opened in **Geldingadalir** — the wether valleys, named after **castrated rams**, because sheep came there for a mouthful of grass. **Hallgrímur J. Ámundason** settled it at **Vísindavefurinn** on **24 March 2021**, five days into the eruption, from the place-name register of the farm **Hraun** in Grindavík.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires

en: **Kristján Sæmundsson** and **Magnús Á. Sigurgeirsson** call **Fagradalsfjall** unlike any other system on the peninsula — no central volcano, no proper fissure swarm, no high-temperature field, roughly **5 km wide and 15 km long.** Its **picrite** comes up fast and from deep without loitering in a chamber, which is why nothing filled up slowly where the instruments could watch it.

en: **Grindavík** was settled ~**934 CE** — one of the first Reykjanes communities and a major North Atlantic **cod harbour.** It even caught the **1627 Barbary corsair** raids. By December 2023 it held about **3,720 people.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌋 Grindavík

en: On **10 November 2023**, thousands of earthquakes in a few hours ripped **fissures metres wide** through roads, gardens and house foundations. The whole town was **evacuated in one night.** In **January 2024**, lava reached the streets for the first time — houses burned, roads buried.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌋 Grindavík

en: Further eruptions followed through 2024 and into 2025 as the **Sundhnúkur crater row** kept reactivating. **6 m earthen barriers** built in days saved some streets and were overrun on others. For all that, **none of this lava ever reached the sea** — it crossed the Grindavíkurvegur road again and again and pushed into the town on **14 January 2024**, but it never made the coast. The last time lava ran into the sea on this peninsula was the **12th century.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌋 Grindavík

en: And then people started coming back. The state buyout company **Þórkatla** bought **over 90% of the homes** and most residents did leave for good — but at **1 April 2026** Þjóðskrá had **874 registered residents** living in Grindavík again, against about **3,720** before the evacuation. The **school is open** for the autumn term, crews have worked all summer to get **Bókasafn Grindavíkur**, the town library, back on its feet, and the **harbour and the power plant never stopped at all.** In **April 2026** Alþingi debated a formal framework for rebuilding the community here. (Not a ghost town. A very small town with an extremely dramatic CV.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌋 Grindavík

en: Between eruptions magma refills a shallow reservoir beneath **Svartsengi**, then runs sideways into the crater row as a **dike** before it surfaces. That sideways run is the only warning there is, and it is short — **Veðurstofa Íslands** puts the historic range at **20 minutes to just over four hours.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌋 Grindavík

en: The **1627** raid was this harbour specifically. On **20 June 1627** corsairs out of **Salé** in Morocco under **Murat Reis** took **12 to 15 Icelanders** along with Danish and Dutch crew and sailed them to **Algiers** — the opening act of the **Tyrkjaránið**, of which only **27** of everyone seized that summer ever made it home, nine years later.

en: Archaeology backs the legend: a turf longhouse wall at **Aðalstræti** lies **under a volcanic ash layer dated to AD 871 ±2** — the founding pinned to within two years by Greenland ice cores. It's on show *in situ* at the **Settlement Exhibition.** (DNA says the "pure Viking" founders were already a **Norse–Gaelic** mix from day one.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Hafnarfjörður → Reykjavík / 🏙️ Reykjavík

en: It's the world's **northernmost capital** at **64°N**, closer to the Arctic than to London. **Two-thirds of all Icelanders** — roughly **250,000 of 394,324** (Hagstofa Íslands, 1 January 2026) — live in the greater city, almost entirely on **geothermal heat**: **80–90°C** water piped to radiators, pools, and snow-free pavements. Reykjavík was the **first major city to quit oil heating**, done by the **1970s.** Skyline: **Hallgrímskirkja**, **Harpa**, and **Esja** behind — the city's free weather app. See Esja = good day. Esja gone = grab a coat.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Hafnarfjörður → Reykjavík / 🏙️ Reykjavík

en: **Höfði house** — the small white seafront mansion — hosted the **Reykjavík Summit, 11–12 October 1986**: **Reagan** and **Gorbachev** met on cutting nuclear arsenals. It officially "failed," then produced the **INF Treaty (1987)**; Berlin Wall down **1989**, USSR gone **1991.** Neutral, army-free Iceland was the trusted middle ground.

en: The street you just got on the bus in is called **Lækjargata — Brook Street.** There is no brook. It is still there, running under the tarmac, and in January it is the reason the ducks in the city pond have anywhere to swim.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏛️ Reykjavík

en: That hill is **Arnarhóll**, and the man on it is **Ingólfur Arnarson**, who the tradition says was Iceland's first settler. The tradition — and say it as a tradition, because that is what it is — has him throwing his **öndvegissúlur**, the carved pillars from either side of a chieftain's high seat, over the side of the ship and settling wherever they washed ashore. They came in below this hill. **What archaeology can actually pin down is different and better:** there were people here **before the ash layer dated to AD 871, give or take two years.** The statue is by **Einar Jónsson**, and it was not a gift from the state — the **Reykjavík craftsmen's guild** paid the **40,000 krónur** and unveiled it on **24 February 1924.** Arnarhóll was a working farm until the **1820s.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏛️ Reykjavík

en: Now the brook. **Lækurinn** ran from the pond down to the sea, the old town grew up on the west side of it, and the street was named **Lækjargata in 1848.** In **1911** they put the brook in a culvert and paved over it. **It is still flowing under us.** And here is the good part: the pond — **Tjörnin** — freezes in winter, except for one patch. Guides will tell you that is a natural hot spring. **It is not.** It is **warm overflow from the city's hot-water system**, coming out at the old brook outlet by Iðnó. One warm corner, and every duck in Reykjavík standing in it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏛️ Reykjavík

en: Off to the right on **Austurvöllur** is the **Alþingishúsið**, the parliament, built **1880 to 1881** by the Danish architect **Ferdinand Meldahl**, out of stone quarried up the hill in **Þingholtin.** And this is where you correct the guidebook. **Alþingi was founded at Þingvellir, traditionally in 930** — the oldest parliamentary institution in the world by date of foundation. **But it is not the oldest continuously running one, and Alþingi does not claim to be.** It was **shut down by royal decree on 6 June 1800** and did not sit again until **1 July 1845.** **Forty-five years of silence.** That gap is the whole reason the Isle of Man gets to argue about this.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏛️ Reykjavík

en: Last one on the skyline: **Hallgrímskirkja**, the concrete tower you can see from most of the city. **About 74 and a half metres** — the parish's own leaflet says 73, and I am not going to pretend that is settled. It was designed by **Guðjón Samúelsson**, and the shape is meant to be **columnar basalt, mountains and glaciers** rather than anything churchy. Building started in **1945** and it was consecrated on **26 October 1986** — **forty-one years.** Guðjón died in **1950** and never saw it. The statue of **Leifur Eiríksson** out front is older than the church behind it: **a gift from the United States** for the **1930 millennium of the Alþingi**, formally handed over on **17 July 1931.**

en: The plant is **ISAL**, the aluminium smelter at **Straumsvík.** Built by the Swiss company **Alusuisse** under a law Alþingi passed on **13 May 1966**, it started producing in **1969** at a modest **33,000 tonnes a year.** Today it runs at about **202,000 tonnes**, with a licence for **230,000**, employs **381 people** (end of 2025) and is owned outright by **Rio Tinto.**

en: Here is the bit that actually matters. To run it, Iceland had to build a power station — so **Landsvirkjun was founded on 1 July 1965** and put up **Búrfellsstöð**, which started on **16 September 1969.** The smelter took **half the station's output, 105 MW.** *(In 2025 it bought **3,334 gigawatt-hours.**)* The **alumina** arrives by ship mostly from **Brazil**, the finished aluminium leaves through **Rotterdam** to around **60 customers**, and it comes out as **billet** — the stuff extruded into window frames and solar-panel rails.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun

en: Now the lava. **Kapelluhraun** poured out of the **Krýsuvíkureldar in 1151** — the same fires we will meet again in an hour. Locals call it **Bruninn**, "the burn", and the medieval name **Nýjahraun** turns up in *Kjalnesinga saga* and in an annal entry for a **1343** shipwreck. People **watched this one arrive.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun

en: And out there in the rock is a tiny ruin called **Kapellan**, the chapel. On **21 May 1950** it was excavated by **Kristján Eldjárn** — later President of Iceland — with three colleagues. The building was **2.4 metres long.** Inside they found, broken into three pieces, a **carved claystone figure of Saint Barbara**, about **3.3 cm** of her surviving from an original of maybe **5.5 cm**, still holding her tower. Pre-Reformation. A wayside shrine where travellers stopped to pray before crossing the lava.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun

en: **Barbara is the patron saint of travellers — and of everyone who works with fire, metal and explosives.** She has been sitting in that lava for five hundred years, and then somebody built an aluminium smelter next door. *(She is now the most appropriately employed saint in the North Atlantic.)*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun

en: The chapel also carries a grim story: that a man from **Bessastaðir** was killed and buried here in the reprisals after the execution of **Bishop Jón Arason.** Kristján Eldjárn dug for it and **found nothing to support it** — and said so. Good man.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun

en: The Road Everyone Said Was A Waste Of Money

en: When they proposed this road in **1936**, the newspapers took it apart. Árni Óla wrote in **1940** that the project had "mostly met with condemnation" and that this exact pass would be the most expensive and difficult stretch of the lot. **We are about to drive the argument.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls

en: The ridge on the right is **Sveifluháls.** It was built underneath a glacier — a fissure eruption erupting into ice, quenching into **móberg**, hyaloclastite, and stacking itself into a wall instead of spreading into a plain. It runs **north-east to south-west**, which is not a coincidence: that is the direction of the rift. The whole **Krýsuvík volcanic system** is about **8 km wide and 50 km long**, and this ridge is drawn along it like a pencil line on a map.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls

en: The road was **Jónas Jónsson and Jón Baldvinsson's** idea, put to Alþingi in **March 1936.** The pitch was weather. The existing route east crossed **Hellisheiði at 370 metres.** This one would top out at **168.** A **snow-free winter road** to the south. That was the whole argument.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls

en: It cost a fortune, it took years, and the stretch past **Kleifarvatn** was not finished until around **1945.** *(Which means the fastest way to make an Icelander build you a road is to point out that the other one gets snowed in.)*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls

en: One more thing you cannot see and should know. The pass is being **quarried** — for exactly the same móberg the ridge is made of. And the local objection is not about the view. **The groundwater under Undirhlíðar runs downhill and comes out at Straumsvík** — the smelter we passed twenty minutes ago. A public consultation on new extraction ran from **25 September to 6 November 2025.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls

en: The Lake That Pulled Its Own Plug
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn

en: In the year 2000 this lake started emptying. Nobody drained it, nobody dammed it. **An earthquake opened a crack in the bottom and the water simply left.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn

en: **Kleifarvatn** is the biggest lake on the peninsula — about **10 km²**, up to **97 metres deep**, sitting roughly **140 metres above sea level** in a closed basin on the eastern edge of the **Krýsuvík fissure swarm.** Vísindavefurinn's answer is that the basin is probably part of a **caldera around 10 km across** — a collapse, not an explosion crater — and that the lake in its present form is roughly **10,000 to 12,000 years old.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn

en: Here is the oddity: **it has no river running out of it.** Before 2000 the water drained north into **Lambhagatjörn** and then underground, all the way to the sea at **Straumsvík.** A lake that empties itself through the floor is already unusual. Then the floor got worse.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn

en: The **earthquakes of 2000** opened and widened fissures at and near the lake's northern end, and over the **following two years the surface dropped about four metres.** Beaches appeared. The jetty ended up a long way from the water. It has since recovered a good deal, but the point stands: on this peninsula even the lakes are provisional.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn

en: It also has a monster, and the sightings are dated. In **1749**, witnesses said they watched the thing haul itself out onto a spit and lie there for **about two hours.** By **1750** people **would not fish here at all**, though the lake was full of fish, because of *"orms eða slöngu sem væri svört að lit"* — a worm or serpent, black, reckoned to be **the size of a medium whale, thirty to forty metres long.** In **1755** something surfaced *"líkasta skötu að lit og lögun"* — closest to a skate in colour and shape, and enormous.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn

en: And when the water finally did drop, Iceland's best-selling crime writer was waiting. **Arnaldur Indriðason's *Kleifarvatn* (2004)** — published in English as ***The Draining Lake*** — opens with the falling water level uncovering **a body that had been down there for decades.** He did not have to invent the setting. He just read the news.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 💧 Kleifarvatn

en: The Fires That Shut The Door
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar

en: This system last erupted in the twelfth century, ran for nearly forty years, and then closed for eight hundred. It has not opened since. That is either reassuring or it isn't.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar

en: The **Krýsuvíkureldar of 1151 to 1188** laid down **Ögmundarhraun**, **Mávahlíðahraun** and **Kapelluhraun** — three flows that between them rewrote the south coast of this peninsula and buried at least one farm.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar

en: Then the system **shut, and has stayed shut for over eight centuries.** Meanwhile its neighbours — Fagradalsfjall in 2021, Svartsengi and Sundhnúkur from 2023 — have been extremely busy. Same peninsula, same rift, completely different diaries.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar

en: That is how the **Reykjanes Fires** work. The peninsula sleeps for centuries, then wakes for decades of eruptions across several systems, then sleeps again. The last full cycle ran roughly **950 to 1240 CE** and laid most of the lava we have driven on today. We are, on the current reading, at the beginning of the next one.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Lækjargata → Seltún / 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar

en: Where They Drilled For The Queen And Got A Crater

en: In October 1999 a borehole here stopped blowing, thought about it for a bit, and then **exploded** — leaving a crater forty-three metres across and throwing mud seven hundred metres up the hillside.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún

en: This is a **high-temperature geothermal field** at the heart of the Krýsuvík system, and the colours are not decoration — they are the rock being eaten. Steam rises off the deep reservoir, condenses near the surface, and brings up **carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide.** Those gases turn the water acid, and the acid digests fresh lava into soft clay. **The mud you are photographing is bedrock that lost an argument with chemistry.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún

en: Those pale yellow mounds have a name and a mechanism. **Brennisteinsþúfur** — sulphur mounds — form where **hydrogen sulphide reaches the surface and oxidises in open air**, dropping pure sulphur out of the gas. Vísindavefurinn puts them at **10 to 20 metres across and 1 to 1.5 metres high**, and — this is the good bit — **hollow inside.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún

en: People mined that sulphur. According to the site's own panels there were two runs: **1754 to 1763**, and again **1858 to 1880**, and contemporary records have **72.5 tonnes of sulphur exported from Krýsuvík in the eighteenth century.** Sulphur meant gunpowder. This muddy field was, briefly, a strategic resource.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún

en: And this is where Iceland's geothermal drilling starts. **Eggert Ólafsson and Bjarni Pálsson** bored here with a hand-turned iron drill in the **autumn of 1755 and the summer of 1756** — the first attempt anywhere in the country. *(Bjarni Pálsson is a name worth keeping: he became Iceland's first* landlæknir*, the first state physician. On the South Coast run he turns up again as Sveinn Pálsson's father-in-law.)*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún

en: Fast forward two centuries. **Rafveita Hafnarfjarðar**, the Hafnarfjörður electricity utility, drilled a research hole here — remembered as **Drottningarholan**, "the Queen's Hole" — and at around **230 metres down the hole blew.** Be straight with the guests about one thing: **the sources give the year as either 1947 or 1949 and I have not been able to settle it.** What nobody disputes is what it did next.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún

en: It blew, on and off, for **half a century.** Then on **Thursday 25 October 1999** it stopped — and shortly afterwards the ground beside it detonated in a steam explosion, opening a crater **about 43 metres across** and flinging mud **700 metres to the north.** The walkways you are standing on were laid out afterwards, by people who had just watched what this ground does when it is annoyed.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún / ♨️ Seltún

en: This is the crater Icelandic geology textbooks use as **the** example of its type. It is roughly **45 metres deep** in a hole only a few hundred metres across. And the reason it is green — **the sources genuinely disagree**, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun

en: **Grænavatn** is a **sprengigígur**, an explosion crater — blown out in a single blast where rising magma met groundwater. Vísindavefur, the University of Iceland's own science service, lists it as the type example for the whole category. Age: **somewhere around six to seven thousand years** — one source says 7,000, another says over 6,000, and nobody has narrowed it further.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun

en: Depth: **about 45 metres**, which is the figure the geologist **Sigurður Þórarinsson** published in **1950.** The official sign at Krýsuvík says **46.** Width: "a few hundred metres" is as precise as anyone will commit to. *(A lake nobody has bothered to measure properly, in a country that measures everything. I love it here.)*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun

en: Now the colour, honestly. **Sigurður Þórarinsson wrote in 1950 that it comes from sulphur compounds in the water.** The **official information board** at the site says it comes from **geothermal algae and crystals absorbing the green light of the sun.** Both are published. Neither has been settled. Take your pick, and if a guest tells you they read something different on the internet, they are probably reading a translation of one of these two.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun

en: The properly weird bit is in the rock thrown out of it. The tephra around Grænavatn contains **gabbro nodules** — lumps of a deep, coarse-grained rock the magma tore off on its way up. **Gabbro has not been found anywhere else in south-west Iceland.** This little hole punched through something nothing else has reached.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 💚 Grænavatn & Augun

en: And in a second we drive **between two more of them.** **Augun** — "the Eyes" — are two small water-filled craters, one on each side of the road, sitting on their own **300-metre crater row.** There are at least **four separate rows** in this cluster, and **Gestsstaðavatn** to the west is the oldest. This is not one volcano. It is a small committee of them.

en: The Church That Burned Down And Was Built Again By Apprentices
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja

en: That church burned to the ground in the small hours of **2 January 2010.** The fire brigade got the call at **02:04** and by the time they arrived **the building had already fallen.** What you are looking at is an **exact replica**, built by carpentry students — and the altarpiece inside is **the original.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja

en: The church that burned was built in **1857** by **Beinteinn Stefánsson**, a tenant farmer and carpenter at Arnarfell, out of **driftwood.** It stopped being a parish church around **1910**, was formally abolished in **1917**, and in **1929** it was deconsecrated and turned into somebody's house. Rebuilt and reconsecrated on **Whit Sunday, 31 May 1964**, taken into the care of the **National Museum** that same year, and legally protected on **1 January 1990.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja

en: Then the fire. It was **arson** — a man in his early twenties was later given a **one-year suspended sentence** for setting it alight. Twenty years of protected status, gone in under an hour.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja

en: Here is the part I like. The replacement was built by the **carpentry school in Hafnarfjörður** — Iðnskólinn, later Tækniskólinn — working with the **National Museum** and a volunteer society, deliberately as a **teaching project in old timber technique.** The insurance payout from the old church bought the materials. It is an **exact copy** and it **seats 40.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja

en: It came back on **9 October 2020**, and could not be lifted onto the old foundation that day because the wind got up. They craned it into place **the next morning.** COVID then delayed the consecration by nearly two years, until **Whit Sunday, 5 June 2022, at two o'clock.** It now belongs to the parish in **Hafnarfjörður.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja

en: And the altarpiece. It was painted for this church by **Sveinn Björnsson** — who was a painter *and* the **chief detective of Hafnarfjörður**, which is a combination I have never encountered anywhere else. Every autumn, after the September service, the picture was taken down and **stored in Hafnarfjarðarkirkja for the winter.** Which is exactly where it was on the night of 2 January 2010. **The painting survived the fire because of a filing habit.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja

en: Sveinn died in **1997** and is buried in that churchyard — the **first burial there since 1917**, and the last. At the 2022 consecration they poured communion wine on his grave.

en: After **1240 the peninsula went quiet for about 800 years** — then on **19 March 2021** a fissure split open at **Fagradalsfjall** and the Fires restarted. That first show ran six months; **more than 50,000 people** hiked out to watch a volcano like it was a gig.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires

en: Then **Meradalir (2022)** and **Litli-Hrútur** ("Little Ram", **2023**), before the action jumped north to the **Sundhnúkur crater row** by Grindavík. **Veðurstofa Íslands counts nine eruptions there.** The ninth began on **16 July 2025** and the Met Office **formally declared it over on 5 August 2025.** That is **twelve eruptions on this peninsula since 2021.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires

en: **And then it stopped.** As of **18 August 2026** Veðurstofan's line is *"Kvikusöfnun og landris heldur áfram við Svartsengi"* — **magma accumulation and uplift are continuing at Svartsengi**, at a rate that has held steady for weeks. Around **ten small earthquakes a day**, most of them north of Grindavík. **No eruption since the fifth of August last year** — which makes today, as we drive across it, **thirteen months of quiet.** The longest pause of the whole series.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires

en: Be careful how you say the next part, because it is the honest one. **The ground is still rising. The magma is still arriving. The Met Office's own assessment is that a new dike intrusion, and possibly a new eruption, remains the most likely outcome.** *(For the exact volume under Svartsengi and today's hazard-zone colours — check vedur.is this morning. Those numbers move and a stale one is worse than none.)*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires

en: **"Could it go off while we're here?"** You will get asked. The honest answer: it could. Here is what matters — when the magma moves it goes **sideways first**, and that dike run is the warning. **Veðurstofa Íslands puts the historic range at twenty minutes to just over four hours.** Iceland has evacuated this ground repeatedly and has **not lost a single person to lava.** If it happens today we will know before it reaches the surface, and we will be somewhere else.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires

en: Two footnotes for the geology-curious. **Kristján Sæmundsson** and **Magnús Á. Sigurgeirsson** describe **Fagradalsfjall** as unlike anything else on the peninsula — **no central volcano, no proper fissure swarm, no high-temperature field**, roughly **5 km wide and 15 km long.** Its **picrite** comes up fast and from deep without loitering in a magma chamber, which is exactly why nothing filled slowly where the instruments could watch it. And the valley the 2021 fissure opened in, **Geldingadalir**, means the **wether valleys** — named for **castrated rams**, because sheep came there for a mouthful of grass. **Hallgrímur J. Ámundason** settled that at **Vísindavefurinn** on **24 March 2021**, five days into the eruption, from the place-name register of the farm **Hraun** in Grindavík.

en: That stripe has a folk tale and a geology paper, and they describe **the same object.** The story says it is a **troll-woman's silver chain.** The geology says it is the **feeder pipe the volcano erupted through.** Both are correct.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli

en: **Festarfjall** is a **stapi** — a tuya. It erupted underneath the ice sheet: móberg breccia below, a cap of grey basalt on top where the eruption finally broke the surface. About **190 metres.** And then the sea did something rare and generous — **it cut the mountain in half.** You are looking at a **cross-section of a volcano's internal plumbing**, which almost never gets exposed.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli

en: The stripe is **Festin**, "the chain": a **basalt dyke**, and — per the geologist **Kristján Sæmundsson** — the **aðfærsluæð**, the conduit the magma actually came up. Harder than the rock around it, so as the sea grinds the cliff back, the dyke stands proud. The mountain is literally wearing its own throat on the outside.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli

en: The tale is recorded in **Rauðskinna**, the folk-tale collection — *not* Jón Árnason, and guides get that wrong. A troll-woman hung a **silver chain** over the cliff and declared that when the farmer at **Hraun** had a daughter named after her, and that girl walked on the sand below, the chain would fall and be hers. **She then neglected to mention her own name.** So the chain is still up there. *(Worst-designed raffle in the North Atlantic.)*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli

en: The farm ahead is **Ísólfsskáli**, documented from **1703** as a Skálholt property. Bishop **Brynjólfur Sveinsson** ran a fishing station from it, and in **1734** the Skálholt boat was lost here with **ten men.** The 1703 land register warned the well was so bad the farm might have to be abandoned for want of water. The **earthquakes of 28–29 January 1905** brought the kitchen down, the farm stood empty **three years**, and in **1916** they rebuilt it **further back from the sea.** For decades it was the **last farm on this whole peninsula living purely off farming.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli

en: One honest correction, because it gets repeated: **the eruptions of 2023 to 2025 did not reach Ísólfsskáli.** Those were all at the **Sundhnúkur crater row above Grindavík.** The drama on *this* road was **2021**, when lava came down into **Nátthagi** and civil protection bulldozed **eight-metre barriers** to keep it off **Suðurstrandarvegur** — because this road is **Grindavík's escape route** and it carries the peninsula's **fibre-optic cable.**

en: The Newest Ground In Europe
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall

en: Everything from here to the ridge is younger than the year 2021. **You are about to walk on land that did not exist when you booked your last holiday.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall

en: The **19 March 2021** eruption ran **six months to the day — to 18 September 2021** — and left roughly **150 million cubic metres** of lava across **4.8 km²**, averaging **more than 30 metres thick**, peaking through May and June at around **twelve cubic metres a second.** For scale: that is a new field of rock deeper than a ten-storey building, poured out of a crack in a valley nobody had heard of.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall

en: What makes it strange is what it was made of. Fagradalsfjall's magma is **picrite**, and it came up **fast, and from deep**, without sitting in a shallow chamber first. Most eruptions are fed by magma that has been parked and stewing. This one was mantle material arriving more or less directly. Geologists were, to use the technical term, delighted.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall

en: **The rule for the next two hours: do not walk on the lava.** That is Safetravel's wording. The crust looks solid and is not, the rock is volcanic glass and will open a hand to the bone, and parts of this field are **still warm underneath** years on. Stay on the marked path, and if you want the photo, take it from the path.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall

en: The other rule is the air. **Check the gas dispersal forecast** — geothermal and volcanic ground gives off **sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide**, both heavier than air, both worst in hollows and dips on a still day. **If it smells strongly of eggs in a dip, go up, not on.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall

en: And look at what is growing. Almost nothing — and that is the lesson. There is **no acid rain here, no baking heat, no forest** to break rock down. Iceland barely weathers. **These 2021 flows will still look like this in a thousand years**, which is exactly why the medieval lava we drove over this morning also looks like last week's.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall

en: That power station accidentally built the Blue Lagoon — and then in 2024 had to be walled off from lava by the metre.

en: It drills **1,000 to 2,000 m** down to water at **240°C**, and now makes **85 MW of electricity** and **190 MW of heat.** The **seventh generating unit came on line on 1 December 2025**, replacing units three and four. That heat is piped across the **Suðurnes**, a region now well over **30,000** people. The **Blue Lagoon** was never planned — just mineral-rich wastewater pooling in the lava next door.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⚡ Svartsengi

en: In **2024**, the eruptions sent lava straight at it. The plant was evacuated and defended with **earthen barriers averaging seven metres**, bulldozed into place in days. **The lava stopped short. It is still running today** — and the same reservoir it drinks from is the one being refilled under our feet right now.

en: The Mountain That Gave The First Warning
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn

en: On **26 January 2020** the Icelandic Met Office published a sentence it had never been able to write before: in **nearly three decades** of precise measurement, **nothing on this peninsula had ever risen this fast.** That was the first alarm of everything that followed. Grindavík was evacuated **three years, nine months and fifteen days later.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn

en: **Þorbjörn** — properly **Þorbjarnarfell** — is **243 metres**, and it is **móberg**, built underneath ice like Sveifluháls this morning. But this one took **two separate glacial periods** to finish, which makes it **one of the older hills on the peninsula** — considerably older than Fagradalsfjall, where we were standing at eleven o'clock. Look at the top: it has **fallen in on itself.** There is a fault and a small rift valley up there, and — this is the odd part — **that fault runs north to south, straight across the south-west-to-north-east grain of every other crack on Reykjanes.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn

en: The cleft splitting the summit is **Þjófagjá**, Thieves' Gorge, and *Huld* — the nineteenth-century folk collection — says **fifteen thieves** once lived in it, robbing Grindavík's sheep. Nobody could get at them. Then a farmer's son from **Hóp** noticed they all bathed at **Baðsvellir** every Saturday, taking turns guarding the clothes. Once they trusted him with the pile, **he turned one shirt-sleeve and one trouser-leg inside out on every single set**, and ran. They lost the race getting dressed, chased him across the lava in their underwear, cut their feet to ribbons, and were caught and hanged at **Gálgaklettar** — Gallows Rocks. The story ends with one of the great Icelandic shrugs: ***"the farmer's son became an unlucky man, but it is not recorded what befell him."***
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn

en: There was a war up there too. **Camp Vail** was a **United States Army Air Forces radar station** — American, not British, and guides get that wrong. The road up the mountain was begun in **early October 1941** by an air-force construction unit working alongside **men hired in Grindavík**, and the station went live on **18 April 1942**: **fourteen Nissen huts** and a generator, down in the crater, with the radar on the summit. It was **the best station in the country for spotting low-flying aircraft over Faxaflói** — and it was **usable only 60% of the time**, because the antenna had to be folded down that often in the wind. Most of it was sold or demolished after the war. **A single stone hearth is still standing up there.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn

en: Now the part that matters. On **21 January 2020** the ground started rising — **3 to 4 millimetres a day**, about **two centimetres** by the time it was announced on the **26th**. Say this next bit accurately, because almost everyone says it wrong: **the centre of the uplift was not under Þorbjörn. It was just west of it.** Underneath, roughly **a million cubic metres of magma at three to five kilometres down.** On the **22nd**, two earthquakes of **magnitude 3.7 and 3.6** were felt as far north as **Borgarnes.** At **17:19 on the 26th**, the National Commissioner declared an **óvissustig** — an uncertainty phase. That was the first alert level of this entire volcanic episode.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn

en: And then nothing happened, for years. The uplift came and went in pulses. That alert stayed in force. **On the night of 10 November 2023, at 23:48, Grindavík was evacuated** — and the eruptions we have been talking about all day began. **The warning arrived first, and it arrived from this hill.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn

en: Two footnotes. There is a **GPS station on that summit, code THOB**, and Benedikt Ófeigsson of the Met Office **installed it at dusk at the end of January 2020** — put there because of exactly this. And note the language has moved on: **the Met Office no longer calls it the Þorbjörn signal. Every bulletin now says Svartsengi.** *(The masts you can actually see up there are telephone and aviation kit, not science. The instrument that matters is small and you cannot see it from here.)*

en: One thing under the wheels. And the response that made it survivable: **real-time monitoring, hours of warning, state-funded buyouts, and barriers built in days.**

en: The Town That Came Back
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík

en: This town stood for a thousand years. On **10 November 2023** the ground tore open beneath it in a single night — and every single person got out. **Then 874 of them moved back in.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík

en: **Grindavík** was settled around **934 CE** — one of the first Reykjanes communities and a major North Atlantic **cod harbour.** By December 2023 it held about **3,720 people.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík

en: On **10 November 2023**, thousands of earthquakes in a few hours drove a **dike roughly 15 kilometres long** under the town. Fissures **metres wide** opened through roads, gardens and house foundations, the ground **subsided about a metre** and **pulled apart by around 120 centimetres.** The whole town was **evacuated in one night.** In **January 2024**, lava reached the streets for the first time — houses burned, roads buried.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík

en: Further eruptions followed through 2024 and into 2025 as the **Sundhnúkur crater row** kept reactivating. **Earthen barriers built in days** — six to ten metres by design, twenty-four at the highest point — saved some streets and were overrun on others. For all that, **none of this lava ever reached the sea.** It crossed the Grindavíkurvegur road again and again and pushed into the town on **14 January 2024**, but it never made the coast. The last time lava ran into the sea on this peninsula was the **twelfth century.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík

en: And then people started coming back. The state buyout company **Þórkatla** bought **over 90% of the homes**, and most residents did leave for good — but at **1 April 2026** Þjóðskrá had **874 registered residents** living here again. The **school is open** for the autumn term, the **library** has been brought back to its feet, and the **harbour and the power plant never stopped at all.** In **April 2026** Alþingi debated a formal framework for rebuilding the community. *(Not a ghost town. A very small town with an extremely dramatic CV.)*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík

en: **Say this bit out loud, because it changes how people behave:** the ground here is still moving and **crevasses are still opening.** That is why we stay on made surfaces and off verges, gardens and shortcuts. People live here. They did not survive all that to have a coach party fall down a hole in their street.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík

en: One older raid, because this harbour has form. On **20 June 1627** corsairs out of **Salé** in Morocco under **Murat Reis** took **12 to 15 Icelanders** from Grindavík, along with Danish and Dutch crew, and sailed them to **Algiers** — the opening act of the **Tyrkjaránið**, the Turkish Raid. Of everyone seized around Iceland that summer, **only 27** ever made it home, **nine years later.**
